10160727 release
10160735 __main__
10160745 .bytecode
10160840 S	r	S
10161085 Record of phased-in incompatible language changes.
10161137 Each line is of the form:
10161164     FeatureName = "_Feature(" OptionalRelease "," MandatoryRelease ","
10161235                               CompilerFlag ")"
10161283 where, normally, OptionalRelease < MandatoryRelease, and both are 5-tuples
10161358 of the same form as sys.version_info:
10161397     (PY_MAJOR_VERSION, # the 2 in 2.1.0a3; an int
10161447      PY_MINOR_VERSION, # the 1; an int
10161486      PY_MICRO_VERSION, # the 0; an int
10161525      PY_RELEASE_LEVEL, # "alpha", "beta", "candidate" or "final"; string
10161598      PY_RELEASE_SERIAL # the 3; an int
10161637     )
10161644 OptionalRelease records the first release in which
10161696     from __future__ import FeatureName
10161736 was accepted.
10161751 In the case of MandatoryReleases that have not yet occurred,
10161812 MandatoryRelease predicts the release in which the feature will become part
10161888 of the language.
10161906 Else MandatoryRelease records when the feature became part of the language;
10161982 in releases at or after that, modules no longer need
10162036     from __future__ import FeatureName
10162076 to use the feature in question, but may continue to use such imports.
10162147 MandatoryRelease may also be None, meaning that a planned feature got
10162217 dropped or that the release version is undetermined.
10162271 Instances of class _Feature have two corresponding methods,
10162331 .getOptionalRelease() and .getMandatoryRelease().
10162382 CompilerFlag is the (bitfield) flag that should be passed in the fourth
10162454 argument to the builtin function compile() to enable the feature in
10162522 dynamically compiled code.  This flag is stored in the .compiler_flag
10162592 attribute on _Future instances.  These values must match the appropriate
10162665 #defines of CO_xxx flags in Include/cpython/compile.h.
10162721 No feature line is ever to be deleted from this file.

10169652 _aix_bos_rter7
10169939 AIX filesets are identified by four decimal values: V.R.M.F.
10170000 V (version) and R (release) can be retrieved using ``uname``
10170061 Since 2007, starting with AIX 5.3 TL7, the M value has been
10170121 included with the fileset bos.rte and represents the Technology
10170185 Level (TL) of AIX. The F (Fix) value also increases, but is not
10170249 relevant for comparing releases and binary compatibility.
10170307 For binary compatibility the so-called builddate is needed.
10170367 Again, the builddate of an AIX release is associated with bos.rte.
10170434 AIX ABI compatibility is described  as guaranteed at: https://www.ibm.com/    support/knowledgecenter/en/ssw_aix_72/install/binary_compatability.html
10170585 For pep425 purposes the AIX platform tag becomes:
10170635 "aix-{:1x}{:1d}{:02d}-{:04d}-{}".format(v, r, tl, builddate, bitsize)
10170705 e.g., "aix-6107-1415-32" for AIX 6.1 TL7 bd 1415, 32-bit
10170762 and, "aix-6107-1415-64" for AIX 6.1 TL7 bd 1415, 64-bit

10209083 Compute the hash value of a set.
10209117 Note that we don't define __hash__: not all sets are hashable.
10209180 But if you define a hashable set type, its __hash__ should
10209239 call this function.
10209260 This must be compatible __eq__.
10209293 All sets ought to compare equal if they contain the same
10209350 elements, regardless of how they are implemented, and
10209404 regardless of the order of the elements; so there's not much
10209465 freedom for __eq__ or __hash__.  We match the algorithm used
10209526 by the built-in frozenset type.

10291064 directly, and then acts as a mix-in class.  You can also register
10291130 unrelated concrete classes (even built-in classes) and unrelated
10291195 ABCs as 'virtual subclasses' -- these and their descendants will

10291324 issubclass() function, but the registering ABC won't show up in

10401056 coefficient), or if an overflow or underflow condition occurs.  The

10401524 operation is subnormal (that is, its adjusted exponent is less than
10401592 Emin, before any rounding).  The result in all cases is unchanged.
10401660 The subnormal signal may be tested (or trapped) to determine if a given

10401936 Numerical overflow.
10401957 This occurs and signals overflow if the adjusted exponent of a result
10402027 (from a conversion or from an operation that is not an attempt to divide
10402100 by zero), after rounding, would be greater than the largest value that
10402171 can be handled by the implementation (the value Emax).
10402227 The result depends on the rounding mode:
10402269 For round-half-up and round-half-even (and for round-half-down and
10402336 round-up, if implemented), the result of the operation is [sign,inf],
10402406 where sign is the sign of the intermediate result.  For round-down, the
10402478 result is the largest finite number that can be represented in the
10402545 current precision, with the sign of the intermediate result.  For
10402611 round-ceiling, the result is the same as for round-down if the sign of
10402682 the intermediate result is 1, or is [0,inf] otherwise.  For round-floor,
10402755 the result is the same as for round-down if the sign of the intermediate
10402828 result is 0, or is [1,inf] otherwise.  In all cases, Inexact and Rounded
10402901 will also be raised.

10468025 S	n	U
10469324 Return self ** other [ % modulo].
10469359 With two arguments, compute self**other.
10469401 With three arguments, compute (self**other) % modulo.  For the
10469464 three argument form, the following restrictions on the
10469519 arguments hold:
10469536  - all three arguments must be integral
10469576  - other must be nonnegative
10469605  - either self or other (or both) must be nonzero
10469655  - modulo must be nonzero and must have at most p digits,
10469713    where p is the context precision.
10469751 If any of these restrictions is violated the InvalidOperation
10469813 flag is raised.
10469830 The result of pow(self, other, modulo) is identical to the
10469889 result that would be obtained by computing (self**other) %
10469948 modulo with unbounded precision, but is computed more
10470002 efficiently.  It is always exact.

10536471 Compares values numerically.
10536501 If the signs of the operands differ, a value representing each
10536564 operand ('-1' if the operand is less than zero, '0' if the operand
10536631 is zero or negative zero, or '1' if the operand is greater than
10536695 zero) is used in place of that operand for the comparison instead of
10536764 the actual operand.
10536785 The comparison is then effected by subtracting the second operand
10536851 from the first and then returning a value according to the result of
10536920 the subtraction: '-1' if the result is less than zero, '0' if the
10536986 result is zero or negative zero, or '1' if the result is greater
10537051 than zero.

10566581 Context.plus
10566744 Raises a to the power of b, to modulo if given.
10566793 With two arguments, compute a**b.  If a is negative then b
10566852 must be integral.  The result will be inexact unless b is
10566910 integral and the result is finite and can be expressed exactly
10566973 in 'precision' digits.
10566997 With three arguments, compute (a**b) % modulo.  For the
10567053 three argument form, the following restrictions on the
10567108 arguments hold:
10567125  - all three arguments must be integral
10567165  - b must be nonnegative
10567190  - at least one of a or b must be nonzero
10567232  - modulo must be nonzero and have at most 'precision' digits
10567295 The result of pow(a, b, modulo) is identical to the result
10567354 that would be obtained by computing (a**b) % modulo with
10567411 unbounded precision, but is computed more efficiently.  It is
10567473 always exact.

10569313 Returns a value equal to 'a' (rounded), having the exponent of 'b'.
10569382 The coefficient of the result is derived from that of the left-hand
10569450 operand.  It may be rounded using the current rounding setting (if
10569517 the exponent is being increased), multiplied by a positive power of
10569585 ten (if the exponent is being decreased), or is unchanged (if the
10569651 exponent is already equal to that of the right-hand operand).
10569714 Unlike other operations, if the length of the coefficient after the
10569782 quantize operation would be greater than precision then an Invalid
10569849 operation condition is raised.  This guarantees that, unless there
10569916 is an error condition, the exponent of the result of a quantize is
10569983 always equal to that of the right-hand operand.
10570032 Also unlike other operations, quantize will never raise Underflow,
10570099 even if the result is subnormal and inexact.

10613554 Open file and return a stream.  Raise OSError upon failure.
10613615     file is either a text or byte string giving the name (and the path
10613686     if the file isn't in the current working directory) of the file to
10613757     be opened or an integer file descriptor of the file to be
10613819     wrapped. (If a file descriptor is given, it is closed when the
10613886     returned I/O object is closed, unless closefd is set to False.)
10613955     mode is an optional string that specifies the mode in which the file
10614028     is opened.  It defaults to 'r' which means open for reading in text
10614100     mode.  Other common values are 'w' for writing (truncating the file if
10614175     it already exists), 'x' for exclusive creation of a new file, and
10614245     'a' for appending (which on some Unix systems, means that all writes
10614318     append to the end of the file regardless of the current seek position).
10614394     In text mode, if encoding is not specified the encoding used is platform
10614471     dependent.  (For reading and writing raw bytes use binary mode and leave
10614548     encoding unspecified.)  The available modes are:
10614602     ========= ==========================================================
10614675     Character Meaning
10614697     --------- ----------------------------------------------------------
10614770     'r'       open for reading (default)
10614811     'w'       open for writing, truncating the file first
10614869     'x'       create a new file and open it for writing
10614925     'a'       open for writing, appending to the end of the file if it
10614996               exists
10615017     'b'       binary mode
10615043     't'       text mode (default)
10615077     '+'       open a disk file for updating (reading and writing)
10615143     ========= ==========================================================
10615217     The default mode is 'rt' (open for reading text). For binary random
10615289     access, the mode 'w+b' opens and truncates the file to 0 bytes, while
10615363     'r+b' opens the file without truncation. The 'x' mode implies 'w' and
10615437     raises an `FileExistsError` if the file already exists.
10615498     Python distinguishes between files opened in binary and text modes,
10615570     even when the underlying operating system doesn't.  Files opened in
10615642     binary mode (appending 'b' to the mode argument) return contents as
10615714     bytes objects without any decoding.  In text mode (the default, or when
10615790     't' is appended to the mode argument), the contents of the file are
10615862     returned as strings, the bytes having been first decoded using a
10615931     platform-dependent encoding or using the specified encoding if given.
10616006     buffering is an optional integer used to set the buffering policy.
10616077     Pass 0 to switch buffering off (only allowed in binary mode), 1 to
10616148     select line buffering (only usable in text mode), and an integer > 1 to
10616224     indicate the size of a fixed-size chunk buffer.  When no buffering
10616295     argument is given, the default buffering policy works as follows:
10616366     * Binary files are buffered in fixed-size chunks; the size of the buffer
10616443 <<<<<<< HEAD
10616456       is chosen using a heuristic trying to determine the underlying device's
10616534       "block size" and falling back on `io.DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE`.
10616599       On many systems, the buffer will typically be 4096 or 8192 bytes long.
10616676 =======
10616684       is max(min(blocksize, 8 MiB), DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE) when the device
10616757       block size is available.
10616788       On most systems, the buffer will typically be 128 kilobytes long.
10616860 >>>>>>> 36137e46a8c ([3.14] gh-150285: Fix too long docstrings in the io module (GH-150287) (GH-150458))
10616966     * "Interactive" text files (files for which isatty() returns True)
10617037       use line buffering.  Other text files use the policy described above
10617112       for binary files.
10617137     encoding is the str name of the encoding used to decode or encode the
10617211     file. This should only be used in text mode. The default encoding is
10617284     platform dependent, but any encoding supported by Python can be
10617352     passed.  See the codecs module for the list of supported encodings.
10617425     errors is an optional string that specifies how encoding errors are to
10617500     be handled---this argument should not be used in binary mode. Pass
10617571     'strict' to raise a ValueError exception if there is an encoding error
10617646     (the default of None has the same effect), or pass 'ignore' to ignore
10617720     errors. (Note that ignoring encoding errors can lead to data loss.)
10617792     See the documentation for codecs.register for a list of the permitted
10617866     encoding error strings.
10617895     newline is a string controlling how universal newlines works (it only
10617969     applies to text mode). It can be None, '', '\n', '\r', and '\r\n'.  It
10618044     works as follows:
10618067     * On input, if newline is None, universal newlines mode is
10618130       enabled. Lines in the input can end in '\n', '\r', or '\r\n', and
10618202       these are translated into '\n' before being returned to the
10618268       caller. If it is '', universal newline mode is enabled, but line
10618339       endings are returned to the caller untranslated. If it has any of
10618411       the other legal values, input lines are only terminated by the given
10618486       string, and the line ending is returned to the caller untranslated.
10618561     * On output, if newline is None, any '\n' characters written are
10618630       translated to the system default line separator, os.linesep. If
10618700       newline is '', no translation takes place. If newline is any of the
10618774       other legal values, any '\n' characters written are translated to
10618846       the given string.
10618871     closedfd is a bool. If closefd is False, the underlying file descriptor
10618947     will be kept open when the file is closed. This does not work when
10619018     a file name is given and must be True in that case.
10619075     The newly created file is non-inheritable.
10619123     A custom opener can be used by passing a callable as *opener*. The
10619194     underlying file descriptor for the file object is then obtained by
10619265     calling *opener* with (*file*, *flags*).  *opener* must return an open
10619340     file descriptor (passing os.open as *opener* results in functionality
10619414     similar to passing None).
10619445     open() returns a file object whose type depends on the mode, and
10619514     through which the standard file operations such as reading and writing
10619589     are performed. When open() is used to open a file in a text mode ('w',
10619664     'r', 'wt', 'rt', etc.), it returns a TextIOWrapper. When used to open
10619738     a file in a binary mode, the returned class varies: in read binary
10619809     mode, it returns a BufferedReader; in write binary and append binary
10619882     modes, it returns a BufferedWriter, and in read/write mode, it returns
10619957     a BufferedRandom.
10619980     It is also possible to use a string or bytearray as a file for both
10620052     reading and writing. For strings StringIO can be used like a file

10623407 IOBasei?
10623423 The abstract base class for all I/O classes.
10623469 This class provides dummy implementations for many methods that
10623533 derived classes can override selectively; the default implementations
10623603 represent a file that cannot be read, written or seeked.
10623661 Even though IOBase does not declare read or write because
10623719 their signatures will vary, implementations and clients should
10623782 consider those methods part of the interface. Also, implementations
10623850 may raise UnsupportedOperation when operations they do not support are
10623921 called.
10623930 The basic type used for binary data read from or written to a file is
10624000 bytes. Other bytes-like objects are accepted as method arguments too.
10624070 Text I/O classes work with str data.
10624108 Note that calling any method (even inquiries) on a closed stream is
10624176 undefined. Implementations may raise OSError in this case.
10624236 IOBase (and its subclasses) support the iterator protocol, meaning
10624303 that an IOBase object can be iterated over yielding the lines in a
10624370 stream.
10624379 IOBase also supports the :keyword:`with` statement. In this example,
10624448 fp is closed after the suite of the with statement is complete:
10624513 with open('spam.txt', 'r') as fp:
10624547     fp.write('Spam and eggs!')
10624686 z@Internal: raise an OSError exception for unsupported operations.

10635845 BufferedIOBasei
10635869 Base class for buffered IO objects.
10635906 The main difference with RawIOBase is that the read() method
10635967 supports omitting the size argument, and does not have a default
10636032 implementation that defers to readinto().
10636075 In addition, read(), readinto() and write() may raise
10636129 BlockingIOError if the underlying raw stream is in non-blocking
10636193 mode and not ready; unlike their raw counterparts, they will never
10636260 return None.
10636274 A typical implementation should not inherit from a RawIOBase
10636335 implementation, but wrap one.
10636436 Read and return up to size bytes, where size is an int.
10636493 If the argument is omitted, None, or negative, reads and
10636550 returns all data until EOF.
10636579 If the argument is positive, and the underlying raw stream is
10636641 not 'interactive', multiple raw reads may be issued to satisfy
10636704 the byte count (unless EOF is reached first).  But for
10636759 interactive raw streams (XXX and for pipes?), at most one raw
10636821 read will be issued, and a short result does not imply that
10636881 EOF is imminent.
10636899 Returns an empty bytes array on EOF.
10636937 Raises BlockingIOError if the underlying raw stream has no
10636996 data at the moment.
10637058 BufferedIOBase.read
10637175 zQRead up to size bytes with at most one read() system call,
10637236 where size is an int.

10675283 Open a file.
10675297 The mode can be 'r' (default), 'w', 'x' or 'a' for reading,
10675357 writing, exclusive creation or appending.  The file will be created
10675425 if it doesn't exist when opened for writing or appending; it will be
10675494 truncated when opened for writing.  A FileExistsError will be raised
10675563 if it already exists when opened for creating.  Opening a file for
10675630 creating implies writing so this mode behaves in a similar way to
10675696 'w'.  Add a '+' to the mode to allow simultaneous reading and
10675758 writing.
10675768 A custom opener can be used by passing a callable as *opener*.
10675831 The underlying file descriptor for the file object is then obtained
10675899 by calling opener with (*name*, *flags*).  *opener* must return
10675963 an open file descriptor (passing os.open as *opener* results in

10693860 Character and line based layer over a BufferedIOBase object, buffer.
10693930 encoding gives the name of the encoding that the stream will be
10693994 decoded or encoded with. It defaults to locale.getencoding().
10694057 errors determines the strictness of encoding and decoding (see the
10694124 codecs.register) and defaults to "strict".
10694168 newline can be None, '', '\n', '\r', or '\r\n'.  It controls the
10694233 handling of line endings. If it is None, universal newlines is
10694296 enabled.  With this enabled, on input, the lines endings '\n', '\r',
10694365 or '\r\n' are translated to '\n' before being returned to the
10694427 caller. Conversely, on output, '\n' is translated to the system
10694491 default line separator, os.linesep. If newline is any other of its
10694558 legal values, that newline becomes the newline when the file is read
10694627 and it is returned untranslated. On output, '\n' is converted to the
10694696 newline.
10694706 If line_buffering is True, a call to flush is implied when a call to
10694775 write contains a newline character.

10722292 Python implementations of some algorithms for use by longobject.c.
10722359 The goal is to provide asymptotically faster algorithms that can be
10722427 used for operations on integers with many digits.  In those cases, the
10722498 performance overhead of the Python implementation is not significant
10722567 since the asymptotic behavior is what dominates runtime. Functions
10722634 provided by this module should be considered private and not part of any
10722707 public API.
10722720 Note: for ease of maintainability, please prefer clear code and avoid
10722790 "micro-optimizations".  This module will only be imported and used for
10722861 integers with a huge number of digits.  Saving a few microseconds with
10722932 tricky or non-obvious code is not worth it.  For people looking for
10723000 maximum performance, they should use something like gmpy2.

10814261 S0S1.
10814325 S,\	\
10814365 g:)<an
10814375 Keymap contains functions for parsing keyspecs and turning keyspecs into
10814448 appropriate sequences.
10814472 A keyspec is a string representing a sequence of key presses that can
10814542 be bound to a command. All characters other than the backslash represent
10814615 themselves. In the traditional manner, a backslash introduces an escape
10814687 sequence.
10814698 pyrepl uses its own keyspec format that is meant to be a strict superset of
10814774 readline's KEYSEQ format. This means that if a spec is found that readline
10814849 accepts that this doesn't, it should be logged as a bug. Note that this means
10814927 we're using the `\C-o' style of readline's keyspec, not the `Control-o' sort.
10815006 The extension to readline is that the sequence \<KEY> denotes the
10815072 sequence of characters produced by hitting KEY.
10815121 Examples:
10815131 `a'      - what you get when you hit the `a' key
10815180 `\EOA'  - Escape - O - A (up, on my terminal)
10815226 `\<UP>' - the up arrow key
10815253 `\<up>' - ditto (keynames are case-insensitive)
10815301 `\C-o', `\c-o'  - control-o
10815329 `\M-.'  - meta-period
10815351 `\E.'   - ditto (that's how meta works for pyrepl)
10815402 `\<tab>', `\<TAB>', `\t', `\011', '\x09', '\X09', '\C-i', '\C-I'
10815467    - all of these are the tab character.

10837625 Reader
10837641 The Reader class implements the bare bones of a command reader,
10837705 handling such details as editing and cursor motion.  What it does
10837771 not support are such things as completion or history support -
10837834 these are implemented elsewhere.
10837868 Instance variables of note include:
10837905   * buffer:
10837917     A *list* (*not* a string at the moment :-) containing all the
10837983     characters that have been entered.
10838022   * console:
10838035     Hopefully encapsulates the OS dependent stuff.
10838086   * pos:
10838095     A 0-based index into `buffer' for where the insertion point
10838159     is.
10838167   * screeninfo:
10838183     Ahem.  This list contains some info needed to move the
10838242     insertion point around reasonably efficiently.
10838293   * cxy, lxy:
10838307     the position of the insertion point in screen ...
10838361   * syntax_table:
10838379     Dictionary mapping characters to `syntax class'; read the
10838441     emacs docs to see what this means :-)
10838483   * commands:
10838497     Dictionary mapping command names to command classes.
10838554   * arg:
10838563     The emacs-style prefix argument.  It will be None if no such
10838628     argument has been provided.
10838660   * dirty:
10838671     True if we need to refresh the display.
10838715   * kill_ring:
10838730     The emacs-style kill-ring; manipulated with yank & yank-pop
10838794   * ps1, ps2, ps3, ps4:
10838818     prompts.  ps1 is the prompt for a one-line input; for a
10838878     multiline input it looks like:
10838913         ps2> first line of input goes here
10838956         ps3> second and further
10838988         ps3> lines get ps3
10839015         ...
10839027         ps4> and the last one gets ps4
10839066     As with the usual top-level, you can set these to instances if
10839133     you like; str() will be called on them (once) at the beginning
10839200     of each command.  Don't put really long or newline containing
10839266     strings here, please!
10839292     This is just the default policy; you can change it freely by
10839357     overriding get_prompt() (and indeed some standard subclasses
10839422     do).
10839431   * finished:
10839445     handle1 will set this to a true value if a command signals
10839508     that we're done.
10839531 console.Consoler

10941896 LocaleTime
10941916 Stores and handles locale-specific information related to time.
10941981 ATTRIBUTES:
10941993     f_weekday -- full weekday names (7-item list)
10942043     a_weekday -- abbreviated weekday names (7-item list)
10942100     f_month -- full month names (13-item list; dummy value in [0], which
10942173                 is added by code)
10942207     a_month -- abbreviated month names (13-item list, dummy value in
10942276                 [0], which is added by code)
10942321     am_pm -- AM/PM representation (2-item list)
10942369     LC_date_time -- format string for date/time representation (string)
10942441     LC_date -- format string for date representation (string)
10942503     LC_time -- format string for time representation (string)
10942565     timezone -- daylight- and non-daylight-savings timezone representation
10942640                 (2-item list of sets)
10942678     lang -- Language used by instance (2-item tuple)
10943202 Set all attributes.
10943223 Order of methods called matters for dependency reasons.
10943280 The locale language is set at the offset and then checked again before
10943351 exiting.  This is to make sure that the attributes were not set with a
10943422 mix of information from more than one locale.  This would most likely
10943492 happen when using threads where one thread calls a locale-dependent
10943560 function while another thread changes the locale while the function in
10943631 the other thread is still running.  Proper coding would call for
10943696 locks to prevent changing the locale while locale-dependent code is
10943764 running.  The check here is done in case someone does not think about
10943834 doing this.
10943847 Only other possible issue is if someone changed the timezone and did
10943916 not call tz.tzset .  That is an issue for the programmer, though,
10943982 since changing the timezone is worthless without that call.

10951548 Find the month format appropriate for the current locale.
10951607 In some locales (for example French and Hebrew), the default month
10951674 used in __calc_date_time has the same name in full and abbreviated
10951741 form.  Also, the month name can by accident match other part of the
10951809 representation: the day of the week name (for example in Morisyen)
10951876 or the month number (for example in Japanese).  Thus, cycle months
10951943 of the year and find all positions that match the month name for
10952008 each month,  If no common positions are found, the representation
10952074 does not use the month name.

10994781 ABCMeta
10994798 Metaclass for defining Abstract Base Classes (ABCs).
10994852 Use this metaclass to create an ABC.  An ABC can be subclassed
10994915 directly, and then acts as a mix-in class.  You can also register
10994981 unrelated concrete classes (even built-in classes) and unrelated
10995046 ABCs as 'virtual subclasses' -- these and their descendants will
10995111 be considered subclasses of the registering ABC by the built-in
10995175 issubclass() function, but the registering ABC won't show up in
10995239 their MRO (Method Resolution Order) nor will method
10995291 implementations defined by the registering ABC be callable (not
10995355 even via super()).

11000461 Command-line parsing library
11000491 This module is an optparse-inspired command-line parsing library that:
11000563     - handles both optional and positional arguments
11000616     - produces highly informative usage messages
11000665     - supports parsers that dispatch to sub-parsers
11000718 The following is a simple usage example that sums integers from the
11000786 command-line and writes the result to a file::
11000834     parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
11000872         description='sum the integers at the command line')
11000932     parser.add_argument(
11000957         'integers', metavar='int', nargs='+', type=int,
11001013         help='an integer to be summed')
11001053     parser.add_argument(
11001078         '--log', default=sys.stdout, type=argparse.FileType('w'),
11001144         help='the file where the sum should be written')
11001201     args = parser.parse_args()
11001232     args.log.write('%s' % sum(args.integers))
11001278     args.log.close()
11001300 The module contains the following public classes:
11001351     - ArgumentParser -- The main entry point for command-line parsing. As the
11001429         example above shows, the add_argument() method is used to populate
11001504         the parser with actions for optional and positional arguments. Then
11001580         the parse_args() method is invoked to convert the args at the
11001650         command-line into an object with attributes.
11001704     - ArgumentError -- The exception raised by ArgumentParser objects when
11001779         there are errors with the parser's actions. Errors raised while
11001851         parsing the command-line are caught by ArgumentParser and emitted
11001925         as command-line messages.
11001960     - FileType -- A factory for defining types of files to be created. As the
11002038         example above shows, instances of FileType are typically passed as
11002113         the type= argument of add_argument() calls.
11002166     - Action -- The base class for parser actions. Typically actions are
11002239         selected by passing strings like 'store_true' or 'append_const' to
11002314         the action= argument of add_argument(). However, for greater
11002383         customization of ArgumentParser actions, subclasses of Action may
11002457         be defined and passed as the action= argument.
11002513     - HelpFormatter, RawDescriptionHelpFormatter, RawTextHelpFormatter,
11002585         ArgumentDefaultsHelpFormatter -- Formatter classes which
11002650         may be passed as the formatter_class= argument to the
11002712         ArgumentParser constructor. HelpFormatter is the default,
11002778         RawDescriptionHelpFormatter and RawTextHelpFormatter tell the parser
11002855         not to change the formatting for help text, and
11002911         ArgumentDefaultsHelpFormatter adds information about argument defaults
11002990         to the help.
11003012 All other classes in this module are considered implementation details.
11003084 (Also note that HelpFormatter and RawDescriptionHelpFormatter are only
11003155 considered public as object names -- the API of the formatter objects is
11003228 still considered an implementation detail.)

11033032 z@An error from trying to convert a command line string to a type.r?
11033305 Information about how to convert command line strings to Python objects.
11033379 Action objects are used by an ArgumentParser to represent the information
11033453 needed to parse a single argument from one or more strings from the
11033521 command line. The keyword arguments to the Action constructor are also
11033592 all attributes of Action instances.
11033629 Keyword Arguments:
11033649     - option_strings -- A list of command-line option strings which
11033717         should be associated with this action.
11033765     - dest -- The name of the attribute to hold the created object(s)
11033836     - nargs -- The number of command-line arguments that should be
11033903         consumed. By default, one argument will be consumed and a single
11033976         value will be produced.  Other values include:
11034031             - N (an integer) consumes N arguments (and produces a list)
11034103             - '?' consumes zero or one arguments
11034152             - '*' consumes zero or more arguments (and produces a list)
11034224             - '+' consumes one or more arguments (and produces a list)
11034295         Note that the difference between the default and nargs=1 is that
11034368         with the default, a single value will be produced, while with
11034438         nargs=1, a list containing a single value will be produced.
11034507     - const -- The value to be produced if the option is specified and the
11034582         option uses an action that takes no values.
11034635     - default -- The value to be produced if the option is not specified.
11034710     - type -- A callable that accepts a single string argument, and
11034778         returns the converted value.  The standard Python types str, int,
11034852         float, and complex are useful examples of such callables.  If None,
11034928         str is used.
11034950     - choices -- A container of values that should be allowed. If not None,
11035026         after a command-line argument has been converted to the appropriate
11035102         type, an exception will be raised if it is not a member of this
11035174         collection.
11035195     - required -- True if the action must always be specified at the
11035264         command line. This is only meaningful for optional command-line
11035336         arguments.
11035356     - help -- The help string describing the argument.
11035412     - metavar -- The name to be used for the option's argument with the
11035484         help string. If None, the 'dest' value will be used as the name.

11106253 The `ast` module helps Python applications to process trees of the Python
11106327 abstract syntax grammar.  The abstract syntax itself might change with
11106398 each Python release; this module helps to find out programmatically what
11106471 the current grammar looks like and allows modifications of it.
11106535 An abstract syntax tree can be generated by passing `ast.PyCF_ONLY_AST` as
11106610 a flag to the `compile()` builtin function or by using the `parse()`
11106679 function from this module.  The result will be a tree of objects whose
11106750 classes all inherit from `ast.AST`.
11106787 A modified abstract syntax tree can be compiled into a Python code object
11106861 using the built-in `compile()` function.
11106903 Additionally various helper functions are provided that make working with
11106977 the trees simpler.  The main intention of the helper functions and this
11107049 module in general is to provide an easy to use interface for libraries
11107120 that work tightly with the python syntax (template engines for example).
11107194 :copyright: Copyright 2008 by Armin Ronacher.
11107240 :license: Python License.

11124477 NodeVisitori
11124499 A node visitor base class that walks the abstract syntax tree and calls a
11124573 visitor function for every node found.  This function may return a value
11124646 which is forwarded by the `visit` method.
11124689 This class is meant to be subclassed, with the subclass adding visitor
11124760 methods.
11124770 Per default the visitor functions for the nodes are ``'visit_'`` +
11124837 class name of the node.  So a `TryFinally` node visit function would
11124906 be `visit_TryFinally`.  This behavior can be changed by overriding
11124973 the `visit` method.  If no visitor function exists for a node
11125035 (return value `None`) the `generic_visit` visitor is used instead.
11125103 Don't use the `NodeVisitor` if you want to apply changes to nodes during
11125176 traversing.  For this a special visitor exists (`NodeTransformer`) that
11125248 allows modifications.
11125412 Visit a node.

11127286 NodeTransformeri
11127312 A :class:`NodeVisitor` subclass that walks the abstract syntax tree and
11127384 allows modification of nodes.
11127415 The `NodeTransformer` will walk the AST and use the return value of the
11127487 visitor methods to replace or remove the old node.  If the return value of
11127562 the visitor method is ``None``, the node will be removed from its location,
11127638 otherwise it is replaced with the return value.  The return value may be the
11127715 original node in which case no replacement takes place.
11127772 Here is an example transformer that rewrites all occurrences of name lookups
11127849 (``foo``) to ``data['foo']``::
11127881    class RewriteName(NodeTransformer):
11127921        def visit_Name(self, node):
11127956            return Subscript(
11127985                value=Name(id='data', ctx=Load()),
11128035                slice=Constant(value=node.id),
11128081                ctx=node.ctx
11128109            )
11128123 Keep in mind that if the node you're operating on has child nodes you must
11128198 either transform the child nodes yourself or call the :meth:`generic_visit`
11128274 method for the node first.
11128302 For nodes that were part of a collection of statements (that applies to all
11128378 statement nodes), the visitor may also return a list of nodes rather than
11128452 just a single node.
11128473 Usually you use the transformer like this::
11128518    node = YourTransformer().visit(node)

11210116 Base implementation of event loop.
11210152 The event loop can be broken up into a multiplexer (the part
11210213 responsible for notifying us of I/O events) and the event loop proper,
11210284 which wraps a multiplexer with functionality for scheduling callbacks,
11210355 immediately or at a given time in the future.
11210402 Whenever a public API takes a callback, subsequent positional
11210464 arguments will be passed to the callback if/when it is called.  This
11210533 avoids the proliferation of trivial lambdas implementing closures.
11210600 Keyword arguments for the callback are not supported; this is a
11210664 conscious design decision, leaving the door open for keyword arguments
11210735 to modify the meaning of the API call itself.

11344843 create_connection
11344861 #AbstractEventLoop.create_connection>
11344949 backlogr
11344963 reuse_address
11344978 reuse_port
11344990 keep_aliver
11345070 A coroutine which creates a TCP server bound to host and port.
11345134 The return value is a Server object which can be used to stop
11345196 the service.
11345210 If host is an empty string or None all interfaces are assumed
11345272 and a list of multiple sockets will be returned (most likely
11345333 one for IPv4 and another one for IPv6). The host parameter can also
11345401 be a sequence (e.g. list) of hosts to bind to.
11345449 family can be set to either AF_INET or AF_INET6 to force the
11345510 socket to use IPv4 or IPv6. If not set it will be determined
11345571 from host (defaults to AF_UNSPEC).
11345607 flags is a bitmask for getaddrinfo().
11345646 sock can optionally be specified in order to use a preexisting
11345709 socket object.
11345725 backlog is the maximum number of queued connections passed to
11345787 listen() (defaults to 100).
11345816 ssl can be set to an SSLContext to enable SSL over the
11345871 accepted connections.
11345894 reuse_address tells the kernel to reuse a local socket in
11345952 TIME_WAIT state, without waiting for its natural timeout to
11346012 expire. If not specified will automatically be set to True on
11346074 UNIX.
11346081 reuse_port tells the kernel to allow this endpoint to be bound to

11392530 Primitive lock objects.
11392555 A primitive lock is a synchronization primitive that is not owned
11392621 by a particular task when locked.  A primitive lock is in one
11392683 of two states, 'locked' or 'unlocked'.
11392723 It is created in the unlocked state.  It has two basic methods,
11392787 acquire() and release().  When the state is unlocked, acquire()
11392851 changes the state to locked and returns immediately.  When the
11392914 state is locked, acquire() blocks until a call to release() in
11392977 another task changes it to unlocked, then the acquire() call
11393038 resets it to locked and returns.  The release() method should only
11393105 be called in the locked state; it changes the state to unlocked
11393169 and returns immediately.  If an attempt is made to release an
11393231 unlocked lock, a RuntimeError will be raised.
11393278 When more than one task is blocked in acquire() waiting for
11393338 the state to turn to unlocked, only one task proceeds when a
11393399 release() call resets the state to unlocked; successive release()
11393465 calls will unblock tasks in FIFO order.
11393506 Locks also support the asynchronous context management protocol.
11393571 'async with lock' statement should be used.
11393616 Usage:
11393624     lock = Lock()
11393642     ...
11393650     await lock.acquire()
11393675     try:
11393684         ...
11393696     finally:
11393709         lock.release()
11393733 Context manager usage:
11393757     lock = Lock()
11393775     ...
11393783     async with lock:
11393804          ...
11393818 Lock objects can be tested for locking state:
11393865     if not lock.locked():
11393891        await lock.acquire()
11393919     else:
11393929        # lock is acquired
11393955        ...

11405988 A Semaphore implementation.
11406017 A semaphore manages an internal counter which is decremented by each
11406086 acquire() call and incremented by each release() call.  The counter
11406154 can never go below zero; when acquire() finds that it is zero, it
11406220 blocks, waiting until some other thread calls release().
11406278 Semaphores also support the context management protocol.
11406336 The optional argument gives the initial value for the internal
11406399 counter; it defaults to 1. If the value given is less than 0,
11406461 ValueError is raised.

11467929 connection_lost
11467946 BaseProtocol.connection_lost
11468025 Called when the transport's buffer goes over the high-water mark.
11468092 Pause and resume calls are paired -- pause_writing() is called
11468155 once when the buffer goes strictly over the high-water mark
11468215 (even if subsequent writes increases the buffer size even
11468273 more), and eventually resume_writing() is called once when the
11468336 buffer size reaches the low-water mark.
11468377 Note that if the buffer size equals the high-water mark,
11468434 pause_writing() is not called -- it must go strictly over.
11468493 Conversely, resume_writing() is called when the buffer size is
11468556 equal or lower than the low-water mark.  These end conditions
11468618 are important to ensure that things go as expected when either
11468681 mark is zero.
11468696 NOTE: This is the only Protocol callback that is not called
11468756 through EventLoop.call_soon() -- if it were, it would have no
11468818 effect when it's most needed (when the app keeps writing
11468875 without yielding until pause_writing() is called).
11468952 pause_writing

11469504 Interface for stream protocol.
11469536 The user should implement this interface.  They can inherit from
11469601 this class but don't need to.  The implementations here do
11469660 nothing (they don't raise exceptions).
11469700 When the user wants to requests a transport, they pass a protocol
11469766 factory to a utility function (e.g., EventLoop.create_connection()).
11469836 When the connection is made successfully, connection_made() is
11469899 called with a suitable transport object.  Then data_received()
11469962 will be called 0 or more times with data (bytes) received from the
11470029 transport; finally, connection_lost() will be called exactly once
11470095 with either an exception object or None as an argument.
11470152 State machine of calls:
11470177   start -> CM [-> DR*] [-> ER?] -> CL -> end
11470223 * CM: connection_made()
11470247 * DR: data_received()
11470269 * ER: eof_received()
11470290 * CL: connection_lost()

11471032 Interface for stream protocol with manual buffer control.
11471091 Event methods, such as `create_server` and `create_connection`,
11471155 accept factories that return protocols that implement this interface.
11471226 The idea of BufferedProtocol is that it allows to manually allocate
11471294 and control the receive buffer.  Event loops can then use the buffer
11471363 provided by the protocol to avoid unnecessary data copies.  This
11471428 can result in noticeable performance improvement for protocols that
11471496 receive big amounts of data.  Sophisticated protocols can allocate
11471563 the buffer only once at creation time.
11471603 State machine of calls:
11471628   start -> CM [-> GB [-> BU?]]* [-> ER?] -> CL -> end
11471683 * CM: connection_made()
11471707 * GB: get_buffer()
11471726 * BU: buffer_updated()
11471749 * ER: eof_received()
11471770 * CL: connection_lost()
11471836 Called to allocate a new receive buffer.
11471878 *sizehint* is a recommended minimal size for the returned
11471936 buffer.  When set to -1, the buffer size can be arbitrary.
11471996 Must return an object that implements the
11472038 :ref:`buffer protocol <bufferobjects>`.
11472078 It is an error to return a zero-sized buffer.

11476321 A queue, useful for coordinating producer and consumer coroutines.
11476389 If maxsize is less than or equal to zero, the queue size is infinite.

11476653 with qsize(), since your single-threaded asyncio application won't be
11476723 interrupted between calling qsize() and doing an operation on the Queue.

11484694 Indicate that a formerly enqueued task is complete.
11484747 Used by queue consumers. For each get() used to fetch a task,
11484809 a subsequent call to task_done() tells the queue that the processing
11484878 on the task is complete.
11484904 If a join() is currently blocking, it will resume when all items
11484969 have been processed (meaning that a task_done() call was received

11485267 Queue.task_done
11485529 Block until all items in the queue have been gotten and processed.
11485597 The count of unfinished tasks goes up whenever an item is added to
11485664 the queue.  The count goes down whenever a consumer calls
11485722 task_done() to indicate that the item was retrieved and all work on
11485790 it is complete.  When the count of unfinished tasks drops to zero,
11485857 join() unblocks.

11486754 Shut-down the queue, making queue gets and puts raise QueueShutDown.
11486824 By default, gets will only raise once the queue is empty. Set

11490323 asyncio\runners.pyr
11490520 A context manager that controls event loop life cycle.
11490576 The context manager always creates a new event loop,
11490629 allows to run async functions inside it,
11490670 and properly finalizes the loop at the context manager exit.
11490732 If debug is True, the event loop will be run in debug mode.
11490792 If loop_factory is passed, it is used for new event loop creation.
11490860 asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)
11490893 is a shortcut for
11490912 with asyncio.Runner(debug=True) as runner:
11490955     runner.run(main())
11490979 The run() method can be called multiple times within the runner's
11491045 context.
11491055 This can be useful for interactive console (e.g. IPython),
11491114 unittest runners, console tools, -- everywhere when async code
11491177 is called from existing sync framework and where the preferred single
11491247 asyncio.run() call doesn't work.

11497399 __doc__r*
11497768 Execute the coroutine and return the result.
11497814 This function runs the passed coroutine, taking care of
11497870 managing the asyncio event loop, finalizing asynchronous
11497927 generators and closing the default executor.
11497973 This function cannot be called when another asyncio event loop is
11498039 running in the same thread.
11498068 If debug is True, the event loop will be run in debug mode.
11498128 If loop_factory is passed, it is used for new event loop creation.
11498196 This function always creates a new event loop and closes it at the end.
11498268 It should be used as a main entry point for asyncio programs, and should
11498341 ideally only be called once.
11498371 The executor is given a timeout duration of 5 minutes to shutdown.
11498438 If the executor hasn't finished within that duration, a warning is
11498505 emitted and the executor is closed.
11498542 Example:
11498552     async def main():
11498574         await asyncio.sleep(1)
11498605         print('hello')
11498629     asyncio.run(main())
11498653 Nz8asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loopr

11570030 Set the high- and low-water limits for write flow control.
11570090 These two values control when to call the protocol's
11570143 pause_writing() and resume_writing() methods.  If specified,
11570204 the low-water limit must be less than or equal to the
11570258 high-water limit.  Neither value can be negative.
11570309 The defaults are implementation-specific.  If only the
11570364 high-water limit is given, the low-water limit defaults to an
11570426 implementation-specific value less than or equal to the
11570482 high-water limit.  Setting high to zero forces low to zero as
11570544 well, and causes pause_writing() to be called whenever the
11570603 buffer becomes non-empty.  Setting low to zero causes
11570657 resume_writing() to be called only once the buffer is empty.
11570718 Use of zero for either limit is generally sub-optimal as it
11570778 reduces opportunities for doing I/O and computation
11570830 concurrently.

11606644 zFSupport for running coroutines in parallel with staggered start times.)
11606720 staggered_race

11606791 loopc
11607542 Run coroutines with staggered start times and take the first to finish.
11607615 This method takes an iterable of coroutine functions. The first one is
11607686 started immediately. From then on, whenever the immediately preceding one
11607760 fails (raises an exception), or when *delay* seconds has passed, the next
11607834 coroutine is started. This continues until one of the coroutines complete
11607908 successfully, in which case all others are cancelled, or until all
11607975 coroutines fail.
11607993 The coroutines provided should be well-behaved in the following way:
11608063 * They should only ``return`` if completed successfully.
11608121 * They should always raise an exception if they did not complete
11608186   successfully. In particular, if they handle cancellation, they should
11608258   probably reraise, like this::
11608291     try:
11608300         # do work
11608318     except asyncio.CancelledError:
11608353         # undo partially completed work
11608393         raise
11608408 Args:
11608414     coro_fns: an iterable of coroutine functions, i.e. callables that
11608484         return a coroutine object when called. Use ``functools.partial`` or
11608560         lambdas to pass arguments.
11608596     delay: amount of time, in seconds, between starting coroutines. If
11608667         ``None``, the coroutines will run sequentially.
11608724     loop: the event loop to use.
11608758 Returns:
11608767     tuple *(winner_result, winner_index, exceptions)* where
11608828     - *winner_result*: the result of the winning coroutine, or ``None``
11608900       if no coroutines won.
11608929     - *winner_index*: the index of the winning coroutine in
11608989       ``coro_fns``, or ``None`` if no coroutines won. If the winning
11609058       coroutine may return None on success, *winner_index* can be used
11609129       to definitively determine whether any coroutine won.
11609189     - *exceptions*: list of exceptions returned by the coroutines.
11609256       ``len(exceptions)`` is equal to the number of coroutines actually
11609328       started, and the order is the same as in ``coro_fns``. The winning
11609401       coroutine's entry is ``None``.

11638582 Read chunk of data from the stream until newline (b'\n') is found.
11638650 On success, return chunk that ends with newline.  If only partial
11638716 line can be read due to EOF, return incomplete line without
11638776 terminating newline.  When EOF was reached while no bytes read,
11638840 empty bytes object is returned.

11638939 newline was found, complete line including newline will be removed
11639006 from internal buffer.  Else, internal buffer will be cleared.

11639129 If stream was paused, this function will automatically resume it if
11639197 needed.

11640761 Read data from the stream until ``separator`` is found.
11640818 On success, the data and separator will be removed from the
11640878 internal buffer (consumed). Returned data will include the
11640937 separator at the end.
11640960 Configured stream limit is used to check result. Limit sets the
11641024 maximal length of data that can be returned, not counting the
11641086 separator.
11641098 If an EOF occurs and the complete separator is still not found,
11641162 an IncompleteReadError exception will be raised, and the internal
11641228 buffer will be reset.  The IncompleteReadError.partial attribute
11641293 may contain the separator partially.
11641331 If the data cannot be read because of over limit, a
11641383 LimitOverrunError exception  will be raised, and the data
11641441 will be left in the internal buffer, so it can be read again.
11641504 The ``separator`` may also be a tuple of separators. In this
11641565 case the return value will be the shortest possible that has any
11641630 separator as the suffix. For the purposes of LimitOverrunError,
11641694 the shortest possible separator is considered to be the one that
11641759 matched.

11659529 	TaskGroup
11659548 events)

11659572 tasksc
11659720 Asynchronous context manager for managing groups of tasks.
11659780 Example use:
11659794     async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
11659839         task1 = group.create_task(some_coroutine(...))
11659894         task2 = group.create_task(other_coroutine(...))
11659950     print("Both tasks have completed now.")
11659995 All tasks are awaited when the context manager exits.
11660050 Any exceptions other than `asyncio.CancelledError` raised within
11660115 a task will cancel all remaining tasks and wait for them to exit.

11674601 limitc
11674685 Return the list of stack frames for this task's coroutine.
11674745 If the coroutine is not done, this returns the stack where it is
11674810 suspended.  If the coroutine has completed successfully or was
11674873 cancelled, this returns an empty list.  If the coroutine was
11674934 terminated by an exception, this returns the list of traceback
11674997 frames.
11675006 The frames are always ordered from oldest to newest.
11675060 The optional limit gives the maximum number of frames to
11675117 return; by default all available frames are returned.  Its
11675176 meaning differs depending on whether a stack or a traceback is
11675239 returned: the newest frames of a stack are returned, but the
11675300 oldest frames of a traceback are returned.  (This matches the
11675362 behavior of the traceback module.)
11675398 For reasons beyond our control, only one stack frame is
11675454 returned for a suspended coroutine.

11676387 Request that this task cancel itself.
11676426 This arranges for a CancelledError to be thrown into the
11676483 wrapped coroutine on the next cycle through the event loop.
11676543 The coroutine then has a chance to clean up or even deny
11676600 the request using try/except/finally.
11676639 Unlike Future.cancel, this does not guarantee that the
11676694 task will be cancelled: the exception might be caught and
11676752 acted upon, delaying cancellation of the task or preventing
11676812 cancellation completely.  The task may also return a value or
11676874 raise a different exception.

11676967 not return True (unless the task was already cancelled).  A
11677027 task will be marked as cancelled when the wrapped coroutine
11677087 terminates with a CancelledError exception (even if cancel()

11694150 "_AsCompletedIterator._wait_for_oner
11694654 Create an iterator of awaitables or their results in completion order.
11694726 Run the supplied awaitables concurrently. The returned object can be
11694795 iterated to obtain the results of the awaitables as they finish.
11694861 The object returned can be iterated as an asynchronous iterator or
11694928 a plain iterator.  When asynchronous iteration is used, the
11694988 originally-supplied awaitables are yielded if they are tasks or
11695052 futures.  This makes it easy to correlate previously-scheduled tasks
11695121 with their results:
11695142     ipv4_connect = create_task(open_connection("127.0.0.1", 80))
11695207     ipv6_connect = create_task(open_connection("::1", 80))
11695266     tasks = [ipv4_connect, ipv6_connect]
11695308     async for earliest_connect in as_completed(tasks):
11695363         # earliest_connect is done. The result can be obtained by
11695429         # awaiting it or calling earliest_connect.result()
11695488         reader, writer = await earliest_connect
11695537         if earliest_connect is ipv6_connect:
11695582             print("IPv6 connection established.")
11695632         else:
11695646             print("IPv4 connection established.")
11695697 During asynchronous iteration, implicitly-created tasks will be
11695761 yielded for supplied awaitables that aren't tasks or futures.
11695824 When used as a plain iterator, each iteration yields a new coroutine
11695893 that returns the result or raises the exception of the next completed
11695963 awaitable.  This pattern is compatible with Python versions older than
11696034 3.13:
11696041     ipv4_connect = create_task(open_connection("127.0.0.1", 80))
11696106     ipv6_connect = create_task(open_connection("::1", 80))
11696165     tasks = [ipv4_connect, ipv6_connect]
11696207     for next_connect in as_completed(tasks):
11696252         # next_connect is not one of the original task objects. It must
11696324         # be awaited to obtain the result value or raise the exception
11696395         # of the awaitable that finishes next.
11696442         reader, writer = await next_connect
11696487 A TimeoutError is raised if the timeout occurs before all awaitables
11696556 are done.  This is raised by the async for loop during asynchronous
11696624 iteration or by the coroutines yielded during plain iteration.

11700485 return_exceptionsc
11701071 Return a future aggregating results from the given coroutines/futures.
11701143 Coroutines will be wrapped in a future and scheduled in the event
11701209 loop. They will not necessarily be scheduled in the same order as
11701275 passed in.
11701287 All futures must share the same event loop.  If all the tasks are
11701353 done successfully, the returned future's result is the list of
11701416 results (in the order of the original sequence, not necessarily
11701480 the order of results arrival).  If *return_exceptions* is True,
11701544 exceptions in the tasks are treated the same as successful
11701603 results, and gathered in the result list; otherwise, the first
11701666 raised exception will be immediately propagated to the returned
11701730 future.
11701739 Cancellation: if the outer Future is cancelled, all children (that
11701806 have not completed yet) are also cancelled.  If any child is
11701867 cancelled, this is treated as if it raised CancelledError --
11701928 the outer Future is *not* cancelled in this case.  (This is to
11701991 prevent the cancellation of one child to cause other children to
11702056 be cancelled.)
11702072 If *return_exceptions* is False, cancelling gather() after it
11702134 has been marked done won't cancel any submitted awaitables.
11702194 For instance, gather can be marked done after propagating an
11702255 exception to the caller, therefore, calling ``gather.cancel()``
11702319 after catching an exception (raised by one of the awaitables) from
11702386 gather won't cancel any other awaitables.

11703903 `       @@@@r'
11704507 Wait for a future, shielding it from cancellation.
11704559 The statement
11704574     task = asyncio.create_task(something())
11704618     res = await shield(task)
11704648 is exactly equivalent to the statement
11704688     res = await something()
11704717 *except* that if the coroutine containing it is cancelled, the
11704780 task running in something() is not cancelled.  From the POV of
11704843 something(), the cancellation did not happen.  But its caller is
11704908 still cancelled, so the yield-from expression still raises
11704967 CancelledError.  Note: If something() is cancelled by other means
11705033 this will still cancel shield().
11705067 If you want to completely ignore cancellation (not recommended)
11705131 you can combine shield() with a try/except clause, as follows:
11705195     task = asyncio.create_task(something())
11705239     try:
11705248         res = await shield(task)
11705281     except CancelledError:
11705308         res = None
11705328 Save a reference to tasks passed to this function, to avoid
11705388 a task disappearing mid-execution. The event loop only keeps
11705449 weak references to tasks. A task that isn't referenced elsewhere
11705514 may get garbage collected at any time, even before it's done.

11720384 Timeout async context manager.
11720416 Useful in cases when you want to apply timeout logic around block
11720482 of code or in cases when asyncio.wait_for is not suitable. For example:
11720555 >>> async with asyncio.timeout(10):  # 10 seconds timeout
11720613 ...     await long_running_task()
11720649 delay - value in seconds or None to disable timeout logic
11720708 long_running_task() is interrupted by raising asyncio.CancelledError,
11720778 the top-most affected timeout() context manager converts CancelledError
11720850 into TimeoutError.
11721055 Schedule the timeout at absolute time.
11721095 Like timeout() but argument gives absolute time in the same clock system
11721168 as loop.time().
11721185 Please note: it is not POSIX time but a time with
11721235 undefined starting base, e.g. the time of the system power on.
11721299 >>> async with asyncio.timeout_at(loop.time() + 10):
11721352 ...     await long_running_task()
11721388 when - a deadline when timeout occurs or None to disable timeout logic
11721460 long_running_task() is interrupted by raising asyncio.CancelledError,
11721530 the top-most affected timeout() context manager converts CancelledError
11721602 into TimeoutError.

11724925 z$Interface for write-only transports.r2
11725016 Set the high- and low-water limits for write flow control.
11725076 These two values control when to call the protocol's
11725129 pause_writing() and resume_writing() methods.  If specified,
11725190 the low-water limit must be less than or equal to the
11725244 high-water limit.  Neither value can be negative.
11725295 The defaults are implementation-specific.  If only the
11725350 high-water limit is given, the low-water limit defaults to an
11725412 implementation-specific value less than or equal to the
11725468 high-water limit.  Setting high to zero forces low to zero as
11725530 well, and causes pause_writing() to be called whenever the
11725589 buffer becomes non-empty.  Setting low to zero causes
11725643 resume_writing() to be called only once the buffer is empty.
11725704 Use of zero for either limit is generally sub-optimal as it
11725764 reduces opportunities for doing I/O and computation
11725816 concurrently.

11728071 Interface representing a bidirectional transport.
11728122 There may be several implementations, but typically, the user does
11728189 not implement new transports; rather, the platform provides some
11728254 useful transports that are implemented using the platform's best
11728319 practices.
11728331 The user never instantiates a transport directly; they call a
11728393 utility function, passing it a protocol factory and other
11728451 information necessary to create the transport and protocol.  (E.g.
11728518 EventLoop.create_connection() or EventLoop.create_server().)
11728580 The utility function will asynchronously create a transport and a
11728646 protocol and hook them up by calling the protocol's
11728698 connection_made() method, passing it the transport.
11728751 The implementation here raises NotImplemented for every method
11728814 except writelines(), which calls write() in a loop.

11821496 A file object providing transparent bzip2 (de)compression.
11821556 A BZ2File can act as a wrapper for an existing file object, or refer

11821805 compresslevelc
11822645 Open a bzip2-compressed file.
11822676 If filename is a str, bytes, or PathLike object, it gives the
11822738 name of the file to be opened. Otherwise, it should be a file
11822800 object, which will be used to read or write the compressed data.
11822866 mode can be 'r' for reading (default), 'w' for (over)writing,
11822928 'x' for creating exclusively, or 'a' for appending. These can
11822990 equivalently be given as 'rb', 'wb', 'xb', and 'ab'.
11823044 If mode is 'w', 'x' or 'a', compresslevel can be a number between 1
11823112 and 9 specifying the level of compression: 1 produces the least
11823176 compression, and 9 (default) produces the most compression.
11823237 If mode is 'r', the input file may be the concatenation of
11823296 multiple compressed streams.

11874898 EPOCHr
11874950 <module>r
11875673 A generic class to build line-oriented command interpreters.
11875735 Interpreters constructed with this class obey the following conventions:
11875809 1. End of file on input is processed as the command 'EOF'.
11875868 2. A command is parsed out of each line by collecting the prefix composed
11875942    of characters in the identchars member.
11875985 3. A command `foo' is dispatched to a method 'do_foo()'; the do_ method
11876057    is passed a single argument consisting of the remainder of the line.
11876129 4. Typing an empty line repeats the last command.  (Actually, it calls the
11876204    method `emptyline', which may be overridden in a subclass.)
11876267 5. There is a predefined `help' method.  Given an argument `topic', it
11876338    calls the command `help_topic'.  With no arguments, it lists all topics
11876413    with defined help_ functions, broken into up to three topics; documented
11876489    commands, miscellaneous help topics, and undocumented commands.
11876556 6. The command '?' is a synonym for `help'.  The command '!' is a synonym
11876630    for `shell', if a do_shell method exists.
11876675 7. If completion is enabled, completing commands will be done automatically,
11876752    and completing of commands args is done by calling complete_foo() with
11876826    arguments text, line, begidx, endidx.  text is string we are matching
11876899    against, all returned matches must begin with it.  line is the current
11876973    input line (lstripped), begidx and endidx are the beginning and end
11877044    indexes of the text being matched, which could be used to provide
11877113    different completion depending upon which position the argument is in.
11877188 The `default' method may be overridden to intercept commands for which there
11877265 is no do_ method.
11877284 The `completedefault' method may be overridden to intercept completions for
11877360 commands that have no complete_ method.
11877401 The data member `self.ruler' sets the character used to draw separator lines
11877478 in the help messages.  If empty, no ruler line is drawn.  It defaults to "=".
11877557 If the value of `self.intro' is nonempty when the cmdloop method is called,
11877633 it is printed out on interpreter startup.  This value may be overridden
11877705 via an optional argument to the cmdloop() method.
11877756 The data members `self.doc_header', `self.misc_header', and
11877816 `self.undoc_header' set the headers used for the help function's
11877881 listings of documented functions, miscellaneous topics, and undocumented
11877954 functions respectively.
11877991 (Cmd) 
11878196 r"S S
11878231 A simple framework for writing line-oriented command interpreters.
11878299 These are often useful for test harnesses, administrative tools, and
11878368 prototypes that will later be wrapped in a more sophisticated interface.
11878442 A Cmd instance or subclass instance is a line-oriented interpreter
11878509 framework.  There is no good reason to instantiate Cmd itself; rather,
11878580 it's useful as a superclass of an interpreter class you define yourself
11878652 in order to inherit Cmd's methods and encapsulate action methods.

11896075 Compile and run some source in the interpreter.
11896124 Arguments are as for compile_command().
11896165 One of several things can happen:
11896200 1) The input is incorrect; compile_command() raised an
11896255 exception (SyntaxError or OverflowError).  A syntax traceback
11896317 will be printed by calling the showsyntaxerror() method.
11896375 2) The input is incomplete, and more input is required;
11896431 compile_command() returned None.  Nothing happens.
11896483 3) The input is complete; compile_command() returned a code
11896543 object.  The code is executed by calling self.runcode() (which
11896606 also handles run-time exceptions, except for SystemExit).
11896665 The return value is True in case 2, False in the other cases (unless
11896734 an exception is raised).  The return value can be used to
11896792 decide whether to use sys.ps1 or sys.ps2 to prompt the next
11896852 line.

11905468 InteractiveConsole.interact
11906530 Push a line to the interpreter.
11906563 The line should not have a trailing newline; it may have
11906620 internal newlines.  The line is appended to a buffer and the
11906681 interpreter's runsource() method is called with the
11906733 concatenated contents of the buffer as source.  If this
11906789 indicates that the command was executed or invalid, the buffer
11906852 is reset; otherwise, the command is incomplete, and the buffer
11906915 is left as it was after the line was appended.  The return
11906974 value is 1 if more input is required, 0 if the line was dealt
11907036 with in some way (this is the same as runsource()).

11913241 Defines the interface for stateless encoders/decoders.
11913297 The .encode()/.decode() methods may use different error
11913353 handling schemes by providing the errors argument. These
11913410 string values are predefined:
11913441  'strict' - raise a ValueError error (or a subclass)
11913494  'ignore' - ignore the character and continue with the next
11913554  'replace' - replace with a suitable replacement character;
11913614             Python will use the official U+FFFD REPLACEMENT
11913674             CHARACTER for the builtin Unicode codecs on
11913730             decoding and '?' on encoding.
11913772  'surrogateescape' - replace with private code points U+DCnn.
11913834  'xmlcharrefreplace' - Replace with the appropriate XML
11913890                        character reference (only for encoding).
11913954  'backslashreplace'  - Replace with backslashed escape sequences.
11914020  'namereplace'       - Replace with \N{...} escape sequences
11914081                        (only for encoding).
11914126 The set of allowed values can be extended via register_error.
11914236 Encodes the object input and returns a tuple (output
11914289 object, length consumed).
11914316 errors defines the error handling to apply. It defaults to
11914375 'strict' handling.
11914395 The method may not store state in the Codec instance. Use
11914453 StreamWriter for codecs which have to keep state in order to
11914514 make encoding efficient.
11914540 The encoder must be able to handle zero length input and
11914597 return an empty object of the output object type in this
11914654 situation.

11937533 encodingre
11937942 StreamRecoder instances translate data from one encoding to another.
11938012 They use the complete set of APIs returned by the
11938062 codecs.lookup() function to implement their task.
11938113 Data written to the StreamRecoder is first decoded into an
11938172 intermediate format (depending on the "decode" codec) and then
11938235 written to the underlying stream using an instance of the provided
11938302 Writer class.
11938317 In the other direction, data is read from the underlying stream using
11938387 a Reader instance and then encoded and returned to the caller.
11938593 Creates a StreamRecoder instance which implements a two-way
11938653 conversion: encode and decode work on the frontend (the
11938709 data visible to .read() and .write()) while Reader and Writer
11938771 work on the backend (the data in stream).
11938814 You can use these objects to do transparent
11938858 transcodings from e.g. latin-1 to utf-8 and back.
11938909 stream must be a file-like object.
11938945 encode and decode must adhere to the Codec interface; Reader and
11939010 Writer must be factory functions or classes providing the
11939068 StreamReader and StreamWriter interfaces resp.
11939116 Error handling is done in the same way as defined for the
11939174 StreamWriter/Readers.

11943140 Note: The wrapped version will only accept the object format
11943201 defined by the codecs, i.e. Unicode objects for most builtin

11943321 Unicode as well.
11943339 If encoding is not None, then the
11943373 underlying encoded files are always opened in binary mode.
11943432 The default file mode is 'r', meaning to open the file in read mode.

11943631 to 'strict' which causes ValueErrors to be raised in case an

11950952 Utilities to compile possibly incomplete Python source code.
11951014 This module provides two interfaces, broadly similar to the builtin
11951082 function compile(), which take program text, a filename and a 'mode'
11951157 - Return code object if the command is complete and valid
11951215 - Return None if the command is incomplete
11951258 - Raise SyntaxError, ValueError or OverflowError if the command is a
11951327   syntax error (OverflowError and ValueError can be produced by
11951391   malformed literals).
11951415 The two interfaces are:
11951440 compile_command(source, filename, symbol):
11951484     Compiles a single command in the manner described above.
11951546 CommandCompiler():
11951566     Instances of this class have __call__ methods identical in
11951629     signature to compile_command; the difference is that if the
11951693     instance compiles program text containing a __future__ statement,
11951763     the instance 'remembers' and compiles all subsequent program texts
11951834     with the statement in force.
11951868 The module also provides another class:
11951909 Compile():
11951921     Instances of this class act like the built-in function compile,
11951989     but with 'memory' in the sense described above.

11979246 or multiset.  Elements are stored as dictionary keys and their counts
11979316 are stored as dictionary values.

11994613 A ChainMap groups multiple dicts (or other mappings) together
11994675 to create a single, updateable view.
11994713 The underlying mappings are stored in a list.  That list is public and can
11994788 be accessed or updated using the *maps* attribute.  There is no other
11994858 state.
11994866 Lookups search the underlying mappings successively until a key is found.
11994940 In contrast, writes, updates, and deletions only operate on the first
11995010 mapping.
11995106 Initialize a ChainMap by setting *maps* to the given mappings.
11995169 If no mappings are provided, a single empty dictionary is used.

12060000 Future.exception
12060647 Mark the future as running or process any cancel notifications.
12060712 Should only be used by Executor implementations and unit tests.
12060777 If the future has been cancelled (cancel() was called and returned
12060844 True) then any threads waiting on the future completing (though
12060908 calls to as_completed() or wait()) are notified and False is
12060969 returned.
12060980 If the future was not cancelled then it is put in the running state
12061048 (future calls to running() will return True) and True is returned.
12061116 This method should be called by Executor implementations before
12061180 executing the work associated with this future. If this method
12061243 returns False then the work should not be executed.
12061296 Returns:
12061305     False if the Future was cancelled, True otherwise.
12061361 Raises:
12061369     RuntimeError: if this method was already called or if
12061427         set_result() or set_exception() was called.
