12068973 Implements ProcessPoolExecutor.
12069006 The following diagram and text describe the data-flow through the system:
12069081 |======================= In-process =====================|== Out-of-process ==|
12069162 +----------+     +----------+       +--------+     +-----------+    +---------+
12069242 |          |  => | Work Ids |       |        |     | Call Q    |    | Process |
12069322 |          |     +----------+       |        |     +-----------+    |  Pool   |
12069402 |          |     | ...      |       |        |     | ...       |    +---------+
12069482 |          |     | 6        |    => |        |  => | 5, call() | => |         |
12069562 |          |     | 7        |       |        |     | ...       |    |         |
12069642 | Process  |     | ...      |       | Local  |     +-----------+    | Process |
12069722 |  Pool    |     +----------+       | Worker |                      |  #1..n  |
12069802 | Executor |                        | Thread |                      |         |
12069882 |          |     +----------- +     |        |     +-----------+    |         |
12069962 |          | <=> | Work Items | <=> |        | <=  | Result Q  | <= |         |
12070042 |          |     +------------+     |        |     +-----------+    |         |
12070122 |          |     | 6: call()  |     |        |     | ...       |    |         |
12070202 |          |     |    future  |     |        |     | 4, result |    |         |
12070282 |          |     | ...        |     |        |     | 3, except |    |         |
12070362 +----------+     +------------+     +--------+     +-----------+    +---------+
12070443 Executor.submit() called:
12070469 - creates a uniquely numbered _WorkItem and adds it to the "Work Items" dict
12070546 - adds the id of the _WorkItem to the "Work Ids" queue
12070602 Local worker thread:
12070623 - reads work ids from the "Work Ids" queue and looks up the corresponding
12070697   WorkItem from the "Work Items" dict: if the work item has been cancelled then
12070777   it is simply removed from the dict, otherwise it is repackaged as a
12070847   _CallItem and put in the "Call Q". New _CallItems are put in the "Call Q"
12070923   until "Call Q" is full. NOTE: the size of the "Call Q" is kept small because
12071002   calls placed in the "Call Q" can no longer be cancelled with Future.cancel().
12071082 - reads _ResultItems from "Result Q", updates the future stored in the
12071153   "Work Items" dict and deletes the dict entry
12071201 Process #1..n:
12071216 - reads _CallItems from "Call Q", executes the calls, and puts the resulting
12071293   _ResultItems in "Result Q"
12071322 z"Brian Quinlan (brian@sweetapp.com)

12115122 S/\+5
12115189 Configuration file parser.
12115217 A configuration file consists of sections, lead by a "[section]" header,
12115290 and followed by "name: value" entries, with continuations and such in
12115360 the style of RFC 822.
12115383 Intrinsic defaults can be specified by passing them into the
12115444 ConfigParser constructor as a dictionary.
12115487 class:
12115495 ConfigParser -- responsible for parsing a list of
12115545                     configuration files, and managing the parsed database.
12115621     methods:
12115635     __init__(defaults=None, dict_type=_default_dict, allow_no_value=False,
12115710              delimiters=('=', ':'), comment_prefixes=('#', ';'),
12115775              inline_comment_prefixes=None, strict=True,
12115831              empty_lines_in_values=True, default_section='DEFAULT',
12115899              interpolation=<unset>, converters=<unset>,
12115955              allow_unnamed_section=False):
12115998         Create the parser. When `defaults` is given, it is initialized into the
12116078         dictionary or intrinsic defaults. The keys must be strings, the values
12116157         must be appropriate for %()s string interpolation.
12116217         When `dict_type` is given, it will be used to create the dictionary
12116293         objects for the list of sections, for the options within a section, and
12116373         for the default values.
12116406         When `delimiters` is given, it will be used as the set of substrings
12116483         that divide keys from values.
12116522         When `comment_prefixes` is given, it will be used as the set of
12116594         substrings that prefix comments in empty lines. Comments can be
12116666         indented.
12116685         When `inline_comment_prefixes` is given, it will be used as the set of
12116764         substrings that prefix comments in non-empty lines.
12116825         When `strict` is True, the parser won't allow for any section or option
12116905         duplicates while reading from a single source (file, string or
12116976         dictionary). Default is True.
12117015         When `empty_lines_in_values` is False (default: True), each empty line
12117094         marks the end of an option. Otherwise, internal empty lines of
12117165         a multiline option are kept as part of the value.
12117224         When `allow_no_value` is True (default: False), options without
12117296         values are accepted; the value presented for these is None.
12117365         When `default_section` is given, the name of the special section is
12117441         named accordingly. By default it is called ``"DEFAULT"`` but this can
12117519         be customized to point to any other valid section name. Its current
12117595         value can be retrieved using the ``parser_instance.default_section``
12117672         attribute and may be modified at runtime.
12117723         When `interpolation` is given, it should be an Interpolation subclass
12117801         instance. It will be used as the handler for option value
12117867         pre-processing when using getters. RawConfigParser objects don't do
12117943         any sort of interpolation, whereas ConfigParser uses an instance of
12118019         BasicInterpolation. The library also provides a ``zc.buildout``
12118091         inspired ExtendedInterpolation implementation.
12118147         When `converters` is given, it should be a dictionary where each key
12118224         represents the name of a type converter and each value is a callable
12118301         implementing the conversion from string to the desired datatype. Every
12118380         converter gets its corresponding get*() method on the parser object and
12118460         section proxies.
12118486         When `allow_unnamed_section` is True (default: False), options
12118557         without section are accepted: the section for these is
12118620         ``configparser.UNNAMED_SECTION``.
12118663     sections()
12118678         Return all the configuration section names, sans DEFAULT.
12118745     has_section(section)
12118770         Return whether the given section exists.
12118820     has_option(section, option)
12118852         Return whether the given option exists in the given section.
12118922     options(section)
12118943         Return list of configuration options for the named section.
12119012     read(filenames, encoding=None)
12119047         Read and parse the iterable of named configuration files, given by
12119122         name.  A single filename is also allowed.  Non-existing files
12119192         are ignored.  Return list of successfully read files.
12119255     read_file(f, filename=None)
12119287         Read and parse one configuration file, given as a file object.
12119358         The filename defaults to f.name; it is only used in error
12119424         messages (if f has no `name` attribute, the string `<???>` is used).
12119502     read_string(string)
12119526         Read configuration from a given string.
12119575     read_dict(dictionary)
12119601         Read configuration from a dictionary. Keys are section names,
12119671         values are dictionaries with keys and values that should be present
12119747         in the section. If the used dictionary type preserves order, sections
12119825         and their keys will be added in order. Values are automatically
12119897         converted to strings.
12119928     get(section, option, raw=False, vars=None, fallback=_UNSET)
12119992         Return a string value for the named option.  All % interpolations are
12120070         expanded in the return values, based on the defaults passed into the
12120147         constructor and the DEFAULT section.  Additional substitutions may be
12120225         provided using the `vars` argument, which must be a dictionary whose
12120302         contents override any pre-existing defaults. If `option` is a key in
12120379         `vars`, the value from `vars` is used.
12120427     getint(section, options, raw=False, vars=None, fallback=_UNSET)
12120495         Like get(), but convert value to an integer.
12120549     getfloat(section, options, raw=False, vars=None, fallback=_UNSET)
12120619         Like get(), but convert value to a float.
12120670     getboolean(section, options, raw=False, vars=None, fallback=_UNSET)
12120742         Like get(), but convert value to a boolean (currently case
12120809         insensitively defined as 0, false, no, off for False, and 1, true,
12120884         yes, on for True).  Returns False or True.
12120936     items(section=_UNSET, raw=False, vars=None)
12120984         If section is given, return a list of tuples with (name, value) for
12121060         each option in the section. Otherwise, return a list of tuples with
12121136         (section_name, section_proxy) for each section, including DEFAULTSECT.
12121216     remove_section(section)
12121244         Remove the given file section and all its options.
12121304     remove_option(section, option)
12121339         Remove the given option from the given section.
12121396     set(section, option, value)
12121428         Set the given option.
12121459     write(fp, space_around_delimiters=True)
12121503         Write the configuration state in .ini format. If
12121560         `space_around_delimiters` is True (the default), delimiters
12121628         between keys and values are surrounded by spaces.

12215139 r'\'\
12215451 r(\(\
12215473 r)\)\
12215495 r*\*\
12215511 r+\+\
12215590 Generic (shallow and deep) copying operations.
12215638 Interface summary:
12215658         import copy
12215679         x = copy.copy(y)                # make a shallow copy of y
12215746         x = copy.deepcopy(y)            # make a deep copy of y
12215810         x = copy.replace(y, a=1, b=2)   # new object with fields replaced, as defined by `__replace__`
12215914 For module specific errors, copy.Error is raised.
12215965 The difference between shallow and deep copying is only relevant for
12216034 compound objects (objects that contain other objects, like lists or
12216102 class instances).
12216121 - A shallow copy constructs a new compound object and then (to the
12216188   extent possible) inserts *the same objects* into it that the
12216251   original contains.
12216273 - A deep copy constructs a new compound object and then, recursively,
12216343   inserts *copies* into it of the objects found in the original.
12216409 Two problems often exist with deep copy operations that don't exist
12216477 with shallow copy operations:
12216508  a) recursive objects (compound objects that, directly or indirectly,
12216578     contain a reference to themselves) may cause a recursive loop
12216645  b) because deep copy copies *everything* it may copy too much, e.g.
12216714     administrative data structures that should be shared even between
12216784     copies
12216796 Python's deep copy operation avoids these problems by:
12216852  a) keeping a table of objects already copied during the current
12216917     copying pass
12216935  b) letting user-defined classes override the copying operation or the
12217006     set of components copied
12217036 This version does not copy types like module, class, function, method,
12217107 nor stack trace, stack frame, nor file, socket, window, nor any
12217171 similar types.
12217187 Classes can use the same interfaces to control copying that they use
12217256 to control pickling: they can define methods called __getinitargs__(),
12217327 __getstate__() and __setstate__().  See the documentation for module
12217396 "pickle" for information on these methods.

12232844 J	r	J
12233128 CSV parsing and writing.
12233154 This module provides classes that assist in the reading and writing
12233222 of Comma Separated Value (CSV) files, and implements the interface
12233289 described by PEP 305.  Although many CSV files are simple to parse,
12233357 the format is not formally defined by a stable specification and
12233422 is subtle enough that parsing lines of a CSV file with something
12233487 like line.split(",") is bound to fail.  The module supports three
12233553 basic APIs: reading, writing, and registration of dialects.
12233615 DIALECT REGISTRATION:
12233638 Readers and writers support a dialect argument, which is a convenient
12233708 handle on a group of settings.  When the dialect argument is a string,
12233779 it identifies one of the dialects previously registered with the module.
12233852 If it is a class or instance, the attributes of the argument are used as
12233925 the settings for the reader or writer:
12233965     class excel:
12233982         delimiter = ','
12234006         quotechar = '"'
12234030         escapechar = None
12234056         doublequote = True
12234083         skipinitialspace = False
12234116         lineterminator = '\r\n'
12234148         quoting = QUOTE_MINIMAL
12234181 SETTINGS:
12234192     * quotechar - specifies a one-character string to use as the
12234257         quoting character.  It defaults to '"'.
12234305     * delimiter - specifies a one-character string to use as the
12234370         field separator.  It defaults to ','.
12234416     * skipinitialspace - specifies how to interpret spaces which
12234481         immediately follow a delimiter.  It defaults to False, which
12234550         means that spaces immediately following a delimiter is part
12234618         of the following field.
12234650     * lineterminator - specifies the character sequence which should
12234719         terminate rows.
12234743     * quoting - controls when quotes should be generated by the writer.
12234815         It can take on any of the following module constants:
12234878         csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL means only when required, for example, when a
12234950             field contains either the quotechar or the delimiter
12235015         csv.QUOTE_ALL means that quotes are always placed around fields.
12235088         csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC means that quotes are always placed around
12235160             fields which do not parse as integers or floating-point
12235228             numbers.
12235249         csv.QUOTE_STRINGS means that quotes are always placed around
12235318             fields which are strings.  Note that the Python value None
12235389             is not a string.
12235418         csv.QUOTE_NOTNULL means that quotes are only placed around fields
12235492             that are not the Python value None.
12235540         csv.QUOTE_NONE means that quotes are never placed around fields.
12235613     * escapechar - specifies a one-character string used to escape
12235680         the delimiter when quoting is set to QUOTE_NONE.
12235737     * doublequote - controls the handling of quotes inside fields.  When
12235810         True, two consecutive quotes are interpreted as one during read,
12235883         and when writing, each quote character embedded in the data is
12235954         written as two quotes

12246569 "Sniffer._guess_quote_and_delimiter
12248947 The delimiter /should/ occur the same number of times on
12249004 each row. However, due to malformed data, it may not. We don't want
12249072 an all or nothing approach, so we allow for small variations in this
12249141 number.
12249149   1) build a table of the frequency of each character on every line.
12249218   2) build a table of frequencies of this frequency (meta-frequency?),
12249289      e.g.  'x occurred 5 times in 10 rows, 6 times in 1000 rows,
12249354      7 times in 2 rows'
12249378   3) use the mode of the meta-frequency to determine the /expected/
12249446      frequency for that character
12249480   4) find out how often the character actually meets that goal
12249543   5) the character that best meets its goal is the delimiter
12249604 For performance reasons, the data is evaluated in chunks, so it can
12249672 try and evaluate the smallest portion of the data possible, evaluating
12249743 additional chunks as necessary.

12298107 Return an object to identify dataclass fields.
12298155 default is the default value of the field.  default_factory is a
12298220 0-argument function called to initialize a field's value.  If init
12298287 is true, the field will be a parameter to the class's __init__()
12298352 function.  If repr is true, the field will be included in the
12298414 object's repr().  If hash is true, the field will be included in the
12298483 object's hash().  If compare is true, the field will be used in
12298547 comparison functions.  metadata, if specified, must be a mapping
12298612 which is stored but not otherwise examined by dataclass.  If kw_only

12340786 Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic.
12340838 This is an implementation of decimal floating-point arithmetic based on
12340910 the General Decimal Arithmetic Specification:
12340957     http://speleotrove.com/decimal/decarith.html
12341007 and IEEE standard 854-1987:
12341036     http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_854-1987
12341084 Decimal floating point has finite precision with arbitrarily large bounds.
12341160 The purpose of this module is to support arithmetic using familiar
12341227 "schoolhouse" rules and to avoid some of the tricky representation
12341294 issues associated with binary floating point.  The package is especially
12341367 useful for financial applications or for contexts where users have
12341434 expectations that are at odds with binary floating point (for instance,
12341506 in binary floating point, 1.00 % 0.1 gives 0.09999999999999995 instead
12341577 of 0.0; Decimal('1.00') % Decimal('0.1') returns the expected
12341639 Decimal('0.00')).

12345218 _calculate_ratior
12345444 SequenceMatcher is a flexible class for comparing pairs of sequences of
12345516 any type, so long as the sequence elements are hashable.  The basic
12345584 algorithm predates, and is a little fancier than, an algorithm
12345647 published in the late 1980's by Ratcliff and Obershelp under the
12345712 hyperbolic name "gestalt pattern matching".  The basic idea is to find
12345783 the longest contiguous matching subsequence that contains no "junk"
12345851 elements (R-O doesn't address junk).  The same idea is then applied
12345919 recursively to the pieces of the sequences to the left and to the right
12345991 of the matching subsequence.  This does not yield minimal edit
12346054 sequences, but does tend to yield matches that "look right" to people.
12346126 SequenceMatcher tries to compute a "human-friendly diff" between two
12346195 sequences.  Unlike e.g. UNIX(tm) diff, the fundamental notion is the
12346264 longest *contiguous* & junk-free matching subsequence.  That's what
12346332 catches peoples' eyes.  The Windows(tm) windiff has another interesting
12346404 notion, pairing up elements that appear uniquely in each sequence.
12346471 That, and the method here, appear to yield more intuitive difference
12346540 reports than does diff.  This method appears to be the least vulnerable
12346612 to syncing up on blocks of "junk lines", though (like blank lines in
12346681 ordinary text files, or maybe "<P>" lines in HTML files).  That may be
12346752 because this is the only method of the 3 that has a *concept* of
12346817 "junk" <wink>.
12346833 Example, comparing two strings, and considering blanks to be "junk":
12346903 >>> s = SequenceMatcher(lambda x: x == " ",
12346947 ...                     "private Thread currentThread;",
12347004 ...                     "private volatile Thread currentThread;")
12347075 .ratio() returns a float in [0, 1], measuring the "similarity" of the
12347145 sequences.  As a rule of thumb, a .ratio() value over 0.6 means the
12347213 sequences are close matches:
12347243 >>> print(round(s.ratio(), 2))
12347284 If you're only interested in where the sequences match,
12347340 .get_matching_blocks() is handy:
12347374 >>> for block in s.get_matching_blocks():
12347416 ...     print("a[%d] and b[%d] match for %d elements" % block)
12347479 a[0] and b[0] match for 8 elements
12347514 a[8] and b[17] match for 21 elements
12347551 a[29] and b[38] match for 0 elements
12347589 Note that the last tuple returned by .get_matching_blocks() is always a
12347661 dummy, (len(a), len(b), 0), and this is the only case in which the last
12347733 tuple element (number of elements matched) is 0.
12347783 If you want to know how to change the first sequence into the second,
12347853 use .get_opcodes():
12347874 >>> for opcode in s.get_opcodes():
12347909 ...     print("%6s a[%d:%d] b[%d:%d]" % opcode)
12347957  equal a[0:8] b[0:8]
12347978 insert a[8:8] b[8:17]
12348000  equal a[8:29] b[17:38]
12348025 See the Differ class for a fancy human-friendly file differencer, which
12348097 uses SequenceMatcher both to compare sequences of lines, and to compare
12348169 sequences of characters within similar (near-matching) lines.
12348232 See also function get_close_matches() in this module, which shows how
12348302 simple code building on SequenceMatcher can be used to do useful work.
12348374 Timing:  Basic R-O is cubic time worst case and quadratic time expected
12348446 case.  SequenceMatcher is quadratic time for the worst case and has
12348514 expected-case behavior dependent in a complicated way on how many
12348580 elements the sequences have in common; best case time is linear.
12348769 Construct a SequenceMatcher.
12348799 Optional arg isjunk is None (the default), or a one-argument
12348860 function that takes a sequence element and returns true iff the
12348924 element is junk.  None is equivalent to passing "lambda x: 0", i.e.
12348992 no elements are considered to be junk.  For example, pass
12349050     lambda x: x in " \t"
12349075 if you're comparing lines as sequences of characters, and don't
12349139 want to synch up on blanks or hard tabs.
12349181 Optional arg a is the first of two sequences to be compared.  By
12349246 default, an empty string.  The elements of a must be hashable.  See
12349314 also .set_seqs() and .set_seq1().
12349349 Optional arg b is the second of two sequences to be compared.  By
12349415 default, an empty string.  The elements of b must be hashable. See
12349482 also .set_seqs() and .set_seq2().
12349517 Optional arg autojunk should be set to False to disable the
12349577 "automatic junk heuristic" that treats popular elements as junk
12349641 (see module documentation for more information).

12354248 Find longest matching block in a[alo:ahi] and b[blo:bhi].
12354307 By default it will find the longest match in the entirety of a and b.
12354378 If isjunk is not defined:
12354405 Return (i,j,k) such that a[i:i+k] is equal to b[j:j+k], where
12354467     alo <= i <= i+k <= ahi
12354494     blo <= j <= j+k <= bhi
12354521 and for all (i',j',k') meeting those conditions,
12354570     k >= k'
12354582     i <= i'
12354594     and if i == i', j <= j'
12354623 In other words, of all maximal matching blocks, return one that
12354687 starts earliest in a, and of all those maximal matching blocks that
12354755 start earliest in a, return the one that starts earliest in b.
12354819 >>> s = SequenceMatcher(None, " abcd", "abcd abcd")
12354871 >>> s.find_longest_match(0, 5, 0, 9)
12354908 Match(a=0, b=4, size=5)
12354933 If isjunk is defined, first the longest matching block is
12354991 determined as above, but with the additional restriction that no
12355056 junk element appears in the block.  Then that block is extended as
12355123 far as possible by matching (only) junk elements on both sides.  So
12355191 the resulting block never matches on junk except as identical junk
12355258 happens to be adjacent to an "interesting" match.
12355309 Here's the same example as before, but considering blanks to be
12355373 junk.  That prevents " abcd" from matching the " abcd" at the tail
12355440 end of the second sequence directly.  Instead only the "abcd" can
12355506 match, and matches the leftmost "abcd" in the second sequence:
12355570 >>> s = SequenceMatcher(lambda x: x==" ", " abcd", "abcd abcd")
12355634 >>> s.find_longest_match(0, 5, 0, 9)
12355671 Match(a=1, b=0, size=4)
12355696 If no blocks match, return (alo, blo, 0).
12355739 >>> s = SequenceMatcher(None, "ab", "c")
12355780 >>> s.find_longest_match(0, 2, 0, 1)
12355817 Match(a=0, b=0, size=0)

12357246 XYXz4
12357743 Return list of triples describing matching subsequences.
12357801 Each triple is of the form (i, j, n), and means that
12357854 a[i:i+n] == b[j:j+n].  The triples are monotonically increasing in
12357921 i and in j.  New in Python 2.5, it's also guaranteed that if
12357982 (i, j, n) and (i', j', n') are adjacent triples in the list, and
12358047 the second is not the last triple in the list, then i+n != i' or
12358112 j+n != j'.  IOW, adjacent triples never describe adjacent equal
12358176 blocks.
12358185 The last triple is a dummy, (len(a), len(b), 0), and is the only
12358250 triple with n==0.
12358269 >>> s = SequenceMatcher(None, "abxcd", "abcd")
12358316 >>> list(s.get_matching_blocks())
12358350 [Match(a=0, b=0, size=2), Match(a=3, b=2, size=2), Match(a=5, b=4, size=0)]

12359421 XAXR4
12359456 Return list of 5-tuples describing how to turn a into b.
12359514 Each tuple is of the form (tag, i1, i2, j1, j2).  The first tuple
12359580 has i1 == j1 == 0, and remaining tuples have i1 == the i2 from the
12359647 tuple preceding it, and likewise for j1 == the previous j2.
12359708 The tags are strings, with these meanings:
12359752 'replace':  a[i1:i2] should be replaced by b[j1:j2]
12359804 'delete':   a[i1:i2] should be deleted.
12359844             Note that j1==j2 in this case.
12359887 'insert':   b[j1:j2] should be inserted at a[i1:i1].
12359940             Note that i1==i2 in this case.
12359983 'equal':    a[i1:i2] == b[j1:j2]
12360017 >>> a = "qabxcd"

12368379 Differ is a class for comparing sequences of lines of text, and
12368443 producing human-readable differences or deltas.  Differ uses
12368504 SequenceMatcher both to compare sequences of lines, and to compare
12368571 sequences of characters within similar (near-matching) lines.
12368634 Each line of a Differ delta begins with a two-letter code:
12368694     '- '    line unique to sequence 1
12368732     '+ '    line unique to sequence 2
12368770     '  '    line common to both sequences
12368812     '? '    line not present in either input sequence
12368867 Lines beginning with '? ' attempt to guide the eye to intraline
12368931 differences, and were not present in either input sequence.  These lines
12369004 can be confusing if the sequences contain tab characters.
12369063 Note that Differ makes no claim to produce a *minimal* diff.  To the
12369132 contrary, minimal diffs are often counter-intuitive, because they synch
12369204 up anywhere possible, sometimes accidental matches 100 pages apart.
12369272 Restricting synch points to contiguous matches preserves some notion of
12369344 locality, at the occasional cost of producing a longer diff.
12369406 Example: Comparing two texts.
12369437 First we set up the texts, sequences of individual single-line strings
12369508 ending with newlines (such sequences can also be obtained from the
12369575 `readlines()` method of file-like objects):
12369620 >>> text1 = '''  1. Beautiful is better than ugly.
12369671 ...   2. Explicit is better than implicit.
12369714 ...   3. Simple is better than complex.
12369754 ...   4. Complex is better than complicated.
12369799 ... '''.splitlines(keepends=True)
12369833 >>> len(text1)
12369850 >>> text1[0][-1]
12369872 >>> text2 = '''  1. Beautiful is better than ugly.
12369923 ...   3.   Simple is better than complex.
12369965 ...   4. Complicated is better than complex.
12370010 ...   5. Flat is better than nested.
12370047 ... '''.splitlines(keepends=True)
12370082 Next we instantiate a Differ object:
12370120 >>> d = Differ()
12370138 Note that when instantiating a Differ object we may pass functions to
12370208 filter out line and character 'junk'.  See Differ.__init__ for details.
12370281 Finally, we compare the two:
12370311 >>> result = list(d.compare(text1, text2))
12370355 'result' is a list of strings, so let's pretty-print it:
12370413 >>> from pprint import pprint as _pprint
12370454 >>> _pprint(result)
12370474 ['    1. Beautiful is better than ugly.\n',
12370518  '-   2. Explicit is better than implicit.\n',
12370565  '-   3. Simple is better than complex.\n',
12370609  '+   3.   Simple is better than complex.\n',
12370655  '?     ++\n',
12370670  '-   4. Complex is better than complicated.\n',
12370719  '?            ^                     ---- ^\n',
12370767  '+   4. Complicated is better than complex.\n',
12370816  '?           ++++ ^                      ^\n',
12370864  '+   5. Flat is better than nested.\n']
12370906 As a single multi-line string it looks like this:
12370957 >>> print(''.join(result), end="")
12370992     1. Beautiful is better than ugly.
12371030 -   2. Explicit is better than implicit.
12371071 -   3. Simple is better than complex.
12371109 +   3.   Simple is better than complex.
12371149 ?     ++
12371158 -   4. Complex is better than complicated.
12371201 ?            ^                     ---- ^
12371243 +   4. Complicated is better than complex.
12371286 ?           ++++ ^                      ^
12371328 +   5. Flat is better than nested.
12371426 Construct a text differencer, with optional filters.
12371480 The two optional keyword parameters are for filter functions:
12371543 - `linejunk`: A function that should accept a single string argument,
12371613   and return true iff the string is junk. The module-level function
12371681   `IS_LINE_JUNK` may be used to filter out lines without visible
12371746   characters, except for at most one splat ('#').  It is recommended
12371815   to leave linejunk None; the underlying SequenceMatcher class has
12371882   an adaptive notion of "noise" lines that's better than any static
12371950   definition the author has ever been able to craft.
12372004 - `charjunk`: A function that should accept a string of length 1. The
12372074   module-level function `IS_CHARACTER_JUNK` may be used to filter out
12372144   whitespace characters (a blank or tab; **note**: bad idea to include
12372215   newline in this!).  Use of IS_CHARACTER_JUNK is recommended.

12380410 Compare two sequences of lines; generate the delta as a unified diff.
12380481 Unified diffs are a compact way of showing line changes and a few
12380547 lines of context.  The number of context lines is set by 'n' which
12380614 defaults to three.
12380634 By default, the diff control lines (those with ---, +++, or @@) are
12380702 created with a trailing newline.  This is helpful so that inputs
12380767 created from file.readlines() result in diffs that are suitable for
12380835 file.writelines() since both the inputs and outputs have trailing
12380901 newlines.
12380912 For inputs that do not have trailing newlines, set the lineterm
12380976 argument to "" so that the output will be uniformly newline free.

12381115 times.  Any or all of these may be specified using strings for
12381178 'fromfile', 'tofile', 'fromfiledate', and 'tofiledate'.

12404057 Returns from/to line lists with tabs expanded and newlines removed.
12404126 Instead of tab characters being replaced by the number of spaces
12404191 needed to fill in to the next tab stop, this function will fill
12404255 the space with tab characters.  This is done so that the difference
12404323 algorithms can identify changes in a file when tabs are replaced by
12404391 spaces and vice versa.  At the end of the HTML generation, the tab
12404458 characters will be replaced with a nonbreakable space.

12469771 Decode encoded word and return (string, charset, lang, defects) tuple.
12469843 An RFC 2047/2243 encoded word has the form:
12469888     =?charset*lang?cte?encoded_string?=
12469929 where '*lang' may be omitted but the other parts may not be.
12469991 This function expects exactly such a string (that is, it does not check the
12470067 syntax and may raise errors if the string is not well formed), and returns
12470142 the encoded_string decoded first from its Content Transfer Encoding and
12470214 then from the resulting bytes into unicode using the specified charset.  If
12470290 the cte-decoded string does not successfully decode using the specified
12470362 character set, a defect is added to the defects list and the unknown octets
12470438 are replaced by the unicode 'unknown' character \uFDFF.
12470495 The specified charset and language are returned.  The default for language,
12470571 which is rarely if ever encountered, is the empty string.

12471676 Encode string using the CTE encoding that produces the shorter result.
12471748 Produces an RFC 2047/2243 encoded word of the form:
12471801     =?charset*lang?cte?encoded_string?=
12471842 where '*lang' is omitted unless the 'lang' parameter is given a value.
12471913 Optional argument charset (defaults to utf-8) specifies the charset to use
12471988 to encode the string to binary before CTE encoding it.  Optional argument
12472062 'encoding' is the cte specifier for the encoding that should be used ('q'
12472136 or 'b'); if it is None (the default) the encoding which produces the
12472205 shortest encoded sequence is used, except that 'q' is preferred if it is up
12472281 to five characters longer.  Optional argument 'lang' (default '') gives the
12472357 RFC 2243 language string to specify in the encoded word.

12476038 Header value parser implementing various email-related RFC parsing rules.
12476113 The parsing methods defined in this module implement various email related
12476188 parsing rules.  Principal among them is RFC 5322, which is the followon
12476260 to RFC 2822 and primarily a clarification of the former.  It also implements
12476337 RFC 2047 encoded word decoding.
12476370 RFC 5322 goes to considerable trouble to maintain backward compatibility with
12476448 RFC 822 in the parse phase, while cleaning up the structure on the generation
12476526 phase.  This parser supports correct RFC 5322 generation by tagging white space
12476606 as folding white space only when folding is allowed in the non-obsolete rule
12476683 sets.  Actually, the parser is even more generous when accepting input than RFC
12476763 5322 mandates, following the spirit of Postel's Law, which RFC 5322 encourages.
12476843 Where possible deviations from the standard are annotated on the 'defects'
12476918 attribute of tokens that deviate.
12476953 The general structure of the parser follows RFC 5322, and uses its terminology
12477032 where there is a direct correspondence.  Where the implementation requires a
12477109 somewhat different structure than that used by the formal grammar, new terms
12477186 that mimic the closest existing terms are used.  Thus, it really helps to have
12477265 a copy of RFC 5322 handy when studying this code.
12477316 Input to the parser is a string that has already been unfolded according to
12477392 RFC 5322 rules.  According to the RFC this unfolding is the very first step, and
12477473 this parser leaves the unfolding step to a higher level message parser, which
12477551 will have already detected the line breaks that need unfolding while
12477620 determining the beginning and end of each header.
12477671 The output of the parser is a TokenList object, which is a list subclass.  A
12477748 TokenList is a recursive data structure.  The terminal nodes of the structure
12477826 are Terminal objects, which are subclasses of str.  These do not correspond
12477902 directly to terminal objects in the formal grammar, but are instead more
12477975 practical higher level combinations of true terminals.
12478031 All TokenList and Terminal objects have a 'value' attribute, which produces the
12478111 semantically meaningful value of that part of the parse subtree.  The value of
12478190 all whitespace tokens (no matter how many sub-tokens they may contain) is a
12478266 single space, as per the RFC rules.  This includes 'CFWS', which is herein
12478341 included in the general class of whitespace tokens.  There is one exception to
12478420 the rule that whitespace tokens are collapsed into single spaces in values: in
12478499 the value of a 'bare-quoted-string' (a quoted-string with no leading or
12478571 trailing whitespace), any whitespace that appeared between the quotation marks
12478650 is preserved in the returned value.  Note that in all Terminal strings quoted
12478728 pairs are turned into their unquoted values.
12478774 All TokenList and Terminal objects also have a string value, which attempts to
12478853 be a "canonical" representation of the RFC-compliant form of the substring that
12478933 produced the parsed subtree, including minimal use of quoted pair quoting.
12479008 Whitespace runs are not collapsed.
12479044 Comment tokens also have a 'content' attribute providing the string found
12479118 between the parens (including any nested comments) with whitespace preserved.
12479197 All TokenList and Terminal objects have a 'defects' attribute which is a
12479270 possibly empty list all of the defects found while creating the token.  Defects
12479350 may appear on any token in the tree, and a composite list of all defects in the
12479430 subtree is available through the 'all_defects' attribute of any node.  (For
12479506 Terminal notes x.defects == x.all_defects.)
12479551 Each object in a parse tree is called a 'token', and each has a 'token_type'
12479628 attribute that gives the name from the RFC 5322 grammar that it represents.
12479704 Not all RFC 5322 nodes are produced, and there is one non-RFC 5322 node that
12479781 may be produced: 'ptext'.  A 'ptext' is a string of printable ascii characters.
12479861 It is returned in place of lists of (ctext/quoted-pair) and
12479921 (qtext/quoted-pair).
12479943 XXX: provide complete list of token types.

12637277 _PolicyBase
12637298 Policy Object basic framework.
12637330 This class is useless unless subclassed.  A subclass should define
12637397 class attributes with defaults for any values that are to be
12637458 managed by the Policy object.  The constructor will then allow
12637521 non-default values to be set for these attributes at instance
12637583 creation time.  The instance will be callable, taking these same
12637648 attributes keyword arguments, and returning a new instance
12637707 identical to the called instance except for those values changed
12637772 by the keyword arguments.  Instances may be added, yielding new
12637836 instances with any non-default values from the right hand
12637894 operand overriding those in the left hand operand.  That is,
12637956     A + B == A(<non-default values of B>)
12637999 The repr of an instance can be used to reconstruct the object
12638061 if and only if the repr of the values can be used to reconstruct
12638126 those values.
12638387 zrCreate new Policy, possibly overriding some defaults.
12638444 See class docstring for a list of overridable attributes.

12642448 _extend_docstringsrO
12642962 Controls for how messages are interpreted and formatted.
12643020 Most of the classes and many of the methods in the email package accept
12643092 Policy objects as parameters.  A Policy object contains a set of values and
12643168 functions that control how input is interpreted and how output is rendered.
12643244 For example, the parameter 'raise_on_defect' controls whether or not an RFC
12643320 violation results in an error being raised or not, while 'max_line_length'
12643395 controls the maximum length of output lines when a Message is serialized.
12643470 Any valid attribute may be overridden when a Policy is created by passing
12643544 it as a keyword argument to the constructor.  Policy objects are immutable,
12643620 but a new Policy object can be created with only certain values changed by
12643695 calling the Policy instance with keyword arguments.  Policy objects can
12643767 also be added, producing a new Policy object in which the non-default
12643837 attributes set in the right hand operand overwrite those specified in the
12643911 left operand.
12643926 Settable attributes:
12643948 raise_on_defect     -- If true, then defects should be raised as errors.
12644021                        Default: False.
12644061 linesep             -- string containing the value to use as separation
12644133                        between output lines.  Default '\n'.
12644194 cte_type            -- Type of allowed content transfer encodings
12644261                        7bit  -- ASCII only
12644304                        8bit  -- Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit is allowed
12644380                        Default: 8bit.  Also controls the disposition of
12644452                        (RFC invalid) binary data in headers; see the
12644521                        documentation of the binary_fold method.
12644586 max_line_length     -- maximum length of lines, excluding 'linesep',
12644655                        during serialization.  None or 0 means no line
12644725                        wrapping is done.  Default is 78.
12644783 mangle_from_        -- a flag that, when True escapes From_ lines in the
12644856                        body of the message by putting a `>' in front of
12644928                        them. This is used when the message is being
12644996                        serialized by a generator. Default: False.
12645063 message_factory     -- the class to use to create new message objects.
12645134                        If the value is None, the default is Message.
12645204 verify_generated_headers
12645229                     -- if true, the generator verifies that each header
12645301                        they are properly folded, so that a parser won't
12645373                        treat it as multiple headers, start-of-body, or
12645444                        part of another header.
12645491                        This is a check against custom Header & fold()
12645561                        implementations.
12645729 Based on policy, either raise defect or call register_defect.
12645792     handle_defect(obj, defect)
12645824 defect should be a Defect subclass, but in any case must be an
12645887 Exception subclass.  obj is the object on which the defect should be
12645956 registered if it is not raised.  If the raise_on_defect is True, the
12646025 defect is raised as an error, otherwise the object and the defect are
12646095 passed to register_defect.
12646123 This method is intended to be called by parsers that discover defects.
12646194 The email package parsers always call it with Defect instances.

12647053 Return the maximum allowed number of headers named 'name'.
12647113 Called when a header is added to a Message object.  If the returned
12647181 value is not 0 or None, and there are already a number of headers with
12647252 the name 'name' equal to the value returned, a ValueError is raised.
12647322 Because the default behavior of Message's __setitem__ is to append the
12647393 value to the list of headers, it is easy to create duplicate headers
12647462 without realizing it.  This method allows certain headers to be limited
12647534 in the number of instances of that header that may be added to a
12647599 Message programmatically.  (The limit is not observed by the parser,
12647668 which will faithfully produce as many headers as exist in the message
12647738 being parsed.)
12647754 The default implementation returns None for all header names.

12654568 <module>r
12654850 Base64 content transfer encoding per RFCs 2045-2047.
12654904 This module handles the content transfer encoding method defined in RFC 2045
12654981 to encode arbitrary 8-bit data using the three 8-bit bytes in four 7-bit
12655054 characters encoding known as Base64.
12655092 It is used in the MIME standards for email to attach images, audio, and text
12655169 using some 8-bit character sets to messages.
12655215 This module provides an interface to encode and decode both headers and bodies
12655294 with Base64 encoding.
12655317 RFC 2045 defines a method for including character set information in an
12655389 `encoded-word' in a header.  This method is commonly used for 8-bit real names
12655468 in To:, From:, Cc:, etc. fields, as well as Subject: lines.
12655529 This module does not do the line wrapping or end-of-line character conversion
12655607 necessary for proper internationalized headers; it only does dumb encoding and
12655686 decoding.  To deal with the various line wrapping issues, use the email.header
12655765 module.

12662186 Map character sets to their email properties.
12662233 This class provides information about the requirements imposed on email
12662305 for a specific character set.  It also provides convenience routines for
12662378 converting between character sets, given the availability of the
12662443 applicable codecs.  Given a character set, it will do its best to provide
12662517 information on how to use that character set in an email in an
12662580 RFC-compliant way.
12662600 Certain character sets must be encoded with quoted-printable or base64
12662671 when used in email headers or bodies.  Certain character sets must be
12662741 converted outright, and are not allowed in email.  Instances of this
12662810 module expose the following information about a character set:
12662874 input_charset: The initial character set specified.  Common aliases
12662942                are converted to their `official' email names (e.g. latin_1
12663017                is converted to iso-8859-1).  Defaults to 7-bit us-ascii.
12663091 header_encoding: If the character set must be encoded before it can be
12663162                  used in an email header, this attribute will be set to
12663234                  charset.QP (for quoted-printable), charset.BASE64 (for
12663306                  base64 encoding), or charset.SHORTEST for the shortest of
12663381                  QP or BASE64 encoding.  Otherwise, it will be None.
12663451 body_encoding: Same as header_encoding, but describes the encoding for the
12663526                mail message's body, which indeed may be different than the
12663601                header encoding.  charset.SHORTEST is not allowed for
12663670                body_encoding.
12663701 output_charset: Some character sets must be converted before they can be
12663774                 used in email headers or bodies.  If the input_charset is
12663848                 one of them, this attribute will contain the name of the
12663921                 charset output will be converted to.  Otherwise, it will
12663994                 be None.
12664020 input_codec: The name of the Python codec used to convert the
12664082              input_charset to Unicode.  If no conversion codec is
12664148              necessary, this attribute will be None.
12664202 output_codec: The name of the Python codec used to convert Unicode
12664269               to the output_charset.  If no conversion codec is necessary,
12664344               this attribute will have the same value as the input_codec.

12695644 FeedParser - An email feed parser.
12695680 The feed parser implements an interface for incrementally parsing an email
12695755 message, line by line.  This has advantages for certain applications, such as
12695833 those reading email messages off a socket.
12695877 FeedParser.feed() is the primary interface for pushing new data into the
12695950 parser.  It returns when there's nothing more it can do with the available
12696025 data.  When you have no more data to push into the parser, call .close().
12696099 This completes the parsing and returns the root message object.
12696164 The other advantage of this parser is that it will never raise a parsing
12696237 exception.  Instead, when it finds something unexpected, it adds a 'defect' to
12696316 the current message.  Defects are just instances that live on the message
12696390 object's .defects attribute.

12743353 Create a MIME-compliant header that can contain many character sets.
12743423 Optional s is the initial header value.  If None, the initial header
12743492 value is not set.  You can later append to the header with .append()
12743561 method calls.  s may be a byte string or a Unicode string, but see the
12743632 .append() documentation for semantics.
12743672 Optional charset serves two purposes: it has the same meaning as the
12743741 charset argument to the .append() method.  It also sets the default
12743809 character set for all subsequent .append() calls that omit the charset
12743880 argument.  If charset is not provided in the constructor, the us-ascii
12743951 charset is used both as s's initial charset and as the default for
12744018 subsequent .append() calls.
12744047 The maximum line length can be specified explicitly via maxlinelen. For
12744119 splitting the first line to a shorter value (to account for the field
12744189 header which isn't included in s, e.g. `Subject') pass in the name of
12744259 the field in header_name.  The default maxlinelen is 78 as recommended
12744330 by RFC 2822.
12744344 continuation_ws must be RFC 2822 compliant folding whitespace (usually
12744415 either a space or a hard tab) which will be prepended to continuation
12744485 lines.
12744493 errors is passed through to the .append() call.

12749590 Encode a message header into an RFC-compliant format.
12749645 There are many issues involved in converting a given string for use in
12749716 an email header.  Only certain character sets are readable in most
12749783 email clients, and as header strings can only contain a subset of
12749849 7-bit ASCII, care must be taken to properly convert and encode (with
12749918 Base64 or quoted-printable) header strings.  In addition, there is a
12749987 75-character length limit on any given encoded header field, so
12750051 line-wrapping must be performed, even with double-byte character sets.
12750123 Optional maxlinelen specifies the maximum length of each generated
12750190 line, exclusive of the linesep string.  Individual lines may be longer
12750261 than maxlinelen if a folding point cannot be found.  The first line
12750329 will be shorter by the length of the header name plus ": " if a header
12750400 name was specified at Header construction time.  The default value for
12750471 maxlinelen is determined at header construction time.
12750526 Optional splitchars is a string containing characters which should be
12750596 given extra weight by the splitting algorithm during normal header
12750663 wrapping.  This is in very rough support of RFC 2822's `higher level
12750732 syntactic breaks':  split points preceded by a splitchar are preferred
12750803 during line splitting, with the characters preferred in the order in
12750872 which they appear in the string.  Space and tab may be included in the
12750943 string to indicate whether preference should be given to one over the
12751013 other as a split point when other split chars do not appear in the line
12751085 being split.  Splitchars does not affect RFC 2047 encoded lines.
12751151 Optional linesep is a string to be used to separate the lines of
12751216 the value.  The default value is the most useful for typical
12751277 Python applications, but it can be set to \r\n to produce RFC-compliant
12751349 line separators when needed.

12770636 BaseHeader
12770656 Base class for message headers.
12770689 Implements generic behavior and provides tools for subclasses.
12770753 A subclass must define a classmethod named 'parse' that takes an unfolded
12770827 value string and a dictionary as its arguments.  The dictionary will
12770896 contain one key, 'defects', initialized to an empty list.  After the call
12770970 the dictionary must contain two additional keys: parse_tree, set to the
12771042 parse tree obtained from parsing the header, and 'decoded', set to the
12771113 string value of the idealized representation of the data from the value.
12771186 (That is, encoded words are decoded, and values that have canonical
12771254 representations are so represented.)
12771292 The defects key is intended to collect parsing defects, which the message
12771366 parser will subsequently dispose of as appropriate.  The parser should not,
12771442 insofar as practical, raise any errors.  Defects should be added to the
12771514 list instead.  The standard header parsers register defects for RFC
12771582 compliance issues, for obsolete RFC syntax, and for unrecoverable parsing
12771656 errors.
12771665 The parse method may add additional keys to the dictionary.  In this case
12771739 the subclass must define an 'init' method, which will be passed the
12771807 dictionary as its keyword arguments.  The method should use (usually by
12771879 setting them as the value of similarly named attributes) and remove all the
12771955 extra keys added by its parse method, and then use super to call its parent
12772031 class with the remaining arguments and keywords.
12772081 The subclass should also make sure that a 'max_count' attribute is defined
12772156 that is either None or 1. XXX: need to better define this API.

12802166 Basic message object.
12802189 A message object is defined as something that has a bunch of RFC 5322
12802259 headers and a payload.  It may optionally have an envelope header
12802325 (a.k.a. Unix-From or From_ header).  If the message is a container (i.e. a
12802400 multipart or a message/rfc822), then the payload is a list of Message
12802470 objects, otherwise it is a string.
12802506 Message objects implement part of the `mapping' interface, which assumes
12802579 there is exactly one occurrence of the header per message.  Some headers
12802652 do in fact appear multiple times (e.g. Received) and for those headers,
12802724 you must use the explicit API to set or get all the headers.  Not all of
12802797 the mapping methods are implemented.
12802993 text/plain)

12825759 Optional failobj is the object to return if there is no Content-Type

12848950 Parser of RFC 5322 and MIME email messages.
12848995 Creates an in-memory object tree representing the email message, which
12849066 can then be manipulated and turned over to a Generator to return the
12849135 textual representation of the message.
12849175 The string must be formatted as a block of RFC 5322 headers and header
12849246 continuation lines, optionally preceded by a 'Unix-from' header.  The
12849316 header block is terminated either by the end of the string or by a
12849383 blank line.
12849396 _class is the class to instantiate for new message objects when they
12849465 must be created.  This class must have a constructor that can take
12849532 zero arguments.  Default is Message.Message.
12849578 The policy keyword specifies a policy object that controls a number of
12849649 aspects of the parser's operation.  The default policy maintains
12849714 backward compatibility.

12855534 \n|\r\n?c
12855707 PROVISIONAL
12855720 The API extensions enabled by this policy are currently provisional.
12855789 Refer to the documentation for details.
12855830 This policy adds new header parsing and folding algorithms.  Instead of
12855902 simple strings, headers are custom objects with custom attributes
12855968 depending on the type of the field.  The folding algorithm fully
12856033 implements RFCs 2047 and 5322.
12856065 In addition to the settable attributes listed above that apply to
12856131 all Policies, this policy adds the following additional attributes:
12856200 utf8                -- if False (the default) message headers will be
12856270                        serialized as ASCII, using encoded words to encode
12856344                        any non-ASCII characters in the source strings.  If
12856419                        True, the message headers will be serialized using
12856493                        utf8 and will not contain encoded words (see RFC
12856565                        6532 for more on this serialization format).
12856634 refold_source       -- if the value for a header in the Message object
12856705                        came from the parsing of some source, this attribute
12856781                        indicates whether or not a generator should refold
12856855                        that value when transforming the message back into
12856929                        stream form.  The possible values are:
12856992                        none  -- all source values use original folding
12857063                        long  -- source values that have any line that is
12857136                                 longer than max_line_length will be
12857204                                 refolded
12857245                        all  -- all values are refolded.
12857302                        The default is 'long'.
12857349 header_factory      -- a callable that takes two arguments, 'name' and
12857420                        'value', where 'name' is a header field name and
12857492                        'value' is an unfolded header field value, and
12857562                        returns a string-like object that represents that
12857635                        header.  A default header_factory is provided that
12857709                        understands some of the RFC5322 header field types.
12857784                        (Currently address fields and date fields have
12857854                        special treatment, while all other fields are
12857923                        treated as unstructured.  This list will be
12857990                        completed before the extension is marked stable.)
12858064 content_manager     -- an object with at least two methods: get_content
12858136                        and set_content.  When the get_content or
12858201                        set_content method of a Message object is called,
12858274                        it calls the corresponding method of this object,
12858347                        passing it the message object as its first argument,
12858423                        and any arguments or keywords that were passed to
12858496                        it as additional arguments.  The default
12858560                        content_manager is
12858602                        :data:`~email.contentmanager.raw_data_manager`.
12858677 longc

12861974 Header folding is controlled by the refold_source policy setting.  A
12862043 value is considered to be a 'source value' if and only if it does not
12862113 have a 'name' attribute (having a 'name' attribute means it is a header
12862185 object of some sort).  If a source value needs to be refolded according

12866072 <module>rz
12866782 Quoted-printable content transfer encoding per RFCs 2045-2047.
12866846 This module handles the content transfer encoding method defined in RFC 2045
12866923 to encode US ASCII-like 8-bit data called `quoted-printable'.  It is used to
12867000 safely encode text that is in a character set similar to the 7-bit US ASCII
12867076 character set, but that includes some 8-bit characters that are normally not
12867153 allowed in email bodies or headers.
12867190 Quoted-printable is very space-inefficient for encoding binary files; use the
12867268 email.base64mime module for that instead.
12867311 This module provides an interface to encode and decode both headers and bodies
12867390 with quoted-printable encoding.
12867423 RFC 2045 defines a method for including character set information in an
12867495 `encoded-word' in a header.  This method is commonly used for 8-bit real names
12867574 in To:/From:/Cc: etc. fields, as well as Subject: lines.
12867632 This module does not do the line wrapping or end-of-line character
12867699 conversion necessary for proper internationalized headers; it only
12867766 does dumb encoding and decoding.  To deal with the various line
12867830 wrapping issues, use the email.header module.

12872484 in an email.
12872498 Each line will be wrapped at, at most, maxlinelen characters before the
12872570 eol string (maxlinelen defaults to 76 characters, the maximum value
12872638 permitted by RFC 2045).  Long lines will have the 'soft line break'
12872706 quoted-printable character "=" appended to them, so the decoded text will
12872780 be identical to the original text.
12872816 The minimum maxlinelen is 4 to have room for a quoted character ("=XX")
12872888 followed by a soft line break.  Smaller values will generate a
12872951 ValueError.

12893208 Standard "encodings" Package
12893238     Standard Python encoding modules are stored in this package
12893302     directory.
12893318     Codec modules must have names corresponding to normalized encoding
12893389     names as defined in the normalize_encoding() function below, e.g.
12893459     'utf-8' must be implemented by the module 'utf_8.py'.
12893518     Each codec module must export the following interface:
12893578     * getregentry() -> codecs.CodecInfo object
12893625     The getregentry() API must return a CodecInfo object with encoder, decoder,
12893705     incrementalencoder, incrementaldecoder, streamwriter and streamreader
12893779     attributes which adhere to the Python Codec Interface Standard.
12893848     In addition, a module may optionally also define the following
12893915     APIs which are then used by the package's codec search function:
12893985     * getaliases() -> sequence of encoding name strings to use as aliases
12894060     Alias names returned by getaliases() must be normalized encoding
12894129     names as defined by normalize_encoding().
12894176 Written by Marc-Andre Lemburg (mal@lemburg.com).
12894226 (c) Copyright CNRI, All Rights Reserved. NO WARRANTY.

13572164 A class that manages the comparison of 2 directories.
13572219 dircmp(a, b, ignore=None, hide=None, *, shallow=True)
13572273   A and B are directories.
13572300   IGNORE is a list of names to ignore,
13572339     defaults to DEFAULT_IGNORES.
13572372   HIDE is a list of names to hide,
13572407     defaults to [os.curdir, os.pardir].
13572447   SHALLOW specifies whether to just check the stat signature (do not read
13572521     the files).
13572537     defaults to True.
13572560 High level usage:
13572578   x = dircmp(dir1, dir2)
13572603   x.report() -> prints a report on the differences between dir1 and dir2
13572676    or
13572682   x.report_partial_closure() -> prints report on differences between dir1
13572756         and dir2, and reports on common immediate subdirectories.
13572822   x.report_full_closure() -> like report_partial_closure,
13572880         but fully recursive.
13572910 Attributes:
13572922  left_list, right_list: The files in dir1 and dir2,
13572974     filtered by hide and ignore.
13573007  common: a list of names in both dir1 and dir2.
13573055  left_only, right_only: names only in dir1, dir2.
13573105  common_dirs: subdirectories in both dir1 and dir2.
13573157  common_files: files in both dir1 and dir2.
13573201  common_funny: names in both dir1 and dir2 where the type differs between
13573275     dir1 and dir2, or the name is not stat-able.
13573324  same_files: list of identical files.
13573362  diff_files: list of filenames which differ.
13573407  funny_files: list of files which could not be compared.
13573464  subdirs: a dictionary of dircmp instances (or MyDirCmp instances if this
13573538    object is of type MyDirCmp, a subclass of dircmp), keyed by names
13573607    in common_dirs.

13584456 This iterates over the lines of all files listed in sys.argv[1:],
13584522 defaulting to sys.stdin if the list is empty.  If a filename is '-' it
13584593 is also replaced by sys.stdin and the optional arguments mode and
13584659 openhook are ignored.  To specify an alternative list of filenames,
13584727 pass it as the argument to input().  A single file name is also allowed.
13584801 Functions filename(), lineno() return the filename and cumulative line
13584872 number of the line that has just been read; filelineno() returns its
13584941 line number in the current file; isfirstline() returns true iff the
13585009 line just read is the first line of its file; isstdin() returns true
13585078 iff the line was read from sys.stdin.  Function nextfile() closes the
13585148 current file so that the next iteration will read the first line from
13585218 the next file (if any); lines not read from the file will not count
13585286 towards the cumulative line count; the filename is not changed until
13585355 after the first line of the next file has been read.  Function close()
13585426 closes the sequence.
13585448 Before any lines have been read, filename() returns None and both line
13585519 numbers are zero; nextfile() has no effect.  After all lines have been
13585590 read, filename() and the line number functions return the values
13585655 pertaining to the last line read; nextfile() has no effect.
13585716 All files are opened in text mode by default, you can override this by
13585787 setting the mode parameter to input() or FileInput.__init__().
13585850 If an I/O error occurs during opening or reading a file, the OSError
13585919 exception is raised.
13585941 If sys.stdin is used more than once, the second and further use will
13586010 return no lines, except perhaps for interactive use, or if it has been
13586081 explicitly reset (e.g. using sys.stdin.seek(0)).
13586131 Empty files are opened and immediately closed; the only time their
13586198 presence in the list of filenames is noticeable at all is when the
13586265 last file opened is empty.
13586293 It is possible that the last line of a file doesn't end in a newline
13586362 character; otherwise lines are returned including the trailing
13586425 newline.
13586435 Class FileInput is the implementation; its methods filename(),
13586498 lineno(), fileline(), isfirstline(), isstdin(), nextfile() and close()
13586569 correspond to the functions in the module.  In addition it has a
13586634 readline() method which returns the next input line, and a
13586693 __getitem__() method which implements the sequence behavior.  The
13586759 sequence must be accessed in strictly sequential order; sequence
13586824 access and readline() cannot be mixed.
13586864 Optional in-place filtering: if the keyword argument inplace=True is
13586933 passed to input() or to the FileInput constructor, the file is moved
13587002 to a backup file and standard output is directed to the input file.
13587070 This makes it possible to write a filter that rewrites its input file
13587140 in place.  If the keyword argument backup=".<some extension>" is also
13587210 given, it specifies the extension for the backup file, and the backup
13587280 file remains around; by default, the extension is ".bak" and it is
13587347 deleted when the output file is closed.  In-place filtering is
13587410 disabled when standard input is read.  XXX The current implementation
13587480 does not work for MS-DOS 8+3 filesystems.

13617095 This class implements rational numbers.
13617136 In the two-argument form of the constructor, Fraction(8, 6) will
13617201 produce a rational number equivalent to 4/3. Both arguments must
13617266 be Rational. The numerator defaults to 0 and the denominator
13617327 defaults to 1 so that Fraction(3) == 3 and Fraction() == 0.
13617388 Fractions can also be constructed from:
13617429   - numeric strings similar to those accepted by the
13617482     float constructor (for example, '-2.3' or '1e10')
13617537   - strings of the form '123/456'
13617572   - float and Decimal instances
13617605   - other Rational instances (including integers)

13630744 Fraction.__format__8
13631154 Generates forward and reverse operators given a purely-rational
13631218 operator and a function from the operator module.
13631269 Use this like:
13631284 __op__, __rop__ = _operator_fallbacks(just_rational_op, operator.op)
13631354 In general, we want to implement the arithmetic operations so
13631416 that mixed-mode operations either call an implementation whose
13631479 author knew about the types of both arguments, or convert both
13631542 to the nearest built in type and do the operation there. In
13631602 Fraction, that means that we define __add__ and __radd__ as:
13631664     def __add__(self, other):
13631694         # Both types have numerators/denominator attributes,
13631755         # so do the operation directly
13631794         if isinstance(other, (int, Fraction)):
13631841             return Fraction(self.numerator * other.denominator +
13631906                             other.numerator * self.denominator,
13631970                             self.denominator * other.denominator)
13632036         # float and complex don't have those operations, but we
13632100         # know about those types, so special case them.
13632156         elif isinstance(other, float):
13632195             return float(self) + other
13632234         elif isinstance(other, complex):
13632275             return complex(self) + other
13632316         # Let the other type take over.
13632356         return NotImplemented
13632387     def __radd__(self, other):
13632418         # radd handles more types than add because there's
13632477         # nothing left to fall back to.
13632517         if isinstance(other, numbers.Rational):
13632565             return Fraction(self.numerator * other.denominator +
13632630                             other.numerator * self.denominator,
13632694                             self.denominator * other.denominator)
13632760         elif isinstance(other, Real):
13632798             return float(other) + float(self)
13632844         elif isinstance(other, Complex):
13632885             return complex(other) + complex(self)
13632935         return NotImplemented
13632967 There are 5 different cases for a mixed-type addition on
13633024 Fraction. I'll refer to all of the above code that doesn't
13633083 refer to Fraction, float, or complex as "boilerplate". 'r'
13633142 will be an instance of Fraction, which is a subtype of
13633197 Rational (r : Fraction <: Rational), and b : B <:
13633247 Complex. The first three involve 'r + b':
13633290     1. If B <: Fraction, int, float, or complex, we handle
13633349        that specially, and all is well.
13633389     2. If Fraction falls back to the boilerplate code, and it
13633451        were to return a value from __add__, we'd miss the
13633509        possibility that B defines a more intelligent __radd__,
13633572        so the boilerplate should return NotImplemented from
13633632        __add__. In particular, we don't handle Rational
13633688        here, even though we could get an exact answer, in case
13633751        the other type wants to do something special.
13633804     3. If B <: Fraction, Python tries B.__radd__ before
13633860        Fraction.__add__. This is ok, because it was
13633912        implemented with knowledge of Fraction, so it can
13633969        handle those instances before delegating to Real or
13634028        Complex.
13634045 The next two situations describe 'b + r'. We assume that b
13634104 didn't know about Fraction in its implementation, and that it
13634166 uses similar boilerplate code:
13634198     4. If B <: Rational, then __radd_ converts both to the
13634257        builtin rational type (hey look, that's us) and
13634312        proceeds.
13634329     5. Otherwise, __radd__ tries to find the nearest common
13634389        base ABC, and fall back to its builtin type. Since this
13634452        class doesn't subclass a concrete type, there's no

13634570        hard as possible to return an actual value, or the user
13634633        will get a TypeError.

13652519 An FTP client class.
13652541 To create a connection, call the class using these arguments:
13652603         host, user, passwd, acct, timeout, source_address, encoding
13652672 The first four arguments are all strings, and have default value ''.
13652741 The parameter 
13652757 timeout
13652766  must be numeric and defaults to None if not
13652811 passed, meaning that no timeout will be set on any ftp socket(s).
13652877 If a timeout is passed, then this is now the default timeout for all ftp
13652950 socket operations for this instance.
13652987 The last parameter is the encoding of filenames, which defaults to utf-8.
13653062 Then use self.connect() with optional host and port argument.
13653125 To download a file, use ftp.retrlines('RETR ' + filename),
13653184 or ftp.retrbinary() with slightly different arguments.
13653239 To upload a file, use ftp.storlines() or ftp.storbinary(),
13653298 which have an open file as argument (see their definitions
13653357 below for details).
13653377 The download/upload functions first issue appropriate TYPE
13653436 and PORT or PASV commands.

13665371 Initiate a transfer over the data connection.
13665418 If the transfer is active, send a port command and the
13665473 transfer command, and accept the connection.  If the server is
13665536 passive, send a pasv command, connect to it, and start the
13665595 transfer command.  Either way, return the socket for the
13665652 connection and the expected size of the transfer.  The
13665707 expected size may be None if it could not be determined.
13665765 Optional `rest' argument can be a string that is sent as the
13665826 argument to a REST command.  This is essentially a server
13665884 marker used to tell the server to skip over any data up to the

13700830 reduce(function, iterable[, initial], /) -> value

13718354 	_c3_mergerP
13719372 Computes the method resolution order using extended C3 linearization.
13719443 If no *abcs* are given, the algorithm works exactly like the built-in C3
13719516 linearization used for method resolution.
13719559 If given, *abcs* is a list of abstract base classes that should be inserted
13719635 into the resulting MRO. Unrelated ABCs are ignored and don't end up in the
13719710 result. The algorithm inserts ABCs where their functionality is introduced,
13719786 i.e. issubclass(cls, abc) returns True for the class itself but returns
13719858 False for all its direct base classes. Implicit ABCs for a given class
13719929 (either registered or inferred from the presence of a special method like
13720003 __len__) are inserted directly after the last ABC explicitly listed in the
13720078 MRO of said class. If two implicit ABCs end up next to each other in the
13720151 resulting MRO, their ordering depends on the order of types in *abcs*.

13742426 Parser for command line options.
13742460 This module helps scripts to parse the command line arguments in
13742525 sys.argv.  It supports the same conventions as the Unix getopt()
13742590 function (including the special meanings of arguments of the form `-'
13742660 and `--').  Long options similar to those supported by GNU software
13742728 may be used as well via an optional third argument.  This module
13742793 provides two functions and an exception:
13742835 getopt() -- Parse command line options
13742874 gnu_getopt() -- Like getopt(), but allow option and non-option arguments
13742947 to be intermixed.
13742965 GetoptError -- exception (class) raised with 'opt' attribute, which is the
13743040 option involved with the exception.
13743080 GetoptError
13743093 error

13744328 getopt(args, options[, long_options]) -> opts, args
13744381 Parses command line options and parameter list.  args is the
13744442 argument list to be parsed, without the leading reference to the
13744507 running program.  Typically, this means "sys.argv[1:]".  shortopts
13744574 is the string of option letters that the script wants to
13744631 recognize, with options that require an argument followed by a
13744694 colon (i.e., the same format that Unix getopt() uses).  If
13744753 specified, longopts is a list of strings with the names of the
13744816 long options which should be supported.  The leading '--'
13744874 characters should not be included in the option name.  Options
13744937 which require an argument should be followed by an equal sign
13744999 ('=').
13745007 The return value consists of two elements: the first is a list of
13745073 (option, value) pairs; the second is the list of program arguments
13745140 left after the option list was stripped (this is a trailing slice
13745206 of the first argument).  Each option-and-value pair returned has
13745271 the option as its first element, prefixed with a hyphen (e.g.,
13745334 '-x'), and the option argument as its second element, or an empty
13745400 string if the option has no argument.  The options occur in the
13745464 list in the same order in which they were found, thus allowing
13745527 multiple occurrences.  Long and short options may be mixed.

13781119 Return a list of paths matching a `pathname` pattern.
13781174 The pattern may contain simple shell-style wildcards a la
13781232 fnmatch. Unlike fnmatch, filenames starting with a
13781283 dot are special cases that are not matched by '*' and '?'
13781341 patterns by default.
13781363 The order of the returned list is undefined. Sort it if you need a
13781430 particular order.
13781449 If `root_dir` is not None, it should be a path-like object specifying
13781519 the root directory for searching.  It has the same effect as changing
13781589 the current directory before calling it (without actually changing it).
13781661 If pathname is relative, the result will contain paths relative to
13781728 `root_dir`.
13781741 If `dir_fd` is not None, it should be a file descriptor referring to a
13781812 directory, and paths will then be relative to that directory.
13781875 If `include_hidden` is true, the patterns '*', '?', '**'  will match
13781944 hidden directories.
13781965 If `recursive` is true, the pattern '**' will match any files and
13782031 zero or more directories and subdirectories.

13805858 Subclass of ValueError raised by TopologicalSorter.prepare if cycles
13805927 exist in the working graph.
13805956 If multiple cycles exist, only one undefined choice among them will be reported
13806036 and included in the exception. The detected cycle can be accessed via the second
13806117 element in the *args* attribute of the exception instance and consists in a list
13806198 of nodes, such that each node is, in the graph, an immediate predecessor of the
13806278 next node in the list. In the reported list, the first and the last node will be
13806359 the same, to make it clear that it is cyclic.

13807738 Add a new node and its predecessors to the graph.
13807789 Both the *node* and all elements in *predecessors* must be hashable.
13807859 If called multiple times with the same node argument, the set of dependencies
