15655221 OpcodeInfo.__init__d
15655646 Push an integer or bool.
15655672       The argument is a newline-terminated decimal literal string.
15655740       The intent may have been that this always fit in a short Python int,
15655815       but INT can be generated in pickles written on a 64-bit box that
15655886       require a Python long on a 32-bit box.  The difference between this
15655960       and LONG then is that INT skips a trailing 'L', and produces a short
15656035       int whenever possible.
15656065       Another difference is due to that, when bool was introduced as a
15656136       distinct type in 2.3, builtin names True and False were also added to
15656212       2.2.2, mapping to ints 1 and 0.  For compatibility in both directions,
15656289       True gets pickled as INT + "I01\n", and False as INT + "I00\n".
15656359       Leading zeroes are never produced for a genuine integer.  The 2.3
15656431       (and later) unpicklers special-case these and return bool instead;
15656504       earlier unpicklers ignore the leading "0" and return the int.
15656572       r
15656585 BININT
15656599 Push a four-byte signed integer.
15656633       This handles the full range of Python (short) integers on a 32-bit
15656706       box, directly as binary bytes (1 for the opcode and 4 for the integer).
15656784       If the integer is non-negative and fits in 1 or 2 bytes, pickling via
15656860       BININT1 or BININT2 saves space.
15656898       
15656906 BININT1
15656918 Push a one-byte unsigned integer.
15656953       This is a space optimization for pickling very small non-negative ints,
15657031       in range(256).
15657052       
15657060 BININT2
15657072 Push a two-byte unsigned integer.
15657107       This is a space optimization for pickling small positive ints, in
15657179       range(256, 2**16).  Integers in range(256) can also be pickled via
15657252       BININT2, but BININT1 instead saves a byte.
15657301       
15657321 Push a long integer.
15657343       The same as INT, except that the literal ends with 'L', and always
15657416       unpickles to a Python long.  There doesn't seem a real purpose to the
15657492       trailing 'L'.
15657513       Note that LONG takes time quadratic in the number of digits when
15657584       unpickling (this is simply due to the nature of decimal->binary
15657654       conversion).  Proto 2 added linear-time (in C; still quadratic-time
15657728       in Python) LONG1 and LONG4 opcodes.
15657770       
15657778 LONG1
15657790 z|Long integer using one-byte length.
15657829       A more efficient encoding of a Python long; the long1 encoding
15657898       says it all.
15657918 LONG4
15657930 z}Long integer using four-byte length.
15657970       A more efficient encoding of a Python long; the long4 encoding
15658039       says it all.
15658059 STRING
15658073 Push a Python string object.
15658103       The argument is a repr-style string, with bracketing quote characters,
15658180       and perhaps embedded escapes.  The argument extends until the next
15658253       newline character.  These are usually decoded into a str instance
15658325       using the encoding given to the Unpickler constructor. or the default,
15658402       'ASCII'.  If the encoding given was 'bytes' however, they will be
15658474       decoded as bytes object instead.
15658513       
15658520 	BINSTRING
15658538 Push a Python string object.
15658568       There are two arguments: the first is a 4-byte little-endian
15658635       signed int giving the number of bytes in the string, and the
15658702       second is that many bytes, which are taken literally as the string
15658775       content.  These are usually decoded into a str instance using the
15658847       encoding given to the Unpickler constructor. or the default,
15658914       'ASCII'.  If the encoding given was 'bytes' however, they will be
15658986       decoded as bytes object instead.
15659025       
15659033 SHORT_BINSTRING
15659056 Push a Python string object.
15659086       There are two arguments: the first is a 1-byte unsigned int giving
15659159       the number of bytes in the string, and the second is that many
15659228       bytes, which are taken literally as the string content.  These are
15659301       usually decoded into a str instance using the encoding given to
15659371       the Unpickler constructor. or the default, 'ASCII'.  If the
15659437       encoding given was 'bytes' however, they will be decoded as bytes
15659509       object instead.

15661920       
15661928 FLOAT
15661941 Newline-terminated decimal float literal.
15661984       The argument is repr(a_float), and in general requires 17 significant
15662060       digits for roundtrip conversion to be an identity (this is so for
15662132       IEEE-754 double precision values, which is what Python float maps to
15662207       on most boxes).
15662230       In general, FLOAT cannot be used to transport infinities, NaNs, or
15662303       minus zero across boxes (or even on a single box, if the platform C
15662377       library can't read the strings it produces for such things -- Windows
15662453       is like that), but may do less damage than BINFLOAT on boxes with
15662525       greater precision or dynamic range than IEEE-754 double.
15662588       
15662596 BINFLOAT
15662612 Float stored in binary form, with 8 bytes of data.
15662664       This generally requires less than half the space of FLOAT encoding.
15662738       In general, BINFLOAT cannot be used to transport infinities, NaNs, or
15662814       minus zero, raises an exception if the exponent exceeds the range of
15662889       an IEEE-754 double, and retains no more than 53 bits of precision (if
15662965       there are more than that, "add a half and chop" rounding is used to
15663039       cut it back to 53 significant bits).

15669626       
15669650 Extension code.
15669667       This code and the similar EXT2 and EXT4 allow using a registry
15669736       of popular objects that are pickled by name, typically classes.
15669806       It is envisioned that through a global negotiation and
15669867       registration process, third parties can set up a mapping between
15669938       ints and object names.
15669968       In order to guarantee pickle interchangeability, the extension
15670037       code registry ought to be global, although a range of codes may
15670107       be reserved for private use.
15670143       EXT1 has a 1-byte integer argument.  This is used to index into the
15670217       extension registry, and the object at that index is pushed on the stack.
15670296       
15670315 zNExtension code.
15670334       See EXT1.  EXT2 has a two-byte integer argument.
15670389       
15670408 zOExtension code.
15670427       See EXT1.  EXT4 has a four-byte integer argument.
15670483       
15670491 GLOBAL
15670505 Push a global object (module.attr) on the stack.
15670555       Two newline-terminated strings follow the GLOBAL opcode.  The first is
15670632       taken as a module name, and the second as a class name.  The class
15670705       object module.class is pushed on the stack.  More accurately, the
15670777       object returned by self.find_class(module, class) is pushed on the
15670850       stack, so unpickling subclasses can override this form of lookup.
15670922       
15670930 STACK_GLOBAL
15670949 z7Push a global object (module.attr) on the stack.
15671000       
15671008 REDUCE
15671022 Push an object built from a callable and an argument tuple.
15671083       The opcode is named to remind of the __reduce__() method.
15671148       Stack before: ... callable pytuple
15671189       Stack after:  ... callable(*pytuple)
15671233       The callable and the argument tuple are the first two items returned
15671308       by a __reduce__ method.  Applying the callable to the argtuple is
15671380       supposed to reproduce the original object, or at least get it started.
15671457       If the __reduce__ method returns a 3-tuple, the last component is an
15671532       argument to be passed to the object's __setstate__, and then the REDUCE
15671610       opcode is followed by code to create setstate's argument, and then a
15671685       BUILD opcode to apply  __setstate__ to that argument.
15671746       If not isinstance(callable, type), REDUCE complains unless the
15671815       callable has been registered with the copyreg module's
15671876       safe_constructors dict, or the callable has a magic
15671934       '__safe_for_unpickling__' attribute with a true value.  I'm not sure
15672009       why it does this, but I've sure seen this complaint often enough when
15672085       I didn't want to <wink>.
15672116       
15672124 BUILD
15672137 Finish building an object, via __setstate__ or dict update.
15672198       Stack before: ... anyobject argument
15672241       Stack after:  ... anyobject
15672276       where anyobject may have been mutated, as follows:
15672334       If the object has a __setstate__ method,
15672382           anyobject.__setstate__(argument)
15672426       is called.
15672444       Else the argument must be a dict, the object must have a __dict__, and
15672521       the object is updated via
15672554           anyobject.__dict__.update(argument)
15672600       
15672620 Build a class instance.
15672645       This is the protocol 0 version of protocol 1's OBJ opcode.
15672710       INST is followed by two newline-terminated strings, giving a
15672777       module and class name, just as for the GLOBAL opcode (and see
15672845       GLOBAL for more details about that).  self.find_class(module, name)
15672919       is used to get a class object.
15672957       In addition, all the objects on the stack following the topmost
15673027       markobject are gathered into a tuple and popped (along with the
15673097       topmost markobject), just as for the TUPLE opcode.
15673155       Now it gets complicated.  If all of these are true:
15673214         + The argtuple is empty (markobject was at the top of the stack
15673286           at the start).
15673312         + The class object does not have a __getinitargs__ attribute.
15673383       then we want to create an old-style class instance without invoking
15673457       its __init__() method (pickle has waffled on this over the years; not
15673533       calling __init__() is current wisdom).  In this case, an instance of
15673608       an old-style dummy class is created, and then we try to rebind its
15673681       __class__ attribute to the desired class object.  If this succeeds,
15673755       the new instance object is pushed on the stack, and we're done.
15673826       Else (the argtuple is not empty, it's not an old-style class object,
15673901       or the class object does have a __getinitargs__ attribute), the code
15673976       first insists that the class object have a __safe_for_unpickling__
15674049       attribute.  Unlike as for the __safe_for_unpickling__ check in REDUCE,
15674126       it doesn't matter whether this attribute has a true or false value, it
15674203       only matters whether it exists (XXX this is a bug).  If
15674265       __safe_for_unpickling__ doesn't exist, UnpicklingError is raised.
15674338       Else (the class object does have a __safe_for_unpickling__ attr),
15674410       the class object obtained from INST's arguments is applied to the
15674482       argtuple obtained from the stack, and the resulting instance object
15674556       is pushed on the stack.
15674587       NOTE:  checks for __safe_for_unpickling__ went away in Python 2.3.
15674660       NOTE:  the distinction between old-style and new-style classes does
15674734              not make sense in Python 3.
15674775       
15674794 Build a class instance.
15674819       This is the protocol 1 version of protocol 0's INST opcode, and is
15674892       very much like it.  The major difference is that the class object
15674964       is taken off the stack, allowing it to be retrieved from the memo
15675036       repeatedly if several instances of the same class are created.  This
15675111       can be much more efficient (in both time and space) than repeatedly
15675185       embedding the module and class names in INST opcodes.
15675246       Unlike INST, OBJ takes no arguments from the opcode stream.  Instead
15675321       the class object is taken off the stack, immediately above the
15675390       topmost markobject:
15675417       Stack before: ... markobject classobject stackslice
15675475       Stack after:  ... new_instance_object
15675520       As for INST, the remainder of the stack above the markobject is
15675590       gathered into an argument tuple, and then the logic seems identical,
15675665       except that no __safe_for_unpickling__ check is done (XXX this is
15675737       a bug).  See INST for the gory details.
15675784       NOTE:  In Python 2.3, INST and OBJ are identical except for how they
15675859       get the class object.  That was always the intent; the implementations
15675936       had diverged for accidental reasons.
15675979       
15675987 NEWOBJ

15676168       top).  Call these cls and args.  They are popped off the stack,
15676238       and the value returned by cls.__new__(cls, *args) is pushed back
15676309       onto the stack.

15681410 Generate all the opcodes in a pickle.
15681449 'pickle' is a file-like object, or string, containing the pickle.
15681516 Each opcode in the pickle is generated, from the current pickle position,
15681590 stopping after a STOP opcode is delivered.  A triple is generated for
15681660 each opcode:
15681674     opcode, arg, pos
15681696 opcode is an OpcodeInfo record, describing the current opcode.
15681760 If the opcode has an argument embedded in the pickle, arg is its decoded
15681833 value, as a Python object.  If the opcode doesn't have an argument, arg
15681905 is None.
15681915 If the pickle has a tell() method, pos was the value of pickle.tell()
15681985 before reading the current opcode.  If the pickle is a bytes object,
15682054 it's wrapped in a BytesIO object, and the latter's tell() result is
15682122 used.  Else (the pickle doesn't have a tell(), and it's not obvious how
15682194 to query its current position) pos is None.

15686530 Produce a symbolic disassembly of a pickle.
15686575 'pickle' is a file-like object, or string, containing a (at least one)
15686646 pickle.  The pickle is disassembled from the current position, through
15686717 the first STOP opcode encountered.
15686753 Optional arg 'out' is a file-like object to which the disassembly is
15686822 printed.  It defaults to sys.stdout.
15686860 Optional arg 'memo' is a Python dict, used as the pickle's memo.  It
15686929 may be mutated by dis(), if the pickle contains PUT or BINPUT opcodes.
15687000 Passing the same memo object to another dis() call then allows disassembly
15687075 to proceed across multiple pickles that were all created by the same
15687144 pickler with the same memo.  Ordinarily you don't need to worry about this.
15687221 Optional arg 'indentlevel' is the number of blanks by which to indent
15687291 a new MARK level.  It defaults to 4.
15687329 Optional arg 'annotate' if nonzero instructs dis() to add short
15687393 description of the opcode on each line of disassembled output.
15687456 The value given to 'annotate' must be an integer and is used as a
15687522 hint for the column where annotation should start.  The default
15687586 value is 0, meaning no annotations.
15687623 In addition to printing the disassembly, some sanity checks are made:
15687694 + All embedded opcode arguments "make sense".
15687741 + Explicit and implicit pop operations have enough items on the stack.
15687813 + When an opcode implicitly refers to a markobject, a markobject is
15687881   actually on the stack.
15687907 + A memo entry isn't referenced before it's defined.
15687961 + The markobject isn't stored in the memo.
15688005 + A memo entry isn't redefined.

15717102 Extend a package's path.
15717128 Intended use is to place the following code in a package's __init__.py:
15717201     from pkgutil import extend_path
15717237     __path__ = extend_path(__path__, __name__)
15717285 For each directory on sys.path that has a subdirectory that
15717345 matches the package name, add the subdirectory to the package's
15717409 __path__.  This is useful if one wants to distribute different
15717472 parts of a single logical package as multiple directories.
15717532 It also looks for *.pkg files beginning where * matches the name
15717597 argument.  This feature is similar to *.pth files (see site.py),
15717662 except that it doesn't special-case lines starting with 'import'.
15717728 A *.pkg file is trusted at face value: apart from checking for
15717791 duplicates, all entries found in a *.pkg file are added to the
15717854 path, regardless of whether they are exist the filesystem.  (This
15717920 is a feature.)
15717936 If the input path is not a list (as is the case for frozen
15717995 packages) it is returned unchanged.  The input path is not
15718054 modified; an extended copy is returned.  Items are only appended
15718119 to the copy at the end.
15718144 It is assumed that sys.path is a sequence.  Items of sys.path that
15718211 are not (unicode or 8-bit) strings referring to existing
15718268 directories are ignored.  Unicode items of sys.path that cause
15718331 errors when used as filenames may cause this function to raise an
15718397 exception (in line with os.path.isdir() behavior).

15719960 Get a resource from a package.
15719992 This is a wrapper round the PEP 302 loader get_data API. The package
15720061 argument should be the name of a package, in standard module format
15720129 (foo.bar). The resource argument should be in the form of a relative
15720198 filename, using '/' as the path separator. The parent directory name '..'
15720272 is not allowed, and nor is a rooted name (starting with a '/').
15720337 The function returns a binary string, which is the contents of the
15720404 specified resource.
15720425 For packages located in the filesystem, which have already been imported,
15720499 this is the rough equivalent of
15720532     d = os.path.dirname(sys.modules[package].__file__)
15720587     data = open(os.path.join(d, resource), 'rb').read()
15720644 If the package cannot be located or loaded, or it uses a PEP 302 loader
15720716 which does not support get_data(), then None is returned.

15721978 Resolve a name to an object.
15722008 It is expected that `name` will be a string in one of the following
15722076 formats, where W is shorthand for a valid Python identifier and dot stands
15722151 for a literal period in these pseudo-regexes:
15722198 W(.W)*
15722205 W(.W)*:(W(.W)*)?
15722223 The first form is intended for backward compatibility only. It assumes that
15722299 some part of the dotted name is a package, and the rest is an object
15722368 somewhere within that package, possibly nested inside other objects.
15722437 Because the place where the package stops and the object hierarchy starts
15722511 can't be inferred by inspection, repeated attempts to import must be done
15722585 with this form.
15722602 In the second form, the caller makes the division point clear through the
15722676 provision of a single colon: the dotted name to the left of the colon is a
15722751 package to be imported, and the dotted name to the right is the object
15722822 hierarchy within that package. Only one import is needed in this form. If
15722896 it ends with the colon, then a module object is returned.
15722955 The function will return an object (which might be a module), or raise one
15723030 of the following exceptions:
15723060 ValueError - if `name` isn't in a recognised format
15723112 ImportError - if an import failed when it shouldn't have
15723169 AttributeError - if a failure occurred when traversing the object hierarchy
15723245                  within the imported package to get to the desired object.
15723328 (?!\d)(\w+)(\.(?!\d)(\w+))*z	^(?P<pkg>z
15723368 )(?P<cln>:(?P<obj>z
15723388 )?)?$z

15747656 Queries the given executable (defaults to the Python interpreter
15747721 binary) for various architecture information.
15747768 Returns a tuple (bits, linkage) which contains information about
15747833 the bit architecture and the linkage format used for the
15747890 executable. Both values are returned as strings.
15747940 Values that cannot be determined are returned as given by the
15748002 parameter presets. If bits is given as '', the sizeof(pointer)
15748065 (or sizeof(long) on Python version < 1.5.2) is used as
15748120 indicator for the supported pointer size.
15748163 The function relies on the system's "file" command to do the
15748224 actual work. This is available on most if not all Unix
15748279 platforms. On some non-Unix platforms where the "file" command
15748342 does not exist and the executable is set to the Python interpreter
15748409 binary defaults from _default_architecture are used.

15770223 This class supports both the minimal and optional command sets.
15770287 Arguments can be strings or integers (where appropriate)
15770344 (e.g.: retr(1) and retr('1') both work equally well.
15770398 Minimal Command Set:
15770419         USER name               user(name)
15770462         PASS string             pass_(string)
15770508         STAT                    stat()
15770547         LIST [msg]              list(msg = None)
15770596         RETR msg                retr(msg)
15770638         DELE msg                dele(msg)
15770680         NOOP                    noop()
15770719         RSET                    rset()
15770758         QUIT                    quit()
15770798 Optional Commands (some servers support these):
15770846         RPOP name               rpop(name)
15770889         APOP name digest        apop(name, digest)
15770940         TOP msg n               top(msg, n)
15770984         UIDL [msg]              uidl(msg = None)
15771033         CAPA                    capa()
15771072         STLS                    stls()
15771111         UTF8                    utf8()
15771151 Raises one exception: 'error_proto'.
15771189 Instantiate with:
15771207         POP3(hostname, port=110)
15771241 NB:     the POP protocol locks the mailbox from user
15771294         authorization until QUIT, so be sure to get in, suck
15771355         the messages, and quit, each time you access the
15771412         mailbox.
15771430         POP is a line-based protocol, which means large mail
15771491         messages consume lots of python cycles reading them
15771551         line-by-line.
15771574         If it's available on your mail server, use IMAP4
15771631         instead, it doesn't suffer from the two problems
15771688         above.

15837231 z0Class for keeping track of an item in inventory.
15837283 total_tt
15837293 func_profilesr+
15837336 __doc__rB
15837680 This class is used for creating reports from data generated by the
15837747 Profile class.  It is a "friend" of that class, and imports data either
15837819 by direct access to members of Profile class, or by reading in a dictionary
15837895 that was emitted (via marshal) from the Profile class.
15837951 The big change from the previous Profiler (in terms of raw functionality)
15838025 is that an "add()" method has been provided to combine Stats from
15838091 several distinct profile runs.  Both the constructor and the add()
15838158 method now take arbitrarily many file names as arguments.
15838217 All the print methods now take an argument that indicates how many lines
15838290 to print.  If the arg is a floating-point number between 0 and 1.0, then
15838363 it is taken as a decimal percentage of the available lines to be printed
15838436 (e.g., .1 means print 10% of all available lines).  If it is an integer,
15838509 it is taken to mean the number of lines of data that you wish to have
15838579 printed.
15838589 The sort_stats() method now processes some additional options (i.e., in
15838661 addition to the old -1, 0, 1, or 2 that are respectively interpreted as
15838733 'stdname', 'calls', 'time', and 'cumulative').  It takes either an
15838800 arbitrary number of quoted strings or SortKey enum to select the sort
15838870 order.
15838878 For example sort_stats('time', 'name') or sort_stats(SortKey.TIME,
15838945 SortKey.NAME) sorts on the major key of 'internal function time', and on
15839018 the minor key of 'the name of the function'.  Look at the two tables in
15839090 sort_stats() and get_sort_arg_defs(self) for more examples.
15839151 All methods return self, so you can string together commands like:
15839218     Stats('foo', 'goo').strip_dirs().sort_stats('calls').                            print_stats(5).print_callers(5)

15883822 n	U	R
15884745 Byte-compile one Python source file to Python bytecode.
15884802 :param file: The source file name.
15884837 :param cfile: The target byte compiled file name.  When not given, this
15884909     defaults to the PEP 3147/PEP 488 location.
15884956 :param dfile: Purported file name, i.e. the file name that shows up in
15885027     error messages.  Defaults to the source file name.
15885082 :param doraise: Flag indicating whether or not an exception should be
15885152     raised when a compile error is found.  If an exception occurs and this
15885227     flag is set to False, a string indicating the nature of the exception
15885301     will be printed, and the function will return to the caller. If an
15885372     exception occurs and this flag is set to True, a PyCompileError
15885440     exception will be raised.
15885470 :param optimize: The optimization level for the compiler.  Valid values
15885542     are -1, 0, 1 and 2.  A value of -1 means to use the optimization
15885611     level of the current interpreter, as given by -O command line options.
15885686 :param invalidation_mode:
15885712 :param quiet: Return full output with False or 0, errors only with 1,
15885782     and no output with 2.
15885809 :return: Path to the resulting byte compiled file.
15885861 Note that it isn't necessary to byte-compile Python modules for
15885925 execution efficiency -- Python itself byte-compiles a module when
15885991 it is loaded, and if it can, writes out the bytecode to the
15886051 corresponding .pyc file.
15886077 However, if a Python installation is shared between users, it is a
15886144 good idea to byte-compile all modules upon installation, since
15886207 other users may not be able to write in the source directories,
15886271 and thus they won't be able to write the .pyc file, and then
15886332 they would be byte-compiling every module each time it is loaded.
15886398 This can slow down program start-up considerably.
15886449 See compileall.py for a script/module that uses this module to
15886512 byte-compile all installed files (or all files in selected
15886571 directories).
15886586 Do note that FileExistsError is raised if cfile ends up pointing at a
15886656 non-regular file or symlink. Because the compilation uses a file renaming,
15886731 the resulting file would be regular and thus not the same type of file as
15886805 it was previously.
15886844 optimizationzc{} is a symlink and will be changed into a regular file if import writes a byte-compiled file to itzk{} is a non-regular file and will be changed into a regular one if import writes a byte-compiled file to itz

15890043 Enumr
15890089 <module>r
15890510 Parse a Python module and describe its classes and functions.
15890573 Parse enough of a Python file to recognize imports and class and
15890638 function definitions, and to find out the superclasses of a class.
15890706 The interface consists of a single function:
15890751     readmodule_ex(module, path=None)
15890788 where module is the name of a Python module, and path is an optional
15890857 list of directories where the module is to be searched.  If present,
15890926 path is prepended to the system search path sys.path.  The return value
15890998 is a dictionary.  The keys of the dictionary are the names of the
15891064 classes and functions defined in the module (including classes that are
15891136 defined via the from XXX import YYY construct).  The values are
15891200 instances of classes Class and Function.  One special key/value pair is
15891272 present for packages: the key '__path__' has a list as its value which
15891343 contains the package search path.
15891378 Classes and Functions have a common superclass: _Object.  Every instance
15891451 has the following attributes:
15891481     module  -- name of the module;
15891516     name    -- name of the object;
15891551     file    -- file in which the object is defined;
15891603     lineno  -- line in the file where the object's definition starts;
15891673     end_lineno -- line in the file where the object's definition ends;
15891744     parent  -- parent of this object, if any;
15891790     children -- nested objects contained in this object.
15891847 The 'children' attribute is a dictionary mapping names to objects.
15891915 Instances of Function describe functions with the attributes from _Object,
15891990 plus the following:
15892010     is_async -- if a function is defined with an 'async' prefix
15892075 Instances of Class describe classes with the attributes from _Object,
15892145 plus the following:
15892165     super   -- list of super classes (Class instances if possible);
15892233     methods -- mapping of method names to beginning line numbers.
15892299 If the name of a super class is not recognized, the corresponding
15892365 entry in the list of super classes is not a class instance but a
15892430 string giving the name of the super class.  Since import statements
15892498 are recognized and imported modules are scanned as well, this
15892560 shouldn't happen often.
15892594 readmodule
15892606 readmodule_ex

15944462 countsc
15945425 Chooses k unique random elements from a population sequence.
15945487 Returns a new list containing elements from the population while
15945552 leaving the original population unchanged.  The resulting list is
15945618 in selection order so that all sub-slices will also be valid random
15945686 samples.  This allows raffle winners (the sample) to be partitioned
15945754 into grand prize and second place winners (the subslices).
15945814 Members of the population need not be hashable or unique.  If the
15945880 population contains repeats, then each occurrence is a possible
15945944 selection in the sample.
15945970 Repeated elements can be specified one at a time or with the optional
15946040 counts parameter.  For example:
15946073     sample(['red', 'blue'], counts=[4, 2], k=5)
15946122 is equivalent to:
15946141     sample(['red', 'red', 'red', 'red', 'blue', 'blue'], k=5)
15946204 To choose a sample from a range of integers, use range() for the
15946269 population argument.  This is especially fast and space efficient
15946335 for sampling from a large population:
15946374     sample(range(10000000), 60)
15946407 zAPopulation must be a sequence.  For dicts or sets, use sorted(d).Nz2The number of counts does not match the populationr
15946534 Counts must be integersz

15968151 \"\,\(5
15968206 Support for regular expressions (RE).
15968245 This module provides regular expression matching operations similar to
15968316 those found in Perl.  It supports both 8-bit and Unicode strings; both
15968387 the pattern and the strings being processed can contain null bytes and
15968458 characters outside the US ASCII range.
15968498 Regular expressions can contain both special and ordinary characters.
15968568 Most ordinary characters, like "A", "a", or "0", are the simplest
15968634 regular expressions; they simply match themselves.  You can
15968694 concatenate ordinary characters, so last matches the string 'last'.
15968763 The special characters are:
15968791     "."      Matches any character except a newline.
15968844     "^"      Matches the start of the string.
15968890     "$"      Matches the end of the string or just before the newline at
15968963              the end of the string.
15968999     "*"      Matches 0 or more (greedy) repetitions of the preceding RE.
15969072              Greedy means that it will match as many repetitions as possible.
15969150     "+"      Matches 1 or more (greedy) repetitions of the preceding RE.
15969223     "?"      Matches 0 or 1 (greedy) of the preceding RE.
15969281     *?,+?,?? Non-greedy versions of the previous three special characters.
15969356     {m,n}    Matches from m to n repetitions of the preceding RE.
15969422     {m,n}?   Non-greedy version of the above.
15969468     "\\"     Either escapes special characters or signals a special sequence.
15969546     []       Indicates a set of characters.
15969590              A "^" as the first character indicates a complementing set.
15969663     "|"      A|B, creates an RE that will match either A or B.
15969726     (...)    Matches the RE inside the parentheses.
15969778              The contents can be retrieved or matched later in the string.
15969853     (?aiLmsux) The letters set the corresponding flags defined below.
15969923     (?:...)  Non-grouping version of regular parentheses.
15969981     (?P<name>...) The substring matched by the group is accessible by name.
15970057     (?P=name)     Matches the text matched earlier by the group named name.
15970133     (?#...)  A comment; ignored.
15970166     (?=...)  Matches if ... matches next, but doesn't consume the string.
15970240     (?!...)  Matches if ... doesn't match next.
15970288     (?<=...) Matches if preceded by ... (must be fixed length).
15970352     (?<!...) Matches if not preceded by ... (must be fixed length).
15970420     (?(id/name)yes|no) Matches yes pattern if the group with id/name matched,
15970498                        the (optional) no pattern otherwise.
15970559 The special sequences consist of "\\" and a character from the list
15970627 below.  If the ordinary character is not on the list, then the
15970690 resulting RE will match the second character.
15970736     \number  Matches the contents of the group of the same number.
15970803     \A       Matches only at the start of the string.
15970857     \Z       Matches only at the end of the string.
15970909     \b       Matches the empty string, but only at the start or end of a word.
15970988     \B       Matches the empty string, but not at the start or end of a word.
15971066     \d       Matches any decimal digit; equivalent to the set [0-9] in
15971137              bytes patterns or string patterns with the ASCII flag.
15971205              In string patterns without the ASCII flag, it will match the whole
15971285              range of Unicode digits.
15971323     \D       Matches any non-digit character; equivalent to [^\d].
15971390     \s       Matches any whitespace character; equivalent to [ \t\n\r\f\v] in
15971468              bytes patterns or string patterns with the ASCII flag.
15971536              In string patterns without the ASCII flag, it will match the whole
15971616              range of Unicode whitespace characters.
15971669     \S       Matches any non-whitespace character; equivalent to [^\s].
15971741     \w       Matches any alphanumeric character; equivalent to [a-zA-Z0-9_]
15971817              in bytes patterns or string patterns with the ASCII flag.
15971888              In string patterns without the ASCII flag, it will match the
15971962              range of Unicode alphanumeric characters (letters plus digits
15972037              plus underscore).
15972068              With LOCALE, it will match the set [0-9_] plus characters defined
15972147              as letters for the current locale.
15972195     \W       Matches the complement of \w.
15972238     \\       Matches a literal backslash.
15972281 This module exports the following functions:
15972326     match     Match a regular expression pattern to the beginning of a string.
15972405     fullmatch Match a regular expression pattern to all of a string.
15972474     search    Search a string for the presence of a pattern.
15972535     sub       Substitute occurrences of a pattern found in a string.
15972604     subn      Same as sub, but also return the number of substitutions made.
15972681     split     Split a string by the occurrences of a pattern.
15972743     findall   Find all occurrences of a pattern in a string.
15972804     finditer  Return an iterator yielding a Match object for each match.
15972877     compile   Compile a pattern into a Pattern object.
15972932     purge     Clear the regular expression cache.
15972982     escape    Backslash all non-alphanumerics in a string.
15973042 Each function other than purge and escape can take an optional 'flags' argument
15973122 consisting of one or more of the following module constants, joined by "|".
15973198 A, L, and U are mutually exclusive.
15973234     A  ASCII       For string patterns, make \w, \W, \b, \B, \d, \D
15973302                    match the corresponding ASCII character categories
15973372                    (rather than the whole Unicode categories, which is the
15973447                    default).
15973476                    For bytes patterns, this flag is the only available
15973547                    behaviour and needn't be specified.
15973602     I  IGNORECASE  Perform case-insensitive matching.
15973656     L  LOCALE      Make \w, \W, \b, \B, dependent on the current locale.
15973729     M  MULTILINE   "^" matches the beginning of lines (after a newline)
15973801                    as well as the string.
15973843                    "$" matches the end of lines (before a newline) as well
15973918                    as the end of the string.
15973963     S  DOTALL      "." matches any character at all, including the newline.
15974039     X  VERBOSE     Ignore whitespace and comments for nicer looking RE's.
15974113     U  UNICODE     For compatibility only. Ignored for string patterns (it
15974188                    is the default), and forbidden for bytes patterns.
15974259 This module also defines exception 'PatternError', aliased to 'error' for
15974333 backward compatibility.

16075256 <module>r
16075632 Word completion for GNU readline.
16075667 The completer completes keywords, built-ins and globals in a selectable
16075739 namespace (which defaults to __main__); when completing NAME.NAME..., it
16075812 evaluates (!) the expression up to the last dot and completes its attributes.
16075891 It's very cool to do "import sys" type "sys.", hit the completion key (twice),
16075970 and see the list of names defined by the sys module!
16076024 Tip: to use the tab key as the completion key, call
16076077     readline.parse_and_bind("tab: complete")
16076123 Notes:
16076131 - Exceptions raised by the completer function are *ignored* (and generally cause
16076212   the completion to fail).  This is a feature -- since readline sets the tty
16076289   device in raw (or cbreak) mode, printing a traceback wouldn't work well
16076363   without some complicated hoopla to save, reset and restore the tty state.
16076440 - The evaluation of the NAME.NAME... form may cause arbitrary application
16076514   defined code to be executed if an object with a __getattr__ hook is found.
16076591   Since it is the responsibility of the application (or the user) to enable this
16076672   feature, I consider this an acceptable risk.  More complicated expressions
16076749   (e.g. function calls or indexing operations) are *not* evaluated.
16076818 - When the original stdin is not a tty device, GNU readline is never
16076887   used, and this module (and the readline module) are silently inactive.
16076968 	Completerc
16077234 Create a new completer for the command line.
16077280 Completer([namespace]) -> completer instance.
16077327 If unspecified, the default namespace where completions are performed
16077397 is __main__ (technically, __main__.__dict__). Namespaces should be
16077464 given as dictionaries.
16077488 Completer instances should be used as the completion mechanism of
16077554 readline via the set_completer() call:
16077594 readline.set_completer(Completer(my_namespace).complete)
16077653 namespace must be a dictionaryN
16077698 isinstance
16077715 	TypeError
16077727 use_main_ns
16077739 	namespace)
16077753 selfr
16077771 rlcompleter.py
16077787 __init__
16077797 Completer.__init__,
16078435 Return the next possible completion for 'text'.
16078484 This is called successively with state == 0, 1, 2, ... until it
16078548 returns None.  The completion should begin with 'text'.

16098513 <module>r
16099153 A generally useful event scheduler class.
16099196 Each instance of this class manages its own queue.
16099247 No multi-threading is implied; you are supposed to hack that
16099308 yourself, or use a single instance per application.
16099361 Each instance is parametrized with two functions, one that is
16099423 supposed to return the current time, one that is supposed to
16099484 implement a delay.  You can implement real-time scheduling by
16099546 substituting time and sleep from built-in module time, or you can
16099612 implement simulated time by writing your own functions.  This can
16099678 also be used to integrate scheduling with STDWIN events; the delay
16099745 function is allowed to modify the queue.  Time can be expressed as
16099812 integers or floating-point numbers, as long as it is consistent.
16099878 Events are specified by tuples (time, priority, action, argument, kwargs).
16099953 As in UNIX, lower priority numbers mean higher priority; in this
16100018 way the queue can be maintained as a priority queue.  Execution of the
16100089 event means calling the action function, passing it the argument
16100154 sequence in "argument" (remember that in Python, multiple function
16100221 arguments are be packed in a sequence) and keyword parameters in "kwargs".
16100296 The action function may be an instance method so it
16100348 has another way to reference private data (besides global variables).
16100428 namedtuple)
16100442 count)

16100762     separates events if time and priority are equal.z?Executing the event means executing

16103404 scheduler.emptyb
16103890 Execute events until the queue is empty.
16103931 If blocking is False executes the scheduled events due to
16103989 expire soonest (if any) and then return the deadline of the
16104049 next scheduled call in the scheduler.
16104088 When there is a positive delay until the first event, the
16104146 delay function is called and the event is left in the queue;
16104207 otherwise, the event is removed from the queue and executed
16104267 (its action function is called, passing it the argument).  If
16104329 the delay function returns prematurely, it is simply
16104382 restarted.
16104394 It is legal for both the delay function and the action
16104449 function to modify the queue or to raise an exception;
16104504 exceptions are not caught but the scheduler's state remains
16104564 well-defined so run() may be called again.
16104608 A questionable hack is added to allow other threads to run:
16104668 just after an event is executed, a delay of 0 is executed, to
16104730 avoid monopolizing the CPU when other threads are also
16104785 runnable.

16112916 BaseSelector
16112938 Selector abstract base class.
16112969 A selector supports registering file objects to be monitored for specific
16113043 I/O events.
16113056 A file object is a file descriptor or any object with a `fileno()` method.
16113131 An arbitrary object can be attached to the file object, which can be used
16113205 for example to store context information, a callback, etc.
16113265 A selector can use various implementations (select(), poll(), epoll()...)
16113339 depending on the platform. The default `Selector` class uses the most
16113409 efficient implementation on the current platform.
16113507 Register a file object.

16113691 SelectorKey instance

16113856         the underlying system call (if a system call is made)

16173457 Recursively copy a directory tree and return the destination directory.
16173530 If exception(s) occur, an Error is raised with a list of reasons.
16173597 If the optional symlinks flag is true, symbolic links in the
16173658 source tree result in symbolic links in the destination tree; if
16173723 it is false, the contents of the files pointed to by symbolic
16173785 links are copied. If the file pointed to by the symlink doesn't
16173849 exist, an exception will be added in the list of errors raised in
16173915 an Error exception at the end of the copy process.
16173967 You can set the optional ignore_dangling_symlinks flag to true if you
16174037 want to silence this exception. Notice that this has no effect on
16174103 platforms that don't support os.symlink.
16174145 The optional ignore argument is a callable. If given, it
16174202 is called with the `src` parameter, which is the directory
16174261 being visited by copytree(), and `names` which is the list of
16174323 `src` contents, as returned by os.listdir():
16174369     callable(src, names) -> ignored_names
16174412 Since copytree() is called recursively, the callable will be
16174473 called once for each directory that is copied. It returns a
16174533 list of names relative to the `src` directory that should
16174591 not be copied.
16174607 The optional copy_function argument is a callable that will be used
16174675 to copy each file. It will be called with the source path and the
16174741 destination path as arguments. By default, copy2() is used, but any
16174809 function that supports the same signature (like copy()) can be used.
16174879 If dirs_exist_ok is false (the default) and `dst` already exists, a
16174947 `FileExistsError` is raised. If `dirs_exist_ok` is true, the copying
16175016 operation will continue if it encounters existing directories, and files
16175089 within the `dst` tree will be overwritten by corresponding files from the
16175163 `src` tree.

16223477 This module provides socket operations and some related functions.
16223544 On Unix, it supports IP (Internet Protocol) and Unix domain sockets.
16223613 On other systems, it only supports IP. Functions specific for a
16223677 socket are available as methods of the socket object.
16223732 Functions:
16223744 socket() -- create a new socket object
16223783 socketpair() -- create a pair of new socket objects [*]
16223839 fromfd() -- create a socket object from an open file descriptor [*]
16223907 send_fds() -- Send file descriptor to the socket.
16223957 recv_fds() -- Receive file descriptors from the socket.
16224013 fromshare() -- create a socket object from data received from socket.share() [*]
16224094 gethostname() -- return the current hostname
16224139 gethostbyname() -- map a hostname to its IP number
16224190 gethostbyaddr() -- map an IP number or hostname to DNS info
16224250 getservbyname() -- map a service name and a protocol name to a port number
16224325 getprotobyname() -- map a protocol name (e.g. 'tcp') to a number
16224390 ntohs(), ntohl() -- convert 16, 32 bit int from network to host byte order
16224465 htons(), htonl() -- convert 16, 32 bit int from host to network byte order
16224540 inet_aton() -- convert IP addr string (123.45.67.89) to 32-bit packed format
16224617 inet_ntoa() -- convert 32-bit packed format IP to string (123.45.67.89)
16224689 socket.getdefaulttimeout() -- get the default timeout value
16224749 socket.setdefaulttimeout() -- set the default timeout value
16224809 create_connection() -- connects to an address, with an optional timeout and
16224885                        optional source address.
16224933 create_server() -- create a TCP socket and bind it to a specified address.
16225009  [*] not available on all platforms!

16240623 sendfile(file[, offset[, count]]) -> sent
16240666 Send a file until EOF is reached by using high-performance
16240725 os.sendfile() and return the total number of bytes which
16240782 were sent.
16240793 *file* must be a regular file object opened in binary mode.
16240853 If os.sendfile() is not available (e.g. Windows) or file is
16240913 not a regular file socket.send() will be used instead.
16240968 *offset* tells from where to start reading the file.

16241084 as opposed to sending the file until EOF is reached.

16241200 which case file.tell() can be used to figure out the number of
16241263 bytes which were sent.

16260812 Resolve host and port into list of address info entries.

16260944 all the necessary arguments for creating a socket connected to that service.
16261021 host is a domain name, a string representation of an IPv4/v6 address or

16264501 S1\#5
16264545 S5\#5
16264568 Generic socket server classes.
16264600 This module tries to capture the various aspects of defining a server:
16264672 For socket-based servers:
16264699 - address family:
16264717         - AF_INET{,6}: IP (Internet Protocol) sockets (default)
16264781         - AF_UNIX: Unix domain sockets
16264820         - others, e.g. AF_DECNET are conceivable (see <socket.h>
16264885 - socket type:
16264900         - SOCK_STREAM (reliable stream, e.g. TCP)
16264950         - SOCK_DGRAM (datagrams, e.g. UDP)
16264994 For request-based servers (including socket-based):
16265047 - client address verification before further looking at the request
16265115         (This is actually a hook for any processing that needs to look
16265186          at the request before anything else, e.g. logging)
16265246 - how to handle multiple requests:
16265281         - synchronous (one request is handled at a time)
16265338         - forking (each request is handled by a new process)
16265399         - threading (each request is handled by a new thread)
16265462 The classes in this module favor the server type that is simplest to
16265531 write: a synchronous TCP/IP server.  This is bad class design, but
16265598 saves some typing.  (There's also the issue that a deep class hierarchy
16265670 slows down method lookups.)
16265699 There are five classes in an inheritance diagram, four of which represent
16265773 synchronous servers of four types:
16265809         +------------+
16265832         | BaseServer |
16265855         +------------+
16265878               |
16265894               v
16265910         +-----------+        +------------------+
16265960         | TCPServer |------->| UnixStreamServer |
16266010         +-----------+        +------------------+
16266060               |
16266076               v
16266092         +-----------+        +--------------------+
16266144         | UDPServer |------->| UnixDatagramServer |
16266196         +-----------+        +--------------------+
16266249 Note that UnixDatagramServer derives from UDPServer, not from
16266311 UnixStreamServer -- the only difference between an IP and a Unix
16266376 stream server is the address family, which is simply repeated in both
16266446 unix server classes.
16266468 Forking and threading versions of each type of server can be created
16266537 using the ForkingMixIn and ThreadingMixIn mix-in classes.  For
16266600 instance, a threading UDP server class is created as follows:
16266663         class ThreadingUDPServer(ThreadingMixIn, UDPServer): pass
16266730 The Mix-in class must come first, since it overrides a method defined
16266800 in UDPServer! Setting the various member variables also changes
16266864 the behavior of the underlying server mechanism.
16266914 To implement a service, you must derive a class from
16266967 BaseRequestHandler and redefine its handle() method.  You can then run
16267038 various versions of the service by combining one of the server classes
16267109 with your request handler class.
16267143 The request handler class must be different for datagram or stream
16267210 services.  This can be hidden by using the request handler
16267269 subclasses StreamRequestHandler or DatagramRequestHandler.
16267329 Of course, you still have to use your head!
16267374 For instance, it makes no sense to use a forking server if the service
16267445 contains state in memory that can be modified by requests (since the
16267514 modifications in the child process would never reach the initial state
16267585 kept in the parent process and passed to each child).  In this case,
16267654 you can use a threading server, but you will probably have to use
16267720 locks to avoid two requests that come in nearly simultaneous to apply
16267790 conflicting changes to the server state.
16267832 On the other hand, if you are building e.g. an HTTP server, where all
16267902 data is stored externally (e.g. in the file system), a synchronous
16267969 class will essentially render the service "deaf" while one request is
16268039 being handled -- which may be for a very long time if a client is slow
16268110 to read all the data it has requested.  Here a threading or forking
16268178 server is appropriate.
16268202 In some cases, it may be appropriate to process part of a request
16268268 synchronously, but to finish processing in a forked child depending on
16268339 the request data.  This can be implemented by using a synchronous
16268405 server and doing an explicit fork in the request handler class
16268468 handle() method.
16268486 Another approach to handling multiple simultaneous requests in an
16268552 environment that supports neither threads nor fork (or where these are
16268623 too expensive or inappropriate for the service) is to maintain an
16268689 explicit table of partially finished requests and to use a selector to
16268760 decide which request to work on next (or whether to handle a new
16268825 incoming request).  This is particularly important for stream services
16268896 where each client can potentially be connected for a long time (if
16268963 threads or subprocesses cannot be used).
16269005 Future work:
16269018 - Standard classes for Sun RPC (which uses either UDP or TCP)
16269080 - Standard mix-in classes to implement various authentication
16269142   and encryption schemes
16269168 XXX Open problems:
16269187 - What to do with out-of-band data?
16269224 BaseServer:
16269236 - split generic "request" functionality out into BaseServer class.
16269303   Copyright (C) 2000  Luke Kenneth Casson Leighton <lkcl@samba.org>
16269372   example: read entries from a SQL database (requires overriding
16269437   get_request() to return a table entry from the database).
16269497   entry is processed by a RequestHandlerClass.

16292140 Base class for request handler classes.
16292181 This class is instantiated for each request to be handled.  The
16292245 constructor sets the instance variables request, client_address
16292309 and server, and then calls the handle() method.  To implement a
16292373 specific service, all you need to do is to derive a class which
16292437 defines a handle() method.
16292465 The handle() method can find the request as self.request, the
16292527 client address as self.client_address, and the server (in case it
16292593 needs access to per-server information) as self.server.  Since a
16292658 separate instance is created for each request, the handle() method
16292725 can define other arbitrary instance variables.

16322657 TLS message callback
16322679 The message callback provides a debugging hook to analyze TLS
16322741 connections. The callback is called for any TLS protocol message
16322806 (header, handshake, alert, and more), but not for application data.
16322874 Due to technical  limitations, the callback can't be used to filter
16322942 traffic or to abort a connection. Any exception raised in the
16323004 callback is delayed until the handshake, read, or write operation
16323070 has been performed.

16330606 	SSLObjecti
16330626 This class implements an interface on top of a low-level SSL object as
16330697 implemented by OpenSSL. This object captures the state of an SSL connection
16330773 but does not provide any network IO itself. IO needs to be performed
16330842 through separate "BIO" objects which are OpenSSL's IO abstraction layer.
16330916 This class does not have a public constructor. Instances are returned by
16330989 ``SSLContext.wrap_bio``. This class is typically used by framework authors
16331064 that want to implement asynchronous IO for SSL through memory buffers.
16331136 When compared to ``SSLSocket``, this object lacks the following features:
16331211  * Any form of network IO, including methods such as ``recv`` and ``send``.
16331287  * The ``do_handshake_on_connect`` and ``suppress_ragged_eofs`` machinery.
16331460 NzU does not have a public constructor. Instances are returned by SSLContext.wrap_bio().

16371828 Basic statistics module.
16371854 This module provides functions for calculating statistics of data, including
16371931 averages, variance, and standard deviation.
16371976 Calculating averages
16371997 --------------------
16372019 ==================  ==================================================
16372090 Function            Description
16372122 ==================  ==================================================
16372193 mean                Arithmetic mean (average) of data.
16372248 fmean               Fast, floating-point arithmetic mean.
16372306 geometric_mean      Geometric mean of data.
16372350 harmonic_mean       Harmonic mean of data.
16372393 median              Median (middle value) of data.
16372444 median_low          Low median of data.
16372484 median_high         High median of data.
16372525 median_grouped      Median, or 50th percentile, of grouped data.
16372590 mode                Mode (most common value) of data.
16372644 multimode           List of modes (most common values of data).
16372708 quantiles           Divide data into intervals with equal probability.
16372779 ==================  ==================================================
16372851 Calculate the arithmetic mean ("the average") of data:
16372907 >>> mean([-1.0, 2.5, 3.25, 5.75])
16372941 2.625
16372949 Calculate the standard median of discrete data:
16372998 >>> median([2, 3, 4, 5])
16373029 Calculate the median, or 50th percentile, of data grouped into class intervals
16373108 centred on the data values provided. E.g. if your data points are rounded to
16373185 the nearest whole number:
16373212 >>> median_grouped([2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4])  #doctest: +ELLIPSIS
16373272 2.8333333333...
16373289 This should be interpreted in this way: you have two data points in the class
16373367 interval 1.5-2.5, three data points in the class interval 2.5-3.5, and one in
16373445 the class interval 3.5-4.5. The median of these data points is 2.8333...
16373520 Calculating variability or spread
16373554 ---------------------------------
16373589 ==================  =============================================
16373655 Function            Description
16373687 ==================  =============================================
16373753 pvariance           Population variance of data.
16373802 variance            Sample variance of data.
16373847 pstdev              Population standard deviation of data.
16373906 stdev               Sample standard deviation of data.
16373961 ==================  =============================================
16374028 Calculate the standard deviation of sample data:
16374078 >>> stdev([2.5, 3.25, 5.5, 11.25, 11.75])  #doctest: +ELLIPSIS
16374141 4.38961843444...
16374159 If you have previously calculated the mean, you can pass it as the optional
16374235 second argument to the four "spread" functions to avoid recalculating it:
16374310 >>> data = [1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6]
16374346 >>> mu = mean(data)
16374366 >>> pvariance(data, mu)
16374396 Statistics for relations between two inputs
16374440 -------------------------------------------
16374485 ==================  ====================================================
16374558 Function            Description
16374590 ==================  ====================================================
16374663 covariance          Sample covariance for two variables.
16374720 correlation         Pearson's correlation coefficient for two variables.
16374793 linear_regression   Intercept and slope for simple linear regression.
16374863 ==================  ====================================================
16374937 Calculate covariance, Pearson's correlation, and simple linear regression
16375011 for two inputs:
16375028 >>> x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
16375064 >>> y = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]
16375100 >>> covariance(x, y)
16375126 >>> correlation(x, y)  #doctest: +ELLIPSIS
16375169 0.31622776601...
16375186 >>> linear_regression(x, y)  #doctest:
16375225 LinearRegression(slope=0.1, intercept=1.5)

16376527 _sum(data) -> (type, sum, count)
16376561 Return a high-precision sum of the given numeric data as a fraction,
16376630 together with the type to be converted to and the count of items.
16376697 Examples
16376706 --------
16376716 >>> _sum([3, 2.25, 4.5, -0.5, 0.25])
16376753 (<class 'float'>, Fraction(19, 2), 5)
16376792 Some sources of round-off error will be avoided:
16376842 # Built-in sum returns zero.
16376871 >>> _sum([1e50, 1, -1e50] * 1000)
16376905 (<class 'float'>, Fraction(1000, 1), 3000)
16376949 Fractions and Decimals are also supported:
16376993 >>> from fractions import Fraction as F
16377033 >>> _sum([F(2, 3), F(7, 5), F(1, 4), F(5, 6)])
16377080 (<class 'fractions.Fraction'>, Fraction(63, 20), 4)
16377133 >>> from decimal import Decimal as D
16377170 >>> data = [D("0.1375"), D("0.2108"), D("0.3061"), D("0.0419")]
16377234 >>> _sum(data)
16377249 (<class 'decimal.Decimal'>, Fraction(6963, 10000), 4)
16377304 Mixed types are currently treated as an error, except that int is
16377370 allowed.

16383676 Rank order a dataset. The lowest value has rank 1.
16383728 Ties are averaged so that equal values receive the same rank:
16383791     >>> data = [31, 56, 31, 25, 75, 18]
16383831     >>> _rank(data)
16383851     [3.5, 5.0, 3.5, 2.0, 6.0, 1.0]
16383887 The operation is idempotent:
16383917     >>> _rank([3.5, 5.0, 3.5, 2.0, 6.0, 1.0])
16383963     [3.5, 5.0, 3.5, 2.0, 6.0, 1.0]

16384060 highest value has rank 1.  Also, a key-function can extract
16384120 the field to be ranked:
16384145     >>> goals = [('eagles', 45), ('bears', 48), ('lions', 44)]

16384262     [2.0, 1.0, 3.0]

16394818 Estimates the median for numeric data binned around the midpoints
16394884 of consecutive, fixed-width intervals.
16394924 The *data* can be any iterable of numeric data with each value being
16394993 exactly the midpoint of a bin.  At least one value must be present.
16395062 The *interval* is width of each bin.
16395100 For example, demographic information may have been summarized into
16395167 consecutive ten-year age groups with each group being represented
16395233 by the 5-year midpoints of the intervals:
16395276     >>> demographics = Counter({
16395309     ...    25: 172,   # 20 to 30 years old
16395352     ...    35: 484,   # 30 to 40 years old
16395395     ...    45: 387,   # 40 to 50 years old
16395438     ...    55:  22,   # 50 to 60 years old
16395481     ...    65:   6,   # 60 to 70 years old
16395524     ... })
16395536 The 50th percentile (median) is the 536th person out of the 1071
16395601 member cohort.  That person is in the 30 to 40 year old age group.
16395669 The regular median() function would assume that everyone in the
16395733 tricenarian age group was exactly 35 years old.  A more tenable
16395797 assumption is that the 484 members of that age group are evenly
16395861 distributed between 30 and 40.  For that, we use median_grouped().
16395929     >>> data = list(demographics.elements())
16395974     >>> median(data)
16395995     35
16396002     >>> round(median_grouped(data, interval=10), 1)
16396054     37.5
16396064 The caller is responsible for making sure the data points are separated
16396136 by exact multiples of *interval*.  This is essential for getting a
16396203 correct result.  The function does not check this precondition.
16396268 Inputs may be any numeric type that can be coerced to a float during
16396337 the interpolation step.
16396376 loz$Value cannot be converted to a floatr9

16398430 cumulativec
16399142 O7S&:X
16399459 Kernel Density Estimation:  Create a continuous probability density
16399527 function or cumulative distribution function from discrete samples.
16399596 The basic idea is to smooth the data using a kernel function
16399657 to help draw inferences about a population from a sample.
16399716 The degree of smoothing is controlled by the scaling parameter h
16399781 which is called the bandwidth.  Smaller values emphasize local
16399844 features while larger values give smoother results.
16399897 The kernel determines the relative weights of the sample data
16399959 points.  Generally, the choice of kernel shape does not matter
16400022 as much as the more influential bandwidth smoothing parameter.
16400086 Kernels that give some weight to every sample point:
16400140    normal (gauss)
16400158    logistic
16400170    sigmoid
16400182 Kernels that only give weight to sample points within
16400236 the bandwidth:
16400252    rectangular (uniform)
16400277    triangular
16400291    parabolic (epanechnikov)
16400319    quartic (biweight)
16400341    triweight
16400354    cosine
16400365 If *cumulative* is true, will return a cumulative distribution function.
16400439 A StatisticsError will be raised if the data sequence is empty.
16400504 Example
16400512 -------
16400521 Given a sample of six data points, construct a continuous
16400579 function that estimates the underlying probability density:
16400640     >>> sample = [-2.1, -1.3, -0.4, 1.9, 5.1, 6.2]
16400691     >>> f_hat = kde(sample, h=1.5)
16400727 Compute the area under the curve:
16400762     >>> area = sum(f_hat(x) for x in range(-20, 20))
16400815     >>> round(area, 4)
16400838     1.0
16400847 Plot the estimated probability density function at
16400898 evenly spaced points from -6 to 10:
16400935     >>> for x in range(-6, 11):
16400967     ...     density = f_hat(x)
16400998     ...     plot = ' ' * int(density * 400) + 'x'
16401048     ...     print(f'{x:2}: {density:.3f} {plot}')
16401098     ...
16401106     -6: 0.002 x
16401122     -5: 0.009    x
16401141     -4: 0.031             x
16401169     -3: 0.070                             x
16401213     -2: 0.111                                             x
16401273     -1: 0.125                                                   x
16401339      0: 0.110                                            x
16401398      1: 0.086                                   x
16401448      2: 0.068                            x
16401491      3: 0.059                        x
16401530      4: 0.066                           x
16401572      5: 0.082                                 x
16401620      6: 0.082                                 x
16401668      7: 0.058                        x
16401707      8: 0.028            x
16401734      9: 0.009    x
16401753     10: 0.002 x
16401770 Estimate P(4.5 < X <= 7.5), the probability that a new sample value
16401838 will be between 4.5 and 7.5:
16401868     >>> cdf = kde(sample, h=1.5, cumulative=True)
16401918     >>> round(cdf(7.5) - cdf(4.5), 2)
16401956     0.22
16401966 References

16402036 https://www.itm-conferences.org/articles/itmconf/pdf/2018/08/itmconf_sam2018_00037.pdf

16402156 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_(statistics)#kernel_functions_in_common_use

16419751 Slope and intercept for simple linear regression.
16419802 Return the slope and intercept of simple linear regression
16419861 parameters estimated using ordinary least squares. Simple linear
16419926 regression describes relationship between an independent variable
16419992 *x* and a dependent variable *y* in terms of a linear function:
16420057     y = slope * x + intercept + noise
16420096 where *slope* and *intercept* are the regression parameters that are
16420165 estimated, and noise represents the variability of the data that was
16420234 not explained by the linear regression (it is equal to the
16420293 difference between predicted and actual values of the dependent
16420357 variable).
16420369 The parameters are returned as a named tuple.
16420416 >>> x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
16420440 >>> noise = NormalDist().samples(5, seed=42)
16420485 >>> y = [3 * x[i] + 2 + noise[i] for i in range(5)]
16420537 >>> linear_regression(x, y)  #doctest: +ELLIPSIS
16420586 LinearRegression(slope=3.17495..., intercept=1.00925...)
16420644 If *proportional* is true, the independent variable *x* and the
16420708 dependent variable *y* are assumed to be directly proportional.
16420772 The data is fit to a line passing through the origin.
16420827 Since the *intercept* will always be 0.0, the underlying linear
16420891 function simplifies to:
16420916     y = slope * x + noise
16420943 >>> y = [3 * x[i] + noise[i] for i in range(5)]
16420991 >>> linear_regression(x, y, proportional=True)  #doctest: +ELLIPSIS
16421059 LinearRegression(slope=2.90475..., intercept=0.0)

16493908 The arguments are the same as for the Popen constructor.  Example:
16493976 >>> check_output(["ls", "-l", "/dev/null"])
16494020 b'crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 1, 3 Oct 18  2007 /dev/null\n'
16494077 The stdout argument is not allowed as it is used internally.
16494138 To capture standard error in the result, use stderr=STDOUT.
16494199 >>> check_output(["/bin/sh", "-c",
16494234 ...               "ls -l non_existent_file ; exit 0"],
16494289 ...              stderr=STDOUT)
16494321 b'ls: non_existent_file: No such file or directory\n'
16494376 There is an additional optional argument, "input", allowing you to
16494443 pass a string to the subprocess's stdin.  If you use this argument
16494510 you may not also use the Popen constructor's "stdin" argument, as
16494576 it too will be used internally.  Example:
16494619 >>> check_output(["sed", "-e", "s/foo/bar/"],
16494665 ...              input=b"when in the course of fooman events\n")
16494730 b'when in the course of barman events\n'
16494772 By default, all communication is in bytes, and therefore any "input"
16494841 should be bytes, and the return value will be bytes.  If in text mode,
16494912 any "input" should be a string, and the return value will be a string
16494982 decoded according to locale encoding, or by "encoding" if set. Text mode
16495055 is triggered by setting any of text, encoding, errors or universal_newlines.

16501121 Translate a sequence of arguments into a command line
16501175 string, using the same rules as the MS C runtime:
16501226 1) Arguments are delimited by white space, which is either a
16501287    space or a tab.
16501307 2) A string surrounded by double quotation marks is
16501359    interpreted as a single argument, regardless of white space
16501422    contained within.  A quoted string can be embedded in an
16501482    argument.
16501496 3) A double quotation mark preceded by a backslash is
16501550    interpreted as a literal double quotation mark.
16501602 4) Backslashes are interpreted literally, unless they
16501656    immediately precede a double quotation mark.
16501705 5) If backslashes immediately precede a double quotation mark,
16501768    every pair of backslashes is interpreted as a literal
16501825    backslash.  If the number of backslashes is odd, the last
16501886    backslash escapes the next double quotation mark as
16501941    described in rule 3.

16680372 z=The TarFile Class provides an interface to tar archives.
16680431     r
16682345 Open an (uncompressed) tar archive `name'. `mode' is either 'r' to
16682412 read from an existing archive, 'a' to append data to an existing
16682477 file or 'w' to create a new file overwriting an existing one. `mode'
16682546 defaults to 'r'.
16682563 If `fileobj' is given, it is used for reading or writing data. If it
16682632 can be determined, `mode' is overridden by `fileobj's mode.
16682692 `fileobj' is not closed, when TarFile is closed.
16682780 !mode must be 'r', 'a', 'w' or 'x'r

16683291 TarFile.__init__
16684073  A"M*
16685207 Open a tar archive for reading, writing or appending. Return
16685268 an appropriate TarFile class.
16685299 mode:
16685305 'r' or 'r:*' open for reading with transparent compression
16685364 'r:'         open for reading exclusively uncompressed
16685419 'r:gz'       open for reading with gzip compression
16685471 'r:bz2'      open for reading with bzip2 compression
16685524 'r:xz'       open for reading with lzma compression
16685576 'a' or 'a:'  open for appending, creating the file if necessary
16685640 'w' or 'w:'  open for writing without compression
16685690 'w:gz'       open for writing with gzip compression
16685742 'w:bz2'      open for writing with bzip2 compression
16685795 'w:xz'       open for writing with lzma compression
16685848 'x' or 'x:'  create a tarfile exclusively without compression, raise
16685917              an exception if the file is already created
16685974 'x:gz'       create a gzip compressed tarfile, raise an exception
16686040              if the file is already created
16686084 'x:bz2'      create a bzip2 compressed tarfile, raise an exception
16686151              if the file is already created
16686195 'x:xz'       create an lzma compressed tarfile, raise an exception

16738309 Temporary files.
16738327 This module provides generic, low- and high-level interfaces for
16738392 creating temporary files and directories.  All of the interfaces
16738457 provided by this module can be used without fear of race conditions

16748906 z&Private accessor for tempfile.tempdir.)
16748990 _gettempdirr
16749186 z Returns tempfile.tempdir as str.)
16749385 z"Returns tempfile.tempdir as bytes.)
16749608 User-callable function to create and return a unique temporary
16749671 file.  The return value is a pair (fd, name) where fd is the
16749732 file descriptor returned by os.open, and name is the filename.
16749796 If 'suffix' is not None, the file name will end with that suffix,
16749862 otherwise there will be no suffix.
16749898 If 'prefix' is not None, the file name will begin with that prefix,
16749966 otherwise a default prefix is used.
16750003 If 'dir' is not None, the file will be created in that directory,
16750069 otherwise a default directory is used.
16750109 If 'text' is specified and true, the file is opened in text
16750169 mode.  Else (the default) the file is opened in binary mode.
16750231 If any of 'suffix', 'prefix' and 'dir' are not None, they must be the
16750301 same type.  If they are bytes, the returned name will be bytes; str
16750369 otherwise.
16750381 The file is readable and writable only by the creating user ID.
16750445 If the operating system uses permission bits to indicate whether a
16750512 file is executable, the file is executable by no one. The file

16778431 Text wrapping and filling.
16778468 TextWrapper
16778493 dedent
16778501 indent
16778509 shortenz
16778968 Object for wrapping/filling text.  The public interface consists of
16779036 the wrap() and fill() methods; the other methods are just there for
16779104 subclasses to override in order to tweak the default behaviour.
16779168 If you want to completely replace the main wrapping algorithm,
16779231 you'll probably have to override _wrap_chunks().
16779281 Several instance attributes control various aspects of wrapping:
16779346   width (default: 70)
16779368     the maximum width of wrapped lines (unless break_long_words
16779432     is false)
16779446   initial_indent (default: "")
16779477     string that will be prepended to the first line of wrapped
16779540     output.  Counts towards the line's width.
16779586   subsequent_indent (default: "")
16779620     string that will be prepended to all lines save the first
16779682     of wrapped output; also counts towards each line's width.
16779744   expand_tabs (default: true)
16779774     Expand tabs in input text to spaces before further processing.
16779841     Each tab will become 0 .. 'tabsize' spaces, depending on its position
16779915     in its line.  If false, each tab is treated as a single character.
16779986   tabsize (default: 8)
16780009     Expand tabs in input text to 0 .. 'tabsize' spaces, unless
16780072     'expand_tabs' is false.
16780100   replace_whitespace (default: true)
16780137     Replace all whitespace characters in the input text by spaces
16780203     after tab expansion.  Note that if expand_tabs is false and
16780267     replace_whitespace is true, every tab will be converted to a
16780332     single space!
16780350   fix_sentence_endings (default: false)
16780390     Ensure that sentence-ending punctuation is always followed
16780453     by two spaces.  Off by default because the algorithm is
16780513     (unavoidably) imperfect.
16780542   break_long_words (default: true)
16780577     Break words longer than 'width'.  If false, those words will not
16780646     be broken, and some lines might be longer than 'width'.
16780706   break_on_hyphens (default: true)
16780741     Allow breaking hyphenated words. If true, wrapping will occur
16780807     preferably on whitespaces and right after hyphens part of
16780869     compound words.
16780889   drop_whitespace (default: true)
16780923     Drop leading and trailing whitespace from lines.
16780976   max_lines (default: None)
16781004     Truncate wrapped lines.
16781032   placeholder (default: ' [...]')
16781066     Append to the last line of truncated text.

16787934 _wrap_chunks(chunks : [string]) -> [string]
16787979 Wrap a sequence of text chunks and return a list of lines of
16788040 length 'self.width' or less.  (If 'break_long_words' is false,
16788103 some lines may be longer than this.)  Chunks correspond roughly
16788167 to words and the whitespace between them: each chunk is
16788223 indivisible (modulo 'break_long_words'), but a line break can

16788473 lines, but apart from that whitespace is preserved.

16802147 Acquire a lock, blocking or non-blocking.
16802190 When invoked without arguments: if this thread already owns the lock,
16802260 increment the recursion level by one, and return immediately. Otherwise,
16802333 if another thread owns the lock, block until the lock is unlocked. Once
16802405 the lock is unlocked (not owned by any thread), then grab ownership, set
16802478 the recursion level to one, and return. If more than one thread is
16802545 blocked waiting until the lock is unlocked, only one at a time will be
16802616 able to grab ownership of the lock. There is no return value in this
16802685 case.
16802692 When invoked with the blocking argument set to true, do the same thing
16802763 as when called without arguments, and return true.
16802815 When invoked with the blocking argument set to false, do not block. If a
16802888 call without an argument would block, return false immediately;
16802952 otherwise, do the same thing as when called without arguments, and
16803019 return true.
16803033 When invoked with the floating-point timeout argument set to a positive
16803105 value, block for at most the number of seconds specified by timeout
16803173 and as long as the lock cannot be acquired.  Return true if the lock has
16803246 been acquired, false if the timeout has elapsed.
