16814995 Acquire a semaphore, decrementing the internal counter by one.
16815059 When invoked without arguments: if the internal counter is larger than
16815130 zero on entry, decrement it by one and return immediately. If it is zero
16815203 on entry, block, waiting until some other thread has called release() to
16815276 make it larger than zero. This is done with proper interlocking so that
16815348 if multiple acquire() calls are blocked, release() will wake exactly one
16815421 of them up. The implementation may pick one at random, so the order in
16815492 which blocked threads are awakened should not be relied on. There is no
16815564 return value in this case.
16815592 When invoked with blocking set to true, do the same thing as when called
16815665 without arguments, and return true.
16815702 When invoked with blocking set to false, do not block. If a call without
16815775 an argument would block, return false immediately; otherwise, do the
16815844 same thing as when called without arguments, and return true.
16815907 When invoked with a timeout other than None, it will block for at
16815973 most timeout seconds.  If acquire does not complete successfully in
16816041 that interval, return false.  Return true otherwise.

16859643 Tool for measuring execution time of small code snippets.
16859702 This module avoids a number of common traps for measuring execution
16859770 times.  See also Tim Peters' introduction to the Algorithms chapter in
16859841 the Python Cookbook, published by O'Reilly.
16859886 Library usage: see the Timer class.
16859923 Command line usage:
16859943     python timeit.py [-n N] [-r N] [-s S] [-p] [-h] [--] [statement]
16860013 Options:
16860022   -n/--number N: how many times to execute 'statement' (default: see below)
16860098   -r/--repeat N: how many times to repeat the timer (default 5)
16860162   -s/--setup S: statement to be executed once initially (default 'pass').
16860236                 Execution time of this setup statement is NOT timed.
16860305   -p/--process: use time.process_time() (default is time.perf_counter())
16860378   -v/--verbose: print raw timing results; repeat for more digits precision
16860453   -u/--unit: set the output time unit (nsec, usec, msec, or sec)
16860518   -h/--help: print this usage message and exit
16860565   --: separate options from statement, use when statement starts with -
16860637   statement: statement to be timed (default 'pass')
16860690 A multi-line statement may be given by specifying each line as a
16860755 separate argument; indented lines are possible by enclosing an
16860818 argument in quotes and using leading spaces.  Multiple -s options are
16860888 treated similarly.
16860908 If -n is not given, a suitable number of loops is calculated by trying
16860979 increasing numbers from the sequence 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, ... until the
16861051 total time is at least 0.2 seconds.
16861088 Note: there is a certain baseline overhead associated with executing a
16861159 pass statement.  It differs between versions.  The code here doesn't try
16861232 to hide it, but you should be aware of it.  The baseline overhead can be
16861305 measured by invoking the program without arguments.

16862073 Class for timing execution speed of small code snippets.
16862131 The constructor takes a statement to be timed, an additional
16862192 statement used for setup, and a timer function.  Both statements
16862257 default to 'pass'; the timer function is platform-dependent (see
16862322 module doc string).  If 'globals' is specified, the code will be
16862387 executed within that namespace (as opposed to inside timeit's
16862449 namespace).

16862524 timeit() method.  The repeat() method is a convenience to call
16862587 timeit() multiple times and return a list of results.

16865882 Timer.timeit
16866170 Call timeit() a few times.
16866198 This is a convenience function that calls the timeit()
16866253 repeatedly, returning a list of results.  The first argument
16866314 specifies how many times to call timeit(), defaulting to 5;
16866374 the second argument specifies the timer argument, defaulting
16866435 to one million.
16866452 Note: it's tempting to calculate mean and standard deviation
16866513 from the result vector and report these.  However, this is not
16866576 very useful.  In a typical case, the lowest value gives a
16866634 lower bound for how fast your machine can run the given code
16866695 snippet; higher values in the result vector are typically not
16866757 caused by variability in Python's speed, but by other
16866811 processes interfering with your timing accuracy.  So the min()
16866874 of the result is probably the only number you should be
16866930 interested in.  After that, you should look at the entire
16866988 vector and apply common sense rather than statistics.

16878906 Tokenization help for Python programs.
16878946 tokenize(readline) is a generator that breaks a stream of bytes into
16879015 Python tokens.  It decodes the bytes according to PEP-0263 for
16879078 determining source file encoding.
16879113 It accepts a readline-like method which is called repeatedly to get the
16879185 next line of input (or b"" for EOF).  It generates 5-tuples with these
16879256 members:
16879266     the token type (see token.py)
16879300     the token (a string)
16879325     the starting (row, column) indices of the token (a 2-tuple of ints)
16879397     the ending (row, column) indices of the token (a 2-tuple of ints)
16879467     the original line (string)
16879499 It is designed to match the working of the Python tokenizer exactly, except
16879575 that it produces COMMENT tokens for comments and gives type OP for all
16879646 operators.  Additionally, all token lists start with an ENCODING token
16879717 which tells you which encoding was used to decode the bytes stream.
16879787 Ka-Ping Yee <ping@lfw.org>zpGvR, ESR, Tim Peters, Thomas Wouters, Fred Drake, Skip Montanaro, Raymond Hettinger, Trent Nelson, Michael Foord

16889360 Untokenizer.compat
16890136 Transform tokens back into Python source code.
16890183 It returns a bytes object, encoded using the ENCODING
16890237 token, which is the first token sequence output by tokenize.
16890299 Each element returned by the iterable must be a token sequence
16890362 with at least two elements, a token number and token value.  If
16890426 only two tokens are passed, the resulting output is poor.
16890485 The result is guaranteed to tokenize back to match the input so
16890549 that the conversion is lossless and round-trips are assured.
16890610 The guarantee applies only to the token type and token string as
16890675 the spacing between tokens (column positions) may change.

16891895 The detect_encoding() function is used to detect the encoding that should
16891969 be used to decode a Python source file.  It requires one argument, readline,
16892046 in the same way as the tokenize() generator.
16892092 It will call readline a maximum of twice, and return the encoding used
16892163 (as a string) and a list of any lines (left as bytes) it has read in.
16892234 It detects the encoding from the presence of a utf-8 bom or an encoding
16892306 cookie as specified in pep-0263.  If both a bom and a cookie are present,
16892380 but disagree, a SyntaxError will be raised.  If the encoding cookie is an
16892454 invalid charset, raise a SyntaxError.  Note that if a utf-8 bom is found,
16892528 'utf-8-sig' is returned.
16892554 If no encoding is specified, then the default of 'utf-8' will be returned.

16894955      r
16895355 The tokenize() generator requires one argument, readline, which
16895419 must be a callable object which provides the same interface as the
16895486 readline() method of built-in file objects.  Each call to the function
16895557 should return one line of input as bytes.  Alternatively, readline
16895624 can be a callable function terminating with StopIteration:
16895683     readline = open(myfile, 'rb').__next__  # Example of alternate readline
16895760 The generator produces 5-tuples with these members: the token type; the
16895832 token string; a 2-tuple (srow, scol) of ints specifying the row and
16895900 column where the token begins in the source; a 2-tuple (erow, ecol) of
16895971 ints specifying the row and column where the token ends in the source;
16896042 and the line on which the token was found.  The line passed is the
16896109 physical line.
16896125 The first token sequence will always be an ENCODING token
16896183 which tells you which encoding was used to decode the bytes stream.

17012860 _ExceptionPrintContext.emit
17013356 An exception ready for rendering.
17013391 The traceback module captures enough attributes from the original exception
17013467 to this intermediary form to ensure that no references are held, while
17013538 still being able to fully print or format it.
17013585 max_group_width and max_group_depth control the formatting of exception
17013657 groups. The depth refers to the nesting level of the group, and the width
17013731 refers to the size of a single exception group's exceptions array. The
17013802 formatted output is truncated when either limit is exceeded.
17013864 Use `from_exception` to create TracebackException instances from exception
17013939 objects, or the constructor to create TracebackException instances from
17014011 individual components.
17014035 - :attr:`__cause__` A TracebackException of the original *__cause__*.
17014105 - :attr:`__context__` A TracebackException of the original *__context__*.
17014179 - :attr:`exceptions` For exception groups - a list of TracebackException
17014252   instances for the nested *exceptions*.  ``None`` for other exceptions.
17014325 - :attr:`__suppress_context__` The *__suppress_context__* value from the
17014398   original exception.
17014420 - :attr:`stack` A `StackSummary` representing the traceback.
17014481 - :attr:`exc_type` (deprecated) The class of the original traceback.

17076774 DynamicClassAttribute
17076805 Route attribute access on a class to __getattr__.
17076856 This is a descriptor, used to define attributes that act differently
17076925 when accessed through an instance and through a class.  Instance access
17076997 remains normal, but access to an attribute through a class will be
17077064 routed to the class's __getattr__ method; this is done by raising
17077130 AttributeError.
17077147 This allows one to have properties active on an instance, and have
17077214 virtual attributes on the class with the same name.  (Enum used this
17077283 between Python versions 3.4 - 3.9 .)
17077321 Subclass from this to use a different method of accessing virtual
17077387 attributes and still be treated properly by the inspect module.  (Enum

17091004 The typing module: Support for gradual typing as defined by PEP 484 and subsequent PEPs.
17091094 Among other things, the module includes the following:
17091149 * Generic, Protocol, and internal machinery to support generic aliases.
17091221   All subscripted types like X[int], Union[int, str] are generic aliases.
17091295 * Various "special forms" that have unique meanings in type annotations:
17091368   Any, Never, ClassVar, Self, Concatenate, Unpack, and others.
17091431 * Classes whose instances can be type arguments to generic classes and functions:
17091513   TypeVar, ParamSpec, TypeVarTuple.
17091549 * Public helper functions: get_type_hints, overload, cast, final, and others.
17091627 * Several protocols to support duck-typing:
17091671   SupportsFloat, SupportsIndex, SupportsAbs, and others.
17091728 * Special types: NewType, NamedTuple, TypedDict.
17091777 * Deprecated aliases for builtin types and collections.abc ABCs.
17091843 Any name not present in __all__ is an implementation detail
17091903 that may be changed without notice. Use at your own risk!

17112753 Special type indicating functions that never return.
17112807 Example::
17112818     from typing import NoReturn
17112851     def stop() -> NoReturn:
17112879         raise Exception('no way')
17112914 NoReturn can also be used as a bottom type, a type that
17112970 has no values. Starting in Python 3.11, the Never type should
17113032 be used for this concept instead. Type checkers should treat the two
17113101 equivalently.
17113117  is not subscriptabler<
17113270 The bottom type, a type that has no members.
17113316 This can be used to define a function that should never be
17113375 called, or a function that never returns::
17113419     from typing import Never
17113449     def never_call_me(arg: Never) -> None:
17113492         pass
17113506     def int_or_str(arg: int | str) -> None:
17113550         never_call_me(arg)  # type checker error
17113599         match arg:
17113618             case int():
17113642                 print("It's an int")
17113679             case str():
17113703                 print("It's a str")
17113739             case _:
17113759                 never_call_me(arg)  # OK, arg is of type Never
17113959 Used to spell the type of "self" in classes.
17114005 Example::
17114016     from typing import Self
17114045     class Foo:
17114060         def return_self(self) -> Self:
17114099             ...
17114115             return self
17114140 This is especially useful for:
17114171     - classmethods that are used as alternative constructors
17114232     - annotating an `__enter__` method which returns self
17114427 Represents an arbitrary literal string.
17114468 Example::
17114479     from typing import LiteralString
17114517     def run_query(sql: LiteralString) -> None:
17114564         ...
17114577     def caller(arbitrary_string: str, literal_string: LiteralString) -> None:
17114655         run_query("SELECT * FROM students")  # OK
17114705         run_query(literal_string)  # OK
17114745         run_query("SELECT * FROM " + literal_string)  # OK
17114804         run_query(arbitrary_string)  # type checker error
17114862         run_query(  # type checker error
17114903             f"SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = {arbitrary_string}"
17114973         )
17114984 Only string literals and other LiteralStrings are compatible
17115045 with LiteralString. This provides a tool to help prevent
17115102 security issues such as SQL injection.
17115300 Special type construct to mark class variables.
17115349 An annotation wrapped in ClassVar indicates that a given
17115406 attribute is intended to be used as a class variable and
17115463 should not be set on instances of that class.
17115510 Usage::
17115519     class Starship:
17115539         stats: ClassVar[dict[str, int]] = {} # class variable
17115601         damage: int = 10                     # instance variable
17115667 ClassVar accepts only types and cannot be further subscribed.

17115783 be used with isinstance() or issubclass().

17116049 Special typing construct to indicate final names to type checkers.
17116117 A final name cannot be re-assigned or overridden in a subclass.
17116182 For example::
17116197     MAX_SIZE: Final = 9000
17116224     MAX_SIZE += 1  # Error reported by type checker
17116277     class Connection:
17116299         TIMEOUT: Final[int] = 10
17116333     class FastConnector(Connection):
17116370         TIMEOUT = 1  # Error reported by type checker
17116425 There is no runtime checking of these properties.
17116501    r|
17116862 Union type; Union[X, Y] means either X or Y.
17116908 On Python 3.10 and higher, the | operator
17116950 can also be used to denote unions;
17116985 X | Y means the same thing to the type checker as Union[X, Y].
17117049 To define a union, use e.g. Union[int, str]. Details:
17117103 - The arguments must be types and there must be at least one.
17117165 - None as an argument is a special case and is replaced by
17117224   type(None).
17117238 - Unions of unions are flattened, e.g.::
17117280     assert Union[Union[int, str], float] == Union[int, str, float]
17117348 - Unions of a single argument vanish, e.g.::
17117394     assert Union[int] == int  # The constructor actually returns int
17117464 - Redundant arguments are skipped, e.g.::
17117507     assert Union[int, str, int] == Union[int, str]
17117559 - When comparing unions, the argument order is ignored, e.g.::
17117623     assert Union[int, str] == Union[str, int]
17117670 - You cannot subclass or instantiate a union.
17117716 - You can use Optional[X] as a shorthand for Union[X, None].
17117782 z Cannot take a Union of no types.z)Union[arg, ...]: each arg must be a type.c

17121926 Special typing construct for marking user-defined type predicate functions.
17122003 ``TypeGuard`` can be used to annotate the return type of a user-defined
17122075 type predicate function.  ``TypeGuard`` only accepts a single type argument.
17122152 At runtime, functions marked this way should return a boolean.
17122216 ``TypeGuard`` aims to benefit *type narrowing* -- a technique used by static
17122293 type checkers to determine a more precise type of an expression within a
17122366 program's code flow.  Usually type narrowing is done by analyzing
17122432 conditional code flow and applying the narrowing to a block of code.  The
17122506 conditional expression here is sometimes referred to as a "type predicate".
17122583 Sometimes it would be convenient to use a user-defined boolean function
17122655 as a type predicate.  Such a function should use ``TypeGuard[...]`` or
17122726 ``TypeIs[...]`` as its return type to alert static type checkers to
17122794 this intention. ``TypeGuard`` should be used over ``TypeIs`` when narrowing
17122870 from an incompatible type (e.g., ``list[object]`` to ``list[int]``) or when
17122946 the function does not return ``True`` for all instances of the narrowed type.
17123025 Using  ``-> TypeGuard[NarrowedType]`` tells the static type checker that
17123098 for a given function:
17123121 1. The return value is a boolean.
17123155 2. If the return value is ``True``, the type of its argument
17123216    is ``NarrowedType``.
17123241 For example::
17123256      def is_str_list(val: list[object]) -> TypeGuard[list[str]]:
17123321          '''Determines whether all objects in the list are strings'''
17123391          return all(isinstance(x, str) for x in val)
17123445      def func1(val: list[object]):
17123480          if is_str_list(val):
17123510              # Type of ``val`` is narrowed to ``list[str]``.
17123571              print(" ".join(val))
17123605          else:
17123620              # Type of ``val`` remains as ``list[object]``.
17123680              print("Not a list of strings!")
17123726 Strict type narrowing is not enforced -- ``TypeB`` need not be a narrower
17123800 form of ``TypeA`` (it can even be a wider form) and this may lead to
17123869 type-unsafe results.  The main reason is to allow for things like
17123935 narrowing ``list[object]`` to ``list[str]`` even though the latter is not
17124009 a subtype of the former, since ``list`` is invariant.  The responsibility of
17124086 writing type-safe type predicates is left to the user.
17124142 ``TypeGuard`` also works with type variables.  For more information, see
17124215 PEP 647 (User-Defined Type Guards).
17124271    r|
17124426 Special typing construct for marking user-defined type predicate functions.
17124503 ``TypeIs`` can be used to annotate the return type of a user-defined
17124572 type predicate function.  ``TypeIs`` only accepts a single type argument.
17124646 At runtime, functions marked this way should return a boolean and accept
17124719 at least one argument.
17124743 ``TypeIs`` aims to benefit *type narrowing* -- a technique used by static
17124817 type checkers to determine a more precise type of an expression within a
17124890 program's code flow.  Usually type narrowing is done by analyzing
17124956 conditional code flow and applying the narrowing to a block of code.  The
17125030 conditional expression here is sometimes referred to as a "type predicate".
17125107 Sometimes it would be convenient to use a user-defined boolean function
17125179 as a type predicate.  Such a function should use ``TypeIs[...]`` or
17125247 ``TypeGuard[...]`` as its return type to alert static type checkers to
17125318 this intention.  ``TypeIs`` usually has more intuitive behavior than
17125387 ``TypeGuard``, but it cannot be used when the input and output types
17125456 are incompatible (e.g., ``list[object]`` to ``list[int]``) or when the
17125527 function does not return ``True`` for all instances of the narrowed type.
17125602 Using  ``-> TypeIs[NarrowedType]`` tells the static type checker that for
17125676 a given function:
17125695 1. The return value is a boolean.
17125729 2. If the return value is ``True``, the type of its argument
17125790    is the intersection of the argument's original type and
17125849    ``NarrowedType``.
17125870 3. If the return value is ``False``, the type of its argument
17125932    is narrowed to exclude ``NarrowedType``.
17125977 For example::
17125992     from typing import assert_type, final, TypeIs
17126043     class Parent: pass
17126066     class Child(Parent): pass
17126096     @final
17126107     class Unrelated: pass
17126134     def is_parent(val: object) -> TypeIs[Parent]:
17126184         return isinstance(val, Parent)
17126224     def run(arg: Child | Unrelated):
17126261         if is_parent(arg):
17126288             # Type of ``arg`` is narrowed to the intersection
17126350             # of ``Parent`` and ``Child``, which is equivalent to
17126416             # ``Child``.
17126441             assert_type(arg, Child)
17126477         else:
17126491             # Type of ``arg`` is narrowed to exclude ``Parent``,
17126556             # so only ``Unrelated`` is left.
17126601             assert_type(arg, Unrelated)
17126642 The type inside ``TypeIs`` must be consistent with the type of the
17126709 function's argument; if it is not, static type checkers will raise
17126776 an error.  An incorrectly written ``TypeIs`` function can lead to
17126842 unsound behavior in the type system; it is the user's responsibility
17126911 to write such functions in a type-safe manner.
17126959 ``TypeIs`` also works with type variables.  For more information, see
17127029 PEP 742 (Narrowing types with ``TypeIs``).

17167021 "_ConcatenateGenericAlias.copy_with.
17167368 Type unpack operator.
17167391 The type unpack operator takes the child types from some container type,
17167464 such as `tuple[int, str]` or a `TypeVarTuple`, and 'pulls them out'.
17167534 For example::
17167549     # For some generic class `Foo`:
17167585     Foo[Unpack[tuple[int, str]]]  # Equivalent to Foo[int, str]
17167650     Ts = TypeVarTuple('Ts')
17167678     # Specifies that `Bar` is generic in an arbitrary number of types.
17167749     # (Think of `Ts` as a tuple of an arbitrary number of individual
17167818     #  `TypeVar`s, which the `Unpack` is 'pulling out' directly into the
17167891     #  `Generic[]`.)
17167912     class Bar(Generic[Unpack[Ts]]): ...
17167952     Bar[int]  # Valid
17167974     Bar[int, str]  # Also valid
17168007 From Python 3.11, this can also be done using the `*` operator::
17168073     Foo[*tuple[int, str]]
17168099     class Bar(Generic[*Ts]): ...
17168133 And from Python 3.12, it can be done using built-in syntax for generics::
17168208     Foo[*tuple[int, str]]
17168234     class Bar[*Ts]: ...
17168259 The operator can also be used along with a `TypedDict` to annotate
17168326 `**kwargs` in a function signature::
17168364     class Movie(TypedDict):
17168392         name: str
17168410         year: int
17168429     # This function expects two keyword arguments - *name* of type `str` and
17168506     # *year* of type `int`.
17168534     def foo(**kwargs: Unpack[Movie]): ...
17168577 Note that there is only some runtime checking of this operator. Not
17168645 everything the runtime allows is accepted by static type checkers.
17168713 For more information, see PEPs 646 and 692.

17179060 Base class for protocol classes.
17179094 Protocol classes are defined as::
17179129     class Proto(Protocol):
17179156         def meth(self) -> int:
17179187             ...
17179204 Such classes are primarily used with static type checkers that recognize
17179277 structural subtyping (static duck-typing).
17179321 For example::
17179336     class C:
17179349         def meth(self) -> int:
17179380             return 0
17179402     def func(x: Proto) -> int:
17179433         return x.meth()
17179458     func(C())  # Passes static type check
17179501 See PEP 544 for details. Protocol classes decorated with
17179558 @typing.runtime_checkable act as simple-minded runtime protocols that check
17179634 only the presence of given attributes, ignoring their type signatures.
17179705 Protocol classes can be generic, they are defined as::
17179761     class GenProto[T](Protocol):
17179794         def meth(self) -> T:
17179823             ...

17184121 Add context-specific metadata to a type.
17184163 Example: Annotated[int, runtime_check.Unsigned] indicates to the
17184228 hypothetical runtime_check module that this type is an unsigned int.
17184297 Every other consumer of this type can ignore this metadata and treat
17184366 this type as int.
17184385 The first argument to Annotated must be a valid type.
17184440 Details:
17184450 - It's an error to call `Annotated` with less than two arguments.
17184516 - Access the metadata via the ``__metadata__`` attribute::
17184576     assert Annotated[int, '$'].__metadata__ == ('$',)
17184631 - Nested Annotated types are flattened::
17184673     assert Annotated[Annotated[T, Ann1, Ann2], Ann3] == Annotated[T, Ann1, Ann2, Ann3]
17184761 - Instantiating an annotated type is equivalent to instantiating the
17184830 underlying type::
17184849     assert Annotated[C, Ann1](5) == C(5)
17184891 - Annotated can be used as a generic type alias::
17184942     type Optimized[T] = Annotated[T, runtime.Optimize()]
17184999     # type checker will treat Optimized[int]
17185044     # as equivalent to Annotated[int, runtime.Optimize()]
17185103     type OptimizedList[T] = Annotated[list[T], runtime.Optimize()]
17185170     # type checker will treat OptimizedList[int]
17185219     # as equivalent to Annotated[list[int], runtime.Optimize()]
17185284 - Annotated cannot be used with an unpacked TypeVarTuple::
17185344     type Variadic[*Ts] = Annotated[*Ts, Ann1]  # NOT valid
17185404   This would be equivalent to::
17185437     Annotated[T1, T2, T3, ..., Ann1]
17185475   where T1, T2 etc. are TypeVars, which would be invalid, because
17185541   only one type should be passed to Annotated.
17185593 zUAnnotated[...] should be used with at least two arguments (a type and an annotation).r
17185685 z?Annotated[...] should not be used with an unpacked TypeVarTuplez$Annotated[t, ...]: t must be a type.Trs
17185864      r|
17186430 Mark a protocol class as a runtime protocol.
17186476 Such protocol can be used with isinstance() and issubclass().
17186538 Raise TypeError if applied to a non-protocol class.
17186590 This allows a simple-minded structural check very similar to
17186651 one-trick ponies in collections.abc such as Iterable.
17186706 For example::
17186721     @runtime_checkable
17186744     class Closable(Protocol):
17186774         def close(self): ...
17186804     assert isinstance(open('/some/file'), Closable)

17186925 not their type signatures!

17187076  is a method member)

17187171 is_callabler
17187192     r|
17187491 Cast a value to a type.
17187516 This returns the value unchanged.  To the type checker this
17187576 signals that the return value has the designated type, but at
17187638 runtime we intentionally don't check anything (we want this
17187698 to be as fast as possible).
17187827 Ask a static type checker to confirm that the value is of the given type.
17187902 At runtime this does nothing: it returns the first argument unchanged with no
17187980 checks or side effects, no matter the actual type of the argument.
17188048 When a static type checker encounters a call to assert_type(), it
17188114 emits an error if the value is not of the specified type::
17188174     def greet(name: str) -> None:
17188208         assert_type(name, str)  # OK
17188245         assert_type(name, int)  # type checker error
17190071 Return type hints for an object.
17190105 This is often the same as inspect.get_annotations(obj) or obj.__annotations__,
17190184 but it handles forward references encoded as string literals and recursively replaces all
17190274 'Annotated[T, ...]' with 'T' (unless 'include_extras=True').
17190336 The argument may be a module, class, method, or function. The annotations
17190410 are returned as a dictionary. For classes, annotations include also
17190478 inherited members.
17190498 TypeError is raised if the argument is not of a type that can contain
17190568 annotations, and an empty dictionary is returned if no annotations are
17190639 present.
17190649 BEWARE -- the behavior of globalns and localns is counterintuitive
17190716 (unless you are familiar with how eval() and exec() work).  The
17190780 search order is locals first, then globals.
17190825 - If no dict arguments are passed, an attempt is made to use the
17190890   globals from obj (or the respective module's globals for classes),
17190959   and these are also used as the locals.  If the object does not appear
17191031   to have globals, an empty dictionary is used.  For classes, the search
17191104   order is globals first then locals.
17191143 - If one dict argument is passed, it is used for both globals and
17191209   locals.
17191220 - If two dict arguments are passed, they specify globals and
17191281   locals, respectively.

17218531  _TypedDictMeta.__subclasscheck__
17219011 A simple typed namespace. At runtime it is equivalent to a plain dict.
17219083 TypedDict creates a dictionary type such that a type checker will expect all
17219160 instances to have a certain set of keys, where each key is
17219219 associated with a value of a consistent type. This expectation
17219282 is not checked at runtime.
17219310 Usage::
17219319     >>> class Point2D(TypedDict):
17219353     ...     x: int
17219372     ...     y: int
17219391     ...     label: str
17219414     ...
17219422     >>> a: Point2D = {'x': 1, 'y': 2, 'label': 'good'}  # OK
17219483     >>> b: Point2D = {'z': 3, 'label': 'bad'}           # Fails type check
17219558     >>> Point2D(x=1, y=2, label='first') == dict(x=1, y=2, label='first')
17219632     True
17219642 The type info can be accessed by calling inspect.get_annotations(Point2D), and
17219721 via the Point2D.__required_keys__ and Point2D.__optional_keys__ frozensets.
17219797 TypedDict supports an additional equivalent form::
17219849     Point2D = TypedDict('Point2D', {'x': int, 'y': int, 'label': str})
17219921 By default, all keys must be present in a TypedDict. It is possible
17219989 to override this by using the NotRequired and Required special forms::
17220061     class Point2D(TypedDict):
17220091         x: int               # the "x" key must always be present (Required is the default)
17220183         y: NotRequired[int]  # the "y" key can be omitted
17220242 This means that a Point2D TypedDict can have the "y" key omitted, but the "x" key must be present.
17220341 Items are required by default, so the Required special form is not necessary in this example.
17220435 In addition, the total argument to the TypedDict function can be used to make all items not required::
17220539     class Point2D(TypedDict, total=False):
17220582         x: int
17220597         y: int
17220613 This means that a Point2D TypedDict can have any of the keys omitted. A type
17220690 checker is only expected to support a literal False or True as the value of
17220766 the total argument. True is the default, and makes all items defined in the
17220842 class body be required. The Required special form can be used to mark individual
17220923 keys as required in a total=False TypedDict.
17220969 The ReadOnly special form can be used
17221007 to mark individual keys as immutable for type checkers::
17221065     class DatabaseUser(TypedDict):
17221100         id: ReadOnly[int]  # the "id" key must not be modified
17221163         username: str      # the "username" key can be changed
17221227 See PEPs 589, 655, and 705 for more information.
17221299  = TypedDict(z
17221314 , {{}})`z
17221324 {name} is deprecated and will be disallowed in Python {remove}. To create a TypedDict class with 0 fields using the functional syntax, pass an empty dictionary, e.g. r

17233653 Decorator to mark an object as providing dataclass-like behavior.
17233720 The decorator can be applied to a function, class, or metaclass.
17233786 Example usage with a decorator function::
17233829     @dataclass_transform()
17233856     def create_model[T](cls: type[T]) -> type[T]:
17233906         ...
17233918         return cls
17233938     @create_model
17233956     class CustomerModel:
17233981         id: int
17233997         name: str
17234016 On a base class::
17234035     @dataclass_transform()
17234062     class ModelBase: ...
17234088     class CustomerModel(ModelBase):
17234124         id: int
17234140         name: str
17234159 On a metaclass::
17234177     @dataclass_transform()
17234204     class ModelMeta(type): ...
17234236     class ModelBase(metaclass=ModelMeta): ...
17234283     class CustomerModel(ModelBase):
17234319         id: int
17234335         name: str
17234354 The ``CustomerModel`` classes defined above will
17234403 be treated by type checkers similarly to classes created with
17234465 ``@dataclasses.dataclass``.
17234493 For example, type checkers will assume these classes have
17234551 ``__init__`` methods that accept ``id`` and ``name``.
17234606 The arguments to this decorator can be used to customize this behavior:
17234678 - ``eq_default`` indicates whether the ``eq`` parameter is assumed to be
17234751     ``True`` or ``False`` if it is omitted by the caller.
17234809 - ``order_default`` indicates whether the ``order`` parameter is
17234874     assumed to be True or False if it is omitted by the caller.
17234938 - ``kw_only_default`` indicates whether the ``kw_only`` parameter is
17235007     assumed to be True or False if it is omitted by the caller.
17235071 - ``frozen_default`` indicates whether the ``frozen`` parameter is
17235138     assumed to be True or False if it is omitted by the caller.
17235202 - ``field_specifiers`` specifies a static list of supported classes
17235270     or functions that describe fields, similar to ``dataclasses.field()``.
17235345 - Arbitrary other keyword arguments are accepted in order to allow for

17235568 It has no other runtime effect.

17236433 Indicate that a method is intended to override a method in a base class.
17236507 Usage::
17236516     class Base:
17236532         def method(self) -> None:
17236566             pass
17236584     class Child(Base):
17236607         @override
17236625         def method(self) -> None:
17236659             super().method()
17236689 When this decorator is applied to a method, the type checker will
17236755 validate that it overrides a method or attribute with the same name on a
17236828 base class.  This helps prevent bugs that may occur when a base class is
17236901 changed without an equivalent change to a child class.
17236957 There is no runtime checking of this property. The decorator attempts to
17237030 set the ``__override__`` attribute to ``True`` on the decorated object to
17237104 allow runtime introspection.
17237134 See PEP 698 for details.

17275723 TestCaseij
17275741 A class whose instances are single test cases.
17275789 By default, the test code itself should be placed in a method named
17275857 'runTest'.
17275869 If the fixture may be used for many test cases, create as
17275927 many test methods as are needed. When instantiating such a TestCase
17275995 subclass, specify in the constructor arguments the name of the test method
17276070 that the instance is to execute.
17276104 Test authors should subclass TestCase for their own tests. Construction
17276176 and deconstruction of the test's environment ('fixture') can be
17276240 implemented by overriding the 'setUp' and 'tearDown' methods respectively.
17276316 If it is necessary to override the __init__ method, the base class
17276383 __init__ method must always be called. It is important that subclasses
17276454 should not change the signature of their __init__ method, since instances
17276528 of the classes are instantiated automatically by parts of the framework
17276600 in order to be run.
17276621 When subclassing TestCase, you can set these attributes:
17276678 * failureException: determines which exception will be raised when
17276745     the instance's assertion methods fail; test methods raising this
17276814     exception will be deemed to have 'failed' rather than 'errored'.
17276883 * longMessage: determines whether long messages (including repr of
17276950     objects used in assert methods) will be printed on failure in *addition*
17277027     to any explicit message passed.
17277063 * maxDiff: sets the maximum length of a diff in failure messages
17277128     by assert methods using difflib. It is looked up as an instance
17277196     attribute so can be configured by individual tests if required.

17340959 n	X@l
17341194 Find and return all test modules from the specified start
17341252 directory, recursing into subdirectories to find them and return all
17341321 tests found within them. Only test files that match the pattern will
17341390 be loaded. (Using shell style pattern matching.)
17341440 All test modules must be importable from the top level of the project.
17341511 If the start directory is not the top level directory then the top
17341578 level directory must be specified separately.
17341625 If a test package name (directory with '__init__.py') matches the
17341691 pattern then the package will be checked for a 'load_tests' function. If
17341764 this exists then it will be called with (loader, tests, pattern) unless
17341836 the package has already had load_tests called from the same discovery
17341906 invocation, in which case the package module object is not scanned for
17341977 tests - this ensures that when a package uses discover to further
17342043 discover child tests that infinite recursion does not happen.
17342106 If load_tests exists then discovery does *not* recurse into the package,
17342179 load_tests is responsible for loading all tests in the package.
17342244 The pattern is deliberately not stored as a loader attribute so that
17342313 packages can continue discovery themselves. top_level_dir is stored so
17342384 load_tests does not need to pass this argument in to loader.discover().
17342457 Paths are sorted before being imported to ensure reproducible execution
17342529 order even on filesystems with non-alphabetical ordering like ext3/4.

17414575  CallableMixin._execute_mock_call
17415094 Create a new `Mock` object. `Mock` takes several optional arguments
17415162 that specify the behaviour of the Mock object:
17415210 * `spec`: This can be either a list of strings or an existing object (a
17415282   class or instance) that acts as the specification for the mock object. If
17415358   you pass in an object then a list of strings is formed by calling dir on
17415433   the object (excluding unsupported magic attributes and methods). Accessing
17415510   any attribute not in this list will raise an `AttributeError`.
17415576   If `spec` is an object (rather than a list of strings) then
17415638   `mock.__class__` returns the class of the spec object. This allows mocks
17415713   to pass `isinstance` tests.
17415744 * `spec_set`: A stricter variant of `spec`. If used, attempting to *set*
17415817   or get an attribute on the mock that isn't on the object passed as
17415886   `spec_set` will raise an `AttributeError`.
17415932 * `side_effect`: A function to be called whenever the Mock is called. See
17416006   the `side_effect` attribute. Useful for raising exceptions or
17416070   dynamically changing return values. The function is called with the same
17416145   arguments as the mock, and unless it returns `DEFAULT`, the return
17416214   value of this function is used as the return value.
17416269   If `side_effect` is an iterable then each call to the mock will return
17416342   the next value from the iterable. If any of the members of the iterable
17416416   are exceptions they will be raised instead of returned.
17416475 * `return_value`: The value returned when the mock is called. By default
17416548   this is a new Mock (created on first access). See the
17416604   `return_value` attribute.
17416633 * `unsafe`: By default, accessing any attribute whose name starts with
17416704   *assert*, *assret*, *asert*, *aseert*, or *assrt* raises an AttributeError.
17416782   Additionally, an AttributeError is raised when accessing
17416841   attributes that match the name of an assertion method without the prefix
17416916   `assert_`, e.g. accessing `called_once` instead of `assert_called_once`.
17416991   Passing `unsafe=True` will allow access to these attributes.
17417055 * `wraps`: Item for the mock object to wrap. If `wraps` is not None then
17417128   calling the Mock will pass the call through to the wrapped object
17417196   (returning the real result). Attribute access on the mock will return a
17417270   Mock object that wraps the corresponding attribute of the wrapped object
17417345   (so attempting to access an attribute that doesn't exist will raise an
17417418   `AttributeError`).
17417440   If the mock has an explicit `return_value` set then calls are not passed
17417515   to the wrapped object and the `return_value` is returned instead.
17417584 * `name`: If the mock has a name then it will be used in the repr of the
17417657   mock. This can be useful for debugging. The name is propagated to child
17417731   mocks.
17417741 Mocks can also be called with arbitrary keyword arguments. These will be
17417814 used to set attributes on the mock after it is created.

17433983 _patch_multipler
17434280 XEXhU
17434300 `patch` acts as a function decorator, class decorator or a context
17434367 manager. Inside the body of the function or with statement, the `target`
17434440 is patched with a `new` object. When the function/with statement exits
17434511 the patch is undone.
17434533 If `new` is omitted, then the target is replaced with an
17434590 `AsyncMock if the patched object is an async function or a
17434649 `MagicMock` otherwise. If `patch` is used as a decorator and `new` is
17434719 omitted, the created mock is passed in as an extra argument to the
17434786 decorated function. If `patch` is used as a context manager the created
17434858 mock is returned by the context manager.
17434900 `target` should be a string in the form `'package.module.ClassName'`. The
17434974 `target` is imported and the specified object replaced with the `new`
17435044 object, so the `target` must be importable from the environment you are
17435116 calling `patch` from. The target is imported when the decorated function
17435189 is executed, not at decoration time.
17435227 The `spec` and `spec_set` keyword arguments are passed to the `MagicMock`
17435301 if patch is creating one for you.
17435336 In addition you can pass `spec=True` or `spec_set=True`, which causes
17435406 patch to pass in the object being mocked as the spec/spec_set object.
17435477 `new_callable` allows you to specify a different class, or callable object,
17435553 that will be called to create the `new` object. By default `AsyncMock` is
17435627 used for async functions and `MagicMock` for the rest.
17435683 A more powerful form of `spec` is `autospec`. If you set `autospec=True`
17435756 then the mock will be created with a spec from the object being replaced.
17435830 All attributes of the mock will also have the spec of the corresponding
17435902 attribute of the object being replaced. Methods and functions being
17435970 mocked will have their arguments checked and will raise a `TypeError` if
17436043 they are called with the wrong signature. For mocks replacing a class,
17436114 their return value (the 'instance') will have the same spec as the class.
17436189 Instead of `autospec=True` you can pass `autospec=some_object` to use an
17436262 arbitrary object as the spec instead of the one being replaced.
17436327 By default `patch` will fail to replace attributes that don't exist. If
17436399 you pass in `create=True`, and the attribute doesn't exist, patch will
17436470 create the attribute for you when the patched function is called, and
17436540 delete it again afterwards. This is useful for writing tests against
17436609 attributes that your production code creates at runtime. It is off by
17436679 default because it can be dangerous. With it switched on you can write
17436750 passing tests against APIs that don't actually exist!
17436805 Patch can be used as a `TestCase` class decorator. It works by
17436868 decorating each test method in the class. This reduces the boilerplate
17436939 code when your test methods share a common patchings set. `patch` finds
17437011 tests by looking for method names that start with `patch.TEST_PREFIX`.
17437082 By default this is `test`, which matches the way `unittest` finds tests.
17437155 You can specify an alternative prefix by setting `patch.TEST_PREFIX`.
17437226 Patch can be used as a context manager, with the with statement. Here the
17437300 patching applies to the indented block after the with statement. If you
17437372 use "as" then the patched object will be bound to the name after the
17437441 "as"; very useful if `patch` is creating a mock object for you.
17437506 Patch will raise a `RuntimeError` if passed some common misspellings of
17437578 the arguments autospec and spec_set. Pass the argument `unsafe` with the
17437651 value True to disable that check.
17437686 `patch` takes arbitrary keyword arguments. These will be passed to
17437753 `AsyncMock` if the patched object is asynchronous, to `MagicMock`
17437819 otherwise or to `new_callable` if specified.
17437865 `patch.dict(...)`, `patch.multiple(...)` and `patch.object(...)` are
17437934 available for alternate use-cases.
17438048            r'

17461961 AsyncMockMixin.reset_mock
17462380 Enhance :class:`Mock` with features allowing to mock
17462433 an async function.
17462453 The :class:`AsyncMock` object will behave so the object is
17462512 recognized as an async function, and the result of a call is an awaitable:
17462588 >>> mock = AsyncMock()
17462611 >>> iscoroutinefunction(mock)
17462646 >>> inspect.isawaitable(mock())
17462685 The result of ``mock()`` is an async function which will have the outcome
17462759 of ``side_effect`` or ``return_value``:
17462800 - if ``side_effect`` is a function, the async function will return the
17462871   result of that function,
17462898 - if ``side_effect`` is an exception, the async function will raise the
17462970   exception,
17462983 - if ``side_effect`` is an iterable, the async function will return the
17463055   next value of the iterable, however, if the sequence of result is
17463123   exhausted, ``StopIteration`` is raised immediately,
17463177 - if ``side_effect`` is not defined, the async function will return the
17463249   value defined by ``return_value``, hence, by default, the async function
17463324   returns a new :class:`AsyncMock` object.
17463368 If the outcome of ``side_effect`` or ``return_value`` is an async function,
17463444 the mock async function obtained when the mock object is called will be this
17463521 async function itself (and not an async function returning an async
17463589 function).
17463601 The test author can also specify a wrapped object with ``wraps``. In this
17463675 case, the :class:`Mock` object behavior is the same as with an
17463738 :class:`.Mock` object: the wrapped object may have methods
17463797 defined as async function functions.
17463835 Based on Martin Richard's asynctest project.

17465352 A tuple for holding the results of a call to a mock, either in the form
17465424 `(args, kwargs)` or `(name, args, kwargs)`.
17465469 If args or kwargs are empty then a call tuple will compare equal to
17465537 a tuple without those values. This makes comparisons less verbose::
17465606     _Call(('name', (), {})) == ('name',)
17465647     _Call(('name', (1,), {})) == ('name', (1,))
17465695     _Call(((), {'a': 'b'})) == ({'a': 'b'},)

17465814     _Call(((1, 2), {'a': 3})) == call(1, 2, a=3)

17548154 Exception classes raised by urllib.
17548191 The base exception class is URLError, which inherits from OSError.  It
17548262 doesn't define any behavior of its own, but is the base class for all
17548332 exceptions defined in this package.
17548369 HTTPError is an exception class that is also a valid HTTP response
17548436 instance.  It behaves this way because HTTP protocol errors are valid
17548506 responses, with a status code, headers, and a body.  In some contexts,
17548577 an application may want to handle an exception like a regular
17548639 response.

17553514 Parse (absolute and relative) URLs.
17553551 urllib.parse module is based upon the following RFC specifications.
17553620 RFC 3986 (STD66): "Uniform Resource Identifiers" by T. Berners-Lee, R. Fielding
17553700 and L.  Masinter, January 2005.
17553733 RFC 2732 : "Format for Literal IPv6 Addresses in URL's by R.Hinden, B.Carpenter
17553813 and L.Masinter, December 1999.
17553845 RFC 2396:  "Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI)": Generic Syntax by T.
17553915 Berners-Lee, R. Fielding, and L. Masinter, August 1998.
17553972 RFC 2368: "The mailto URL scheme", by P.Hoffman , L Masinter, J. Zawinski, July 1998.
17554059 RFC 1808: "Relative Uniform Resource Locators", by R. Fielding, UC Irvine, June
17554139 1995.
17554146 RFC 1738: "Uniform Resource Locators (URL)" by T. Berners-Lee, L. Masinter, M.
17554225 McCahill, December 1994
17554250 RFC 3986 is considered the current standard and any future changes to
17554320 urllib.parse module should conform with it.  The urllib.parse module is
17554392 currently not entirely compliant with this RFC due to defacto
17554454 scenarios for parsing, and for backward compatibility purposes, some
17554523 parsing quirks from older RFCs are retained. The testcases in
17554585 test_urlparse.py provides a good indicator of parsing behavior.
17554650 The WHATWG URL Parser spec should also be considered.  We are not compliant with
17554731 it either due to existing user code API behavior expectations (Hyrum's Law).
17554808 It serves as a useful guide when making changes.

17566669 Parse a URL into 6 components:
17566700 <scheme>://<netloc>/<path>;<params>?<query>#<fragment>
17566756 The result is a named 6-tuple with fields corresponding to the
17566819 above. It is either a ParseResult or ParseResultBytes object,
17566881 depending on the type of the url parameter.
17566926 The username, password, hostname, and port sub-components of netloc
17566994 can also be accessed as attributes of the returned object.
17567054 The scheme argument provides the default value of the scheme
17567115 component when no scheme is found in url.
17567158 If allow_fragments is False, no attempt is made to separate the
17567222 fragment component from the previous component, which can be either
17567290 path or query.
17567306 Note that % escapes are not expanded.

17585626 quote('abc def') -> 'abc%20def'
17585659 Each part of a URL, e.g. the path info, the query, etc., has a
17585722 different set of reserved characters that must be quoted. The
17585784 quote function offers a cautious (not minimal) way to quote a
17585846 string for most of these parts.
17585879 RFC 3986 Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax lists
17585944 the following (un)reserved characters.
17585984 unreserved    = ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "." / "_" / "~"
17586038 reserved      = gen-delims / sub-delims
17586078 gen-delims    = ":" / "/" / "?" / "#" / "[" / "]" / "@"
17586134 sub-delims    = "!" / "$" / "&" / "'" / "(" / ")"
17586184               / "*" / "+" / "," / ";" / "="
17586229 Each of the reserved characters is reserved in some component of a URL,
17586301 but not necessarily in all of them.
17586338 The quote function %-escapes all characters that are neither in the
17586406 unreserved chars ("always safe") nor the additional chars set via the
17586476 safe arg.
17586487 The default for the safe arg is '/'. The character is reserved, but in
17586558 typical usage the quote function is being called on a path where the
17586627 existing slash characters are to be preserved.
17586675 Python 3.7 updates from using RFC 2396 to RFC 3986 to quote URL strings.
17586748 Now, "~" is included in the set of unreserved characters.
17586807 string and safe may be either str or bytes objects. encoding and errors
17586879 must not be specified if string is a bytes object.
17586931 The optional encoding and errors parameters specify how to deal with
17587000 non-ASCII characters, as accepted by the str.encode method.
17587060 By default, encoding='utf-8' (characters are encoded with UTF-8), and
17587130 errors='strict' (unsupported characters raise a UnicodeEncodeError).
17587209 z,quote() doesn't support 'encoding' for bytesz*quote() doesn't support 'errors' for bytes)
17587353     r@
17587776 Like quote(), but also replace ' ' with '+', as required for quoting
17587845 HTML form values. Plus signs in the original string are escaped unless
17587916 they are included in safe. It also does not have safe default to '/'.

17604130 An extensible library for opening URLs using a variety of protocols
17604199 The simplest way to use this module is to call the urlopen function,
17604268 which accepts a string containing a URL or a Request object (described
17604339 below).  It opens the URL and returns the results as file-like
17604402 object; the returned object has some extra methods described below.
17604471 The OpenerDirector manages a collection of Handler objects that do
17604538 all the actual work.  Each Handler implements a particular protocol or
17604609 option.  The OpenerDirector is a composite object that invokes the
17604676 Handlers needed to open the requested URL.  For example, the
17604737 HTTPHandler performs HTTP GET and POST requests and deals with
17604800 non-error returns.  The HTTPRedirectHandler automatically deals with
17604869 HTTP 301, 302, 303, 307, and 308 redirect errors, and the
17604927 HTTPDigestAuthHandler deals with digest authentication.
17604984 urlopen(url, data=None) -- Basic usage is the same as original
17605047 urllib.  pass the url and optionally data to post to an HTTP URL, and
17605117 get a file-like object back.  One difference is that you can also pass
17605188 a Request instance instead of URL.  Raises a URLError (subclass of
17605255 OSError); for HTTP errors, raises an HTTPError, which can also be
17605321 treated as a valid response.
17605351 build_opener -- Function that creates a new OpenerDirector instance.
17605420 Will install the default handlers.  Accepts one or more Handlers as
17605488 arguments, either instances or Handler classes that it will
17605548 instantiate.  If one of the argument is a subclass of the default
17605614 handler, the argument will be installed instead of the default.
17605679 install_opener -- Installs a new opener as the default opener.
17605743 objects of interest:
17605765 OpenerDirector -- Sets up the User Agent as the Python-urllib client and manages
17605846 the Handler classes, while dealing with requests and responses.
17605911 Request -- An object that encapsulates the state of a request.  The
17605979 state can be as simple as the URL.  It can also include extra HTTP
17606046 headers, e.g. a User-Agent.
17606075 BaseHandler --
17606091 internals:
17606102 BaseHandler and parent
17606125 _call_chain conventions

17606166 import urllib.request
17606189 # set up authentication info
17606218 authinfo = urllib.request.HTTPBasicAuthHandler()
17606267 authinfo.add_password(realm='PDQ Application',
17606314                       uri='https://mahler:8092/site-updates.py',
17606379                       user='klem',
17606414                       passwd='geheim$parole')
17606461 proxy_support = urllib.request.ProxyHandler({"http" : "http://ahad-haam:3128"})
17606542 # build a new opener that adds authentication and caching FTP handlers

17606675                                      urllib.request.CacheFTPHandler)

17607922 Open the URL url, which can be either a string or a Request object.
17607991 *data* must be an object specifying additional data to be sent to
17608057 the server, or None if no such data is needed.  See Request for
17608121 details.
17608131 urllib.request module uses HTTP/1.1 and includes a "Connection:close"
17608201 header in its HTTP requests.
17608231 The optional *timeout* parameter specifies a timeout in seconds for
17608299 blocking operations like the connection attempt (if not specified, the
17608370 global default timeout setting will be used). This only works for HTTP,
17608442 HTTPS and FTP connections.
17608470 If *context* is specified, it must be a ssl.SSLContext instance describing
17608545 the various SSL options. See HTTPSConnection for more details.
17608610 This function always returns an object which can work as a
17608669 context manager and has the properties url, headers, and status.
17608734 See urllib.response.addinfourl for more detail on these properties.
17608803 For HTTP and HTTPS URLs, this function returns a http.client.HTTPResponse
17608877 object slightly modified. In addition to the three new methods above, the
17608951 msg attribute contains the same information as the reason attribute ---
17609023 the reason phrase returned by the server --- instead of the response
17609092 headers as it is specified in the documentation for HTTPResponse.
17609159 For FTP, file, and data URLs and requests explicitly handled by legacy
17609230 URLopener and FancyURLopener classes, this function returns a
17609292 urllib.response.addinfourl object.
17609328 Note that None may be returned if no handler handles the request (though
17609401 the default installed global OpenerDirector uses UnknownHandler to ensure
17609475 this never happens).
17609497 In addition, if proxy settings are detected (for example, when a *_proxy
17609570 environment variable like http_proxy is set), ProxyHandler is default
17609640 installed and makes sure the requests are handled through the proxy.

17741083 A context manager that copies and restores the warnings filter upon
17741151 exiting the context.
17741173 The 'record' argument specifies whether warnings should be captured by a
17741246 custom implementation of warnings.showwarning() and be appended to a list
17741320 returned by the context manager. Otherwise None is returned by the context
17741395 manager. The objects appended to the list are arguments whose attributes
17741468 mirror the arguments to showwarning().
17741508 The 'module' argument is to specify an alternative module to the module
17741580 named 'warnings' and imported under that name. This argument is only useful
17741656 when testing the warnings module itself.
17741698 If the 'action' argument is not None, the remaining arguments are passed
17741771 to warnings.simplefilter() as if it were called immediately on entering the
17741847 context.

17744955 Indicate that a class, function or overload is deprecated.
17745015 When this decorator is applied to an object, the type checker
17745077 will generate a diagnostic on usage of the deprecated object.
17745140 Usage:
17745148     @deprecated("Use B instead")
17745181     class A:
17745194         pass
17745208     @deprecated("Use g instead")
17745241     def f():
17745254         pass
17745268     @overload
17745282     @deprecated("int support is deprecated")
17745327     def g(x: int) -> int: ...
17745357     @overload
17745371     def g(x: str) -> int: ...
17745402 The warning specified by *category* will be emitted at runtime
17745465 on use of deprecated objects. For functions, that happens on calls;
17745533 for classes, on instantiation and on creation of subclasses.
17745594 If the *category* is ``None``, no warning is emitted at runtime.
17745659 The *stacklevel* determines where the
17745697 warning is emitted. If it is ``1`` (the default), the warning
17745759 is emitted at the direct caller of the deprecated object; if it
17745823 is higher, it is emitted further up the stack.
17745870 Static type checker behavior is not affected by the *category*
17745933 and *stacklevel* arguments.
17745962 The deprecation message passed to the decorator is saved in the
17746026 ``__deprecated__`` attribute on the decorated object.
17746080 If applied to an overload, the decorator
17746121 must be after the ``@overload`` decorator for the attribute to
17746184 exist on the overload as returned by ``get_overloads()``.
17746243 See PEP 702 for details.

17778075 Class for finalization of weakrefable objects
17778122 finalize(obj, func, *args, **kwargs) returns a callable finalizer
17778188 object which will be called when obj is garbage collected. The
17778251 first time the finalizer is called it evaluates func(*arg, **kwargs)
17778320 and returns the result. After this the finalizer is dead, and
17778382 calling it just returns None.
17778413 When the program exits any remaining finalizers for which the
17778475 atexit attribute is true will be run in reverse order of creation.
17778542 By default atexit is true.

17918136 Class with methods to open, read, write, close, list zip files.
17918201 z = ZipFile(file, mode="r", compression=ZIP_STORED, allowZip64=True,
17918270             compresslevel=None)
17918303 file: Either the path to the file, or a file-like object.
17918361       If it is a path, the file will be opened and closed by ZipFile.
17918431 mode: The mode can be either read 'r', write 'w', exclusive create 'x',
17918503       or append 'a'.
17918524 compression: ZIP_STORED (no compression), ZIP_DEFLATED (requires zlib),
17918596       ZIP_BZIP2 (requires bz2) or ZIP_LZMA (requires lzma).
17918656 allowZip64: if True ZipFile will create files with ZIP64 extensions
17918724       when needed, otherwise it will raise an exception when this
17918790       would be necessary.
17918816 compresslevel: None (default for the given compression type) or
17918880       an integer specifying the level to pass to the compressor.
17918945       When using ZIP_STORED or ZIP_LZMA this keyword has no effect.
17919013       When using ZIP_DEFLATED integers 0 through 9 are accepted.
17919078       When using ZIP_BZIP2 integers 1 through 9 are accepted.

17980394 A :class:`importlib.resources.abc.Traversable` interface for zip files.
17980467 Implements many of the features users enjoy from
17980516 :class:`pathlib.Path`.
17980540 Consider a zip file with this structure::
17980583     .
17980602  a.txt
17980625         
17980642  c.txt
17980649         
17980669             
17980690  e.txt
17980698 >>> data = io.BytesIO()
17980722 >>> zf = ZipFile(data, 'w')
17980750 >>> zf.writestr('a.txt', 'content of a')
17980791 >>> zf.writestr('b/c.txt', 'content of c')
17980834 >>> zf.writestr('b/d/e.txt', 'content of e')
17980879 >>> zf.filename = 'mem/abcde.zip'
17980914 Path accepts the zipfile object itself or a filename
17980968 >>> path = Path(zf)
17980989 From there, several path operations are available.
17981041 Directory iteration (including the zip file itself):
17981095 >>> a, b = path.iterdir()
17981121 >>> a
17981127 Path('mem/abcde.zip', 'a.txt')
17981158 >>> b
17981164 Path('mem/abcde.zip', 'b/')
17981193 name property:
17981209 >>> b.name
17981225 join with divide operator:
17981253 >>> c = b / 'c.txt'
17981273 >>> c
17981279 Path('mem/abcde.zip', 'b/c.txt')
17981312 >>> c.name
17981323 'c.txt'
17981332 Read text:
17981344 >>> c.read_text(encoding='utf-8')
17981378 'content of c'
17981394 existence:
17981406 >>> c.exists()
17981426 >>> (b / 'missing.txt').exists()
17981459 False
17981466 Coercion to string:
17981487 >>> import os
17981501 >>> str(c).replace(os.sep, posixpath.sep)
17981543 'mem/abcde.zip/b/c.txt'
17981568 At the root, ``name``, ``filename``, and ``parent``
17981620 resolve to the zipfile.
17981645 >>> str(path)

17981676 >>> path.name
17981690 'abcde.zip'
17981702 >>> path.filename == pathlib.Path('mem/abcde.zip')
17981758 >>> str(path.parent)
17981779 'mem'

17981826 attributes are not
17981845 valid and accessing them will raise an Exception.
17981896 >>> zf.filename = None

18243864 aitems
18243871 uCreate a new task collection/namespace.
18243913         `.Collection` offers a set of methods for building a collection of
18243988         tasks from scratch, plus a convenient constructor wrapping said API.
18244066         In either case:
18244091         * The first positional argument may be a string, which (if given) is
18244168           used as the collection's default name when performing namespace
18244242           lookups;
18244261         * A ``loaded_from`` keyword argument may be given, which sets metadata
18244340           indicating the filesystem path the collection was loaded from. This
18244418           is used as a guide when loading per-project :ref:`configuration files
18244498           <config-hierarchy>`.
18244529         * An ``auto_dash_names`` kwarg may be given, controlling whether task
18244607           and collection names have underscores turned to dashes in most cases;
18244687           it defaults to ``True`` but may be set to ``False`` to disable.
18244762           The CLI machinery will pass in the value of the
18244820           ``tasks.auto_dash_names`` config value to this kwarg.
18244885         **The method approach**
18244918         May initialize with no arguments and use methods (e.g.
18244981         `.add_task`/`.add_collection`) to insert objects::
18245041             c = Collection()
18245070             c.add_task(some_task)
18245105         If an initial string argument is given, it is used as the default name
18245184         for this collection, should it be inserted into another collection as a
18245264         sub-namespace::
18245289             docs = Collection('docs')
18245327             docs.add_task(doc_task)
18245363             ns = Collection()
18245393             ns.add_task(top_level_task)
18245433             ns.add_collection(docs)
18245469             # Valid identifiers are now 'top_level_task' and 'docs.doc_task'
18245546             # (assuming the task objects were actually named the same as the
18245623             # variables we're using :))
18245664         For details, see the API docs for the rest of the class.
18245730         **The constructor approach**
18245768         All ``*args`` given to `.Collection` (besides the abovementioned
18245841         optional positional 'name' argument and ``loaded_from`` kwarg) are
18245916         expected to be `.Task` or `.Collection` instances which will be passed
18245995         to `.add_task`/`.add_collection` as appropriate. Module objects are
18246071         also valid (as they are for `.add_collection`). For example, the below
18246150         snippet results in the same two task identifiers as the one above::
18246227             ns = Collection(top_level_task, Collection('docs', doc_task))
18246302         If any ``**kwargs`` are given, the keywords are used as the initial
18246378         name arguments for the respective values::
18246430             ns = Collection(
18246459                 top_level_task=some_other_task,
18246507                 docs=Collection(doc_task)
18246549             )
18246564         That's exactly equivalent to::
18246604             docs = Collection(doc_task)
18246644             ns = Collection()
18246674             ns.add_task(some_other_task, 'top_level_task')
18246733             ns.add_collection(docs, 'docs')
18246778         See individual methods' API docs for details.
18246832

18247841 aconfigure
18247852 uReturn a new `.Collection` created from ``module``.
18247906         Inspects ``module`` for any `.Task` instances and adds them to a new
18247983         `.Collection`, returning it. If any explicit namespace collections
18248058         exist (named ``ns`` or ``namespace``) a copy of that collection object
18248137         is preferentially loaded instead.
18248180         When the implicit/default collection is generated, it will be named
18248256         after the module's ``__name__`` attribute, or its last dotted section
18248334         if it's a submodule. (I.e. it should usually map to the actual ``.py``
18248413         filename.)
18248433         Explicitly given collections will only be given that module-derived
18248509         name if they don't already have a valid ``.name`` attribute.
18248579         If the module has a docstring (``__doc__``) it is copied onto the
18248653         resulting `.Collection` (and used for display in help, list etc
18248725         output.)
18248743         :param str name:
18248768             A string, which if given will override any automatically derived
18248845             collection name (or name set on the module's root namespace, if it
18248924             has one.)
18248947         :param dict config:
18248975             Used to set config options on the newly created `.Collection`
18249049             before returning it (saving you a call to `.configure`.)
18249119             If the imported module had a root namespace object, ``config`` is
18249197             merged on top of it (i.e. overriding any conflicts.)
18249263         :param str loaded_from:
18249295             Identical to the same-named kwarg from the regular class
18249364             constructor - should be the path where the module was
18249430             found.
18249450         :param bool auto_dash_names:
18249487             Identical to the same-named kwarg from the regular class
18249556             constructor - determines whether emitted names are auto-dashed.
18249633         .. versionadded:: 1.0
18249663

18264567 amerge
18264574 uCreates a new config object.
18264605         :param dict defaults:
18264635             A dict containing default (lowest level) config data. Default:
18264710             `global_defaults`.
18264742         :param dict overrides:
18264773             A dict containing override-level config data. Default: ``{}``.
18264849         :param str system_prefix:
18264883             Base path for the global config file location; combined with the
18264960             prefix and file suffixes to arrive at final file path candidates.
18265039             Default: ``/etc/`` (thus e.g. ``/etc/invoke.yaml`` or
18265105             ``/etc/invoke.json``).
18265141         :param str user_prefix:
18265173             Like ``system_prefix`` but for the per-user config file. These
18265248             variables are joined as strings, not via path-style joins, so they
18265327             may contain partial file paths; for the per-user config file this
18265405             often means a leading dot, to make the final result a hidden file
18265483             on most systems.
18265513             Default: ``~/.`` (e.g. ``~/.invoke.yaml``).
18265570         :param str project_location:
18265607             Optional directory path of the currently loaded `.Collection` (as
18265685             loaded by `.Loader`). When non-empty, will trigger seeking of
18265759             per-project config files in this directory.
18265816         :param str runtime_path:
18265849             Optional file path to a runtime configuration file.
18265914             Used to fill the penultimate slot in the config hierarchy. Should
18265992             be a full file path to an existing file, not a directory path or a
18266071             prefix.
18266092         :param bool lazy:
18266118             Whether to automatically load some of the lower config levels.
18266194             By default (``lazy=False``), ``__init__`` automatically calls
18266268             `load_system` and `load_user` to load system and user config files,
18266348             respectively.
18266375             For more control over what is loaded when, you can say
18266442             ``lazy=True``, and no automatic loading is done.
18266504             .. note::
18266526                 If you give ``defaults`` and/or ``overrides`` as ``__init__``
18266604                 kwargs instead of waiting to use `load_defaults` or
18266672                 `load_overrides` afterwards, those *will* still end up 'loaded'
18266752                 immediately.

18273269 acopy
18273275 uReturn a copy of this configuration object.
18273321         The new object will be identical in terms of configured sources and any
18273401         loaded (or user-manipulated) data, but will be a distinct object with
18273479         as little shared mutable state as possible.
18273532         Specifically, all `dict` values within the config are recursively
18273606         recreated, with non-dict leaf values subjected to `copy.copy` (note:
18273683         *not* `copy.deepcopy`, as this can cause issues with various objects
18273760         such as compiled regexen or threading locks, often found buried deep
18273837         within rich aggregates like API or DB clients).
18273894         The only remaining config values that may end up shared between a
18273968         config and its clone are thus those 'rich' objects that do not
18274039         `copy.copy` cleanly, or compound non-dict objects (such as lists or
18274115         tuples).
18274133         :param into:
18274154             A `.Config` subclass that the new clone should be "upgraded" to.
18274232             Used by client libraries which have their own `.Config` subclasses
18274311             that e.g. define additional defaults; cloning "into" one of these
18274389             subclasses ensures that any new keys/subtrees are added gracefully,
18274469             without overwriting anything that may have been pre-defined.
18274543             Default: ``None`` (just clone into another regular `.Config`).
18274619         :returns:
18274637             A `.Config`, or an instance of the class given to ``into``.
18274710         .. versionadded:: 1.0
