18279302 a__prepare__
18279315 aConfig
18279323 u%s.__prepare__() must return a mapping, not %s
18279371 u<metaclass>
18279384 uInvoke's primary configuration handling class.
18279433     See :doc:`/concepts/configuration` for details on the configuration system
18279512     this class implements, including the :ref:`configuration hierarchy
18279583     <config-hierarchy>`. The rest of this class' documentation assumes
18279654     familiarity with that document.
18279691     **Access**
18279707     Configuration values may be accessed and/or updated using dict syntax::
18279784         config['foo']
18279807     or attribute syntax::
18279834         config.foo
18279854     Nesting works the same way - dict config values are turned into objects
18279930     which honor both the dictionary protocol and the attribute-access method::
18280010        config['foo']['bar']
18280038        config.foo.bar
18280061     **A note about attribute access and methods**
18280112     This class implements the entire dictionary protocol: methods such as
18280186     ``keys``, ``values``, ``items``, ``pop`` and so forth should all function
18280264     as they do on regular dicts. It also implements new config-specific methods
18280344     such as `load_system`, `load_collection`, `merge`, `clone`, etc.
18280414     .. warning::
18280431         Accordingly, this means that if you have configuration options sharing
18280510         names with these methods, you **must** use dictionary syntax (e.g.
18280585         ``myconfig['keys']``) to access the configuration data.
18280650     **Lifecycle**
18280669     At initialization time, `.Config`:
18280709     - creates per-level data structures;
18280750     - stores any levels supplied to `__init__`, such as defaults or overrides,
18280829       as well as the various config file paths/filename patterns;
18280895     - and loads config files, if found (though typically this just means system
18280975       and user-level files, as project and runtime files need more info before
18281054       they can be found and loaded.)
18281092         - This step can be skipped by specifying ``lazy=True``.
18281157     At this point, `.Config` is fully usable - and because it pre-emptively
18281233     loads some config files, those config files can affect anything that
18281306     comes after, like CLI parsing or loading of task collections.
18281373     In the CLI use case, further processing is done after instantiation, using
18281452     the ``load_*`` methods such as `load_overrides`, `load_project`, etc:
18281527     - the result of argument/option parsing is applied to the overrides level;
18281606     - a project-level config file is loaded, as it's dependent on a loaded
18281681       tasks collection;
18281705     - a runtime config file is loaded, if its flag was supplied;
18281770     - then, for each task being executed:
18281813         - per-collection data is loaded (only possible now that we have
18281885           collection & task in hand);
18281923         - shell environment data is loaded (must be done at end of process due
18282002           to using the rest of the config as a guide for interpreting env var
18282080           names.)
18282099     At this point, the config object is handed to the task being executed, as
18282177     part of its execution `.Context`.
18282216     Any modifications made directly to the `.Config` itself after this point
18282293     end up stored in their own (topmost) config level, making it easier to
18282368     debug final values.
18282393     Finally, any *deletions* made to the `.Config` (e.g. applications of
18282466     dict-style mutators like ``pop``, ``clear`` etc) are also tracked in their
18282545     own structure, allowing the config object to honor such method calls
18282618     without mutating the underlying source data.
18282668     **Special class attributes**
18282702     The following class-level attributes are used for low-level configuration
18282780     of the config system itself, such as which file paths to load. They are
18282856     primarily intended for overriding by subclasses.
18282910     - ``prefix``: Supplies the default value for ``file_prefix`` (directly) and
18282990       ``env_prefix`` (uppercased). See their descriptions for details. Its
18283065       default value is ``"invoke"``.
18283102     - ``file_prefix``: The config file 'basename' default (though it is not a
18283180       literal basename; it can contain path parts if desired) which is appended
18283260       to the configured values of ``system_prefix``, ``user_prefix``, etc, to
18283338       arrive at the final (pre-extension) file paths.
18283393       Thus, by default, a system-level config file path concatenates the
18283466       ``system_prefix`` of ``/etc/`` with the ``file_prefix`` of ``invoke`` to
18283545       arrive at paths like ``/etc/invoke.json``.
18283595       Defaults to ``None``, meaning to use the value of ``prefix``.
18283664     - ``env_prefix``: A prefix used (along with a joining underscore) to
18283737       determine which environment variables are loaded as the env var
18283807       configuration level. Since its default is the value of ``prefix``
18283879       capitalized, this means env vars like ``INVOKE_RUN_ECHO`` are sought by
18283957       default.
18283973       Defaults to ``None``, meaning to use the value of ``prefix``.
18284042     .. versionadded:: 1.0

18288959 a_sudo
18288966 uExecute a shell command via ``sudo`` with password auto-response.
18289034         **Basics**
18289054         This method is identical to `run` but adds a handful of
18289118         convenient behaviors around invoking the ``sudo`` program. It doesn't
18289196         do anything users could not do themselves by wrapping `run`, but the
18289273         use case is too common to make users reinvent these wheels themselves.
18289353         .. note::
18289371             If you intend to respond to sudo's password prompt by hand, just
18289448             use ``run("sudo command")`` instead! The autoresponding features in
18289528             this method will just get in your way.
18289580         Specifically, `sudo`:
18289611         * Places a `.FailingResponder` into the ``watchers`` kwarg (see
18289683           :doc:`/concepts/watchers`) which:
18289728             * searches for the configured ``sudo`` password prompt;
18289796             * responds with the configured sudo password (``sudo.password``
18289872               from the :doc:`configuration </concepts/configuration>`);
18289944             * can tell when that response causes an authentication failure
18290019               (e.g. if the system requires a password and one was not
18290089               configured), and raises `.AuthFailure` if so.
18290150         * Builds a ``sudo`` command string using the supplied ``command``
18290224           argument, prefixed by various flags (see below);
18290283         * Executes that command via a call to `run`, returning the result.
18290359         **Flags used**
18290383         ``sudo`` flags used under the hood include:
18290436         - ``-S`` to allow auto-responding of password via stdin;
18290501         - ``-p <prompt>`` to explicitly state the prompt to use, so we can be
18290579           sure our auto-responder knows what to look for;
18290637         - ``-u <user>`` if ``user`` is not ``None``, to execute the command as
18290716           a user other than ``root``;
18290754         - When ``-u`` is present, ``-H`` is also added, to ensure the
18290824           subprocess has the requested user's ``$HOME`` set properly.
18290895         **Configuring behavior**
18290929         There are a couple of ways to change how this method behaves:
18291000         - Because it wraps `run`, it honors all `run` config parameters and
18291076           keyword arguments, in the same way that `run` does.
18291139             - Thus, invocations such as ``c.sudo('command', echo=True)`` are
18291216               possible, and if a config layer (such as a config file or env
18291292               var) specifies that e.g. ``run.warn = True``, that too will take
18291371               effect under `sudo`.
18291407         - `sudo` has its own set of keyword arguments (see below) and they are
18291486           also all controllable via the configuration system, under the
18291558           ``sudo.*`` tree.
18291586             - Thus you could, for example, pre-set a sudo user in a config
18291661               file; such as an ``invoke.json`` containing ``{"sudo": {"user":
18291739               "someuser"}}``.
18291770         :param str password: Runtime override for ``sudo.password``.
18291839         :param str user: Runtime override for ``sudo.user``.
18291901         .. versionadded:: 1.0
18291931

18292480 u && 
18292486 uPrefixes ``command`` with all prefixes found in ``command_prefixes``.
18292558         ``command_prefixes`` is a list of strings which is modified by the
18292633         `prefix` context manager.
18292667         
18292676 uPrefix all nested `run`/`sudo` commands with given command plus ``&&``.
18292750         Most of the time, you'll want to be using this alongside a shell script
18292830         which alters shell state, such as ones which export or alter shell
18292905         environment variables.
18292937         For example, one of the most common uses of this tool is with the
18293011         ``workon`` command from `virtualenvwrapper
18293062         <https://virtualenvwrapper.readthedocs.io/en/latest/>`_::
18293129             with c.prefix('workon myvenv'):
18293173                 c.run('./manage.py migrate')
18293219         In the above snippet, the actual shell command run would be this::
18293295             $ workon myvenv && ./manage.py migrate
18293347         This context manager is compatible with `cd`, so if your virtualenv
18293423         doesn't ``cd`` in its ``postactivate`` script, you could do the
18293495         following::
18293516             with c.cd('/path/to/app'):
18293555                 with c.prefix('workon myvenv'):
18293603                     c.run('./manage.py migrate')
18293652                     c.run('./manage.py loaddata fixture')
18293711         Which would result in executions like so::
18293763             $ cd /path/to/app && workon myvenv && ./manage.py migrate
18293833             $ cd /path/to/app && workon myvenv && ./manage.py loaddata fixture
18293913         Finally, as alluded to above, `prefix` may be nested if desired, e.g.::
18293994             with c.prefix('workon myenv'):
18294037                 c.run('ls')
18294065                 with c.prefix('source /some/script'):
18294119                     c.run('touch a_file')
18294162         The result::
18294184             $ workon myenv && ls
18294217             $ workon myenv && source /some/script && touch a_file
18294284         Contrived, but hopefully illustrative.
18294332         .. versionadded:: 1.0

18294529 ajoin
18294535 uReturn the current working directory, accounting for uses of `cd`.
18294604         .. versionadded:: 1.0
18294634         
18294643 uContext manager that keeps directory state when executing commands.
18294713         Any calls to `run`, `sudo`, within the wrapped block will implicitly
18294790         have a string similar to ``"cd <path> && "`` prefixed in order to give
18294869         the sense that there is actually statefulness involved.
18294934         Because use of `cd` affects all such invocations, any code making use
18295012         of the `cwd` property will also be affected by use of `cd`.
18295081         Like the actual 'cd' shell builtin, `cd` may be called with relative
18295158         paths (keep in mind that your default starting directory is your user's
18295238         ``$HOME``) and may be nested as well.
18295285         Below is a "normal" attempt at using the shell 'cd', which doesn't work
18295365         since all commands are executed in individual subprocesses -- state is
18295444         **not** kept between invocations of `run` or `sudo`::
18295507             c.run('cd /var/www')
18295540             c.run('ls')
18295565         The above snippet will list the contents of the user's ``$HOME``
18295638         instead of ``/var/www``. With `cd`, however, it will work as expected::
18295719             with c.cd('/var/www'):
18295754                 c.run('ls')  # Turns into "cd /var/www && ls"
18295817         Finally, a demonstration (see inline comments) of nesting::
18295886             with c.cd('/var/www'):
18295921                 c.run('ls') # cd /var/www && ls
18295969                 with c.cd('website1'):
18296008                     c.run('ls')  # cd /var/www/website1 && ls
18296071         .. note::
18296089             Space characters will be escaped automatically to make dealing with
18296169             such directory names easier.
18296211         .. versionadded:: 1.0
18296241         .. versionchanged:: 1.5
18296273             Explicitly cast the ``path`` argument (the only argument) to a
18296348             string; this allows any object defining ``__str__`` to be handed in
18296428             (such as the various ``Path`` objects out there), and not just
18296503             string literals.

18296815 awraps
18296822 uCreate a ``Context``-like object whose methods yield `.Result` objects.
18296896         :param config:
18296919             A Configuration object to use. Identical in behavior to `.Context`.
18297000         :param run:
18297020             A data structure indicating what `.Result` objects to return from
18297098             calls to the instantiated object's `~.Context.run` method (instead
18297177             of actually executing the requested shell command).
18297242             Specifically, this kwarg accepts:
18297289             - A single `.Result` object.
18297330             - A boolean; if True, yields a `.Result` whose ``exited`` is ``0``,
18297410               and if False, ``1``.
18297445             - An iterable of the above values, which will be returned on each
18297523               subsequent call to ``.run`` (the first item on the first call,
18297600               the second on the second call, etc).
18297651             - A dict mapping command strings or compiled regexen to the above
18297729               values (including an iterable), allowing specific
18297793               call-and-response semantics instead of assuming a call order.
18297870         :param sudo:
18297891             Identical to ``run``, but whose values are yielded from calls to
18297968             `~.Context.sudo`.
18297999         :param bool repeat:
18298027             A flag determining whether results yielded by this class' methods
18298105             repeat or are consumed.
18298142             For example, when a single result is indicated, it will normally
18298219             only be returned once, causing ``NotImplementedError`` afterwards.
18298298             But when ``repeat=True`` is given, that result is returned on
18298372             every call, forever.
18298406             Similarly, iterable results are normally exhausted once, but when
18298484             this setting is enabled, they are wrapped in `itertools.cycle`.
18298561             Default: ``True``.
18298593         :raises:
18298610             ``TypeError``, if the values given to ``run`` or other kwargs
18298684             aren't of the expected types.
18298727         .. versionchanged:: 1.5
18298759             Added support for boolean and string result values.
18298823         .. versionchanged:: 1.5
18298855             Added support for regex dict keys.
18298902         .. versionchanged:: 1.5
18298934             Added the ``repeat`` keyword argument.
18298985         .. versionchanged:: 2.0
18299017             Changed ``repeat`` default value from ``False`` to ``True``.

18300737 uinvoke.context
18300753 uContext-aware API wrapper & state-passing object.
18300805     `.Context` objects are created during command-line parsing (or, if desired,
18300885     by hand) and used to share parser and configuration state with executed
18300961     tasks (see :ref:`why-context`).
18300998     Specifically, the class offers wrappers for core API calls (such as `.run`)
18301078     which take into account CLI parser flags, configuration files, and/or
18301152     changes made at runtime. It also acts as a proxy for its `~.Context.config`
18301232     attribute - see that attribute's documentation for details.
18301297     Instances of `.Context` may be shared between tasks when executing
18301368     sub-tasks - either the same context the caller was given, or an altered
18301444     copy thereof (or, theoretically, a brand new one).
18301500     .. versionadded:: 1.0

18308553 aFailure
18308562 uException subclass representing failure of a command execution.
18308628     "Failure" may mean the command executed and the shell indicated an unusual
18308707     result (usually, a non-zero exit code), or it may mean something else, like
18308787     a ``sudo`` command which was aborted when the supplied password failed
18308862     authentication.
18308883     Two attributes allow introspection to determine the nature of the problem:
18308963     * ``result``: a `.Result` instance with info about the command being
18309036       executed and, if it ran to completion, how it exited.
18309096     * ``reason``: a wrapped exception instance if applicable (e.g. a
18309165       `.StreamWatcher` raised `WatcherError`) or ``None`` otherwise, in which
18309243       case, it's probably a `Failure` subclass indicating its own specific
18309318       nature, such as `UnexpectedExit` or `CommandTimedOut`.
18309380     This class is only rarely raised by itself; most of the time `.Runner.run`
18309459     (or a wrapper of same, such as `.Context.sudo`) will raise a specific
18309533     subclass like `UnexpectedExit` or `AuthFailure`.
18309587     .. versionadded:: 1.0

18311143 aExit
18311149 uSimple custom stand-in for SystemExit.
18311190     Replaces scattered sys.exit calls, improves testability, allows one to
18311265     catch an exit request without intercepting real SystemExits (typically an
18311343     unfriendly thing to do, as most users calling `sys.exit` rather expect it
18311421     to truly exit.)
18311442     Defaults to a non-printing, exit-0 friendly termination behavior if the
18311518     exception is uncaught.
18311546     If ``code`` (an int) given, that code is used to exit.
18311606     If ``message`` (a string) given, it is printed to standard error, and the
18311684     program exits with code ``1`` by default (unless overridden by also giving
18311763     ``code`` explicitly.)

18315925 akwargs
18315933 uExecute one or more ``tasks`` in sequence.
18315978         :param tasks:
18316000             An all-purpose iterable of "tasks to execute", each member of which
18316080             may take one of the following forms:
18316130             **A string** naming a task from the Executor's `.Collection`. This
18316209             name may contain dotted syntax appropriate for calling namespaced
18316287             tasks, e.g. ``subcollection.taskname``. Such tasks are executed
18316363             without arguments.
18316395             **A two-tuple** whose first element is a task name string (as
18316469             above) and whose second element is a dict suitable for use as
18316543             ``**kwargs`` when calling the named task. E.g.::
18316605                 [
18316623                     ('task1', {}),
18316658                     ('task2', {'arg1': 'val1'}),
18316707                     ...
18316731                 ]
18316750             is equivalent, roughly, to::
18316792                 task1()
18316816                 task2(arg1='val1')
18316852             **A `.ParserContext`** instance, whose ``.name`` attribute is used
18316931             as the task name and whose ``.as_kwargs`` attribute is used as the
18317010             task kwargs (again following the above specifications).
18317079             .. note::
18317101                 When called without any arguments at all (i.e. when ``*tasks``
18317180                 is empty), the default task from ``self.collection`` is used
18317257                 instead, if defined.
18317295         :returns:
18317313             A dict mapping task objects to their return values.
18317378             This dict may include pre- and post-tasks if any were executed. For
18317458             example, in a collection with a ``build`` task depending on another
18317538             task named ``setup``, executing ``build`` will result in a dict
18317614             with two keys, one for ``build`` and one for ``setup``.
18317683         .. versionadded:: 1.0

18324816 uinvoke.parser.argument
18324840 uA command-line argument/flag.
18324872     :param name:
18324889         Syntactic sugar for ``names=[<name>]``. Giving both ``name`` and
18324962         ``names`` is invalid.
18324992     :param names:
18325010         List of valid identifiers for this argument. For example, a "help"
18325085         argument may be defined with a name list of ``['-h', '--help']``.
18325159     :param kind:
18325176         Type factory & parser hint. E.g. ``int`` will turn the default text
18325252         value parsed, into a Python integer; and ``bool`` will tell the
18325324         parser not to expect an actual value but to treat the argument as a
18325400         toggle/flag.
18325421     :param default:
18325441         Default value made available to the parser if no value is given on the
18325520         command line.

18341543 uCreate a new, parameterized `.Program` instance.
18341594         :param str version:
18341622             The program's version, e.g. ``"0.1.0"``. Defaults to ``"unknown"``.
18341703         :param namespace:
18341729             A `.Collection` to use as this program's subcommands.
18341796             If ``None`` (the default), the program will behave like ``invoke``,
18341876             seeking a nearby task namespace with a `.Loader` and exposing
18341950             arguments such as :option:`--list` and :option:`--collection` for
18342028             inspecting or selecting specific namespaces.
18342086             If given a `.Collection` object, will use it as if it had been
18342161             handed to :option:`--collection`. Will also update the parser to
18342238             remove references to tasks and task-related options, and display
18342315             the subcommands in ``--help`` output. The result will be a program
18342394             that has a static set of subcommands.
18342445         :param str name:
18342470             The program's name, as displayed in ``--version`` output.
18342541             If ``None`` (default), is a capitalized version of the first word
18342619             in the ``argv`` handed to `.run`. For example, when invoked from a
18342698             binstub installed as ``foobar``, it will default to ``Foobar``.
18342775         :param str binary:
18342802             Descriptive lowercase binary name string used in help text.
18342875             For example, Invoke's own internal value for this is ``inv[oke]``,
18342954             denoting that it is installed as both ``inv`` and ``invoke``. As
18343031             this is purely text intended for help display, it may be in any
18343107             format you wish, though it should match whatever you've put into
18343184             your ``setup.py``'s ``console_scripts`` entry.
18343244             If ``None`` (default), uses the first word in ``argv`` verbatim (as
18343324             with ``name`` above, except not capitalized).
18343383         :param binary_names:
18343412             List of binary name strings, for use in completion scripts.
18343485             This list ensures that the shell completion scripts generated by
18343562             :option:`--print-completion-script` instruct the shell to use
18343636             that completion for all of this program's installed names.
18343708             For example, Invoke's internal default for this is ``["inv",
18343781             "invoke"]``.
18343807             If ``None`` (the default), the first word in ``argv`` (in the
18343881             invocation of :option:`--print-completion-script`) is used in a
18343957             single-item list.
18343988         :param loader_class:
18344017             The `.Loader` subclass to use when loading task collections.
18344091             Defaults to `.FilesystemLoader`.
18344137         :param executor_class:
18344168             The `.Executor` subclass to use when executing tasks.
18344235             Defaults to `.Executor`; may also be overridden at runtime by the
18344313             :ref:`configuration system <default-values>` and its
18344378             ``tasks.executor_class`` setting (anytime that setting is not
18344452             ``None``).
18344476         :param config_class:
18344505             The `.Config` subclass to use for the base config object.
18344576             Defaults to `.Config`.

18344644             Added the ``binary_names`` argument.

18357672 a_run_body
18357683 astop
18357689 uExecute ``command``, returning an instance of `Result` once complete.
18357761         By default, this method is synchronous (it only returns once the
18357834         subprocess has completed), and allows interactive keyboard
18357901         communication with the subprocess.
18357945         It can instead behave asynchronously (returning early & requiring
18358019         interaction with the resulting object to manage subprocess lifecycle)
18358097         if you specify ``asynchronous=True``. Furthermore, you can completely
18358175         disassociate the subprocess from Invoke's control (allowing it to
18358249         persist on its own after Python exits) by saying ``disown=True``. See
18358327         the per-kwarg docs below for details on both of these.
18358391         .. note::
18358409             All kwargs will default to the values found in this instance's
18358484             `~.Runner.context` attribute, specifically in its configuration's
18358562             ``run`` subtree (e.g. ``run.echo`` provides the default value for
18358640             the ``echo`` keyword, etc). The base default values are described
18358718             in the parameter list below.
18358760         :param str command: The shell command to execute.
18358819         :param bool asynchronous:
18358853             When set to ``True`` (default ``False``), enables asynchronous
18358928             behavior, as follows:
18358963             - Connections to the controlling terminal are disabled, meaning you
18359043               will not see the subprocess output and it will not respond to
18359119               your keyboard input - similar to ``hide=True`` and
18359184               ``in_stream=False`` (though explicitly given
18359243               ``(out|err|in)_stream`` file-like objects will still be honored
18359321               as normal).
18359347             - `.run` returns immediately after starting the subprocess, and its
18359427               return value becomes an instance of `Promise` instead of
18359498               `Result`.
18359522             - `Promise` objects are primarily useful for their `~Promise.join`
18359601               method, which blocks until the subprocess exits (similar to
18359675               threading APIs) and either returns a final `~Result` or raises an
18359755               exception, just as a synchronous ``run`` would.
18359818                 - As with threading and similar APIs, users of
18359881                   ``asynchronous=True`` should make sure to ``join`` their
18359956                   `Promise` objects to prevent issues with interpreter
18360027                   shutdown.
18360055                 - One easy way to handle such cleanup is to use the `Promise`
18360133                   as a context manager - it will automatically ``join`` at the
18360212                   exit of the context block.
18360258             .. versionadded:: 1.4
18360293         :param bool disown:
18360321             When set to ``True`` (default ``False``), returns immediately like
18360400             ``asynchronous=True``, but does not perform any background work
18360476             related to that subprocess (it is completely ignored). This allows
18360555             subprocesses using shell backgrounding or similar techniques (e.g.
18360634             trailing ``&``, ``nohup``) to persist beyond the lifetime of the
18360711             Python process running Invoke.
18360755             .. note::
18360777                 If you're unsure whether you want this or ``asynchronous``, you
18360857                 probably want ``asynchronous``!
18360906             Specifically, ``disown=True`` has the following behaviors:
18360978             - The return value is still a `Result`, but it is severely limited
18361057               in functionality & data, per below.
18361107             - No I/O worker threads are spun up, so you will have no access to
18361186               the subprocess' stdout/stderr (those attributes on the result
18361262               will be empty strings), your stdin will not be forwarded,
18361334               ``(out|err|in)_stream`` will be ignored, and features like
18361407               ``watchers`` will not function.
18361453             - No exit code is checked for, so you will not receive any errors
18361531               if the subprocess fails to exit cleanly, the result's ``exited``
18361610               will be ``None``, and convenience properties like `ok` and
18361683               `failed` will not be reliable.
18361728             - ``pty=True`` may not function correctly (subprocesses may not run
18361808               at all; this seems to be a potential bug in Python's
18361875               ``pty.fork``) unless your command line includes tools such as
18361951               ``nohup`` or (the shell builtin) ``disown``.
18362011             .. versionadded:: 1.4
18362045             .. versionchanged:: 3.0
18362081                 The return value when ``disown=True`` changed from `None` to
18362158                 `Result`.
18362185         :param bool dry:
18362210             Whether to dry-run instead of truly invoking the given command. See
18362290             :option:`--dry` (which flips this on globally) for details on this
18362369             behavior.
18362392             .. versionadded:: 1.3
18362427         :param bool echo:
18362453             Controls whether `.run` prints the command string to local stdout
18362531             prior to executing it. Default: ``False``.
18362587             .. note::
18362609                 ``hide=True`` will override ``echo=True`` if both are given.
18362687         :param echo_format:
18362715             A string, which when passed to Python's inbuilt ``.format`` method,
18362795             will change the format of the output when ``run.echo`` is set to
18362872             true.
18362891             Currently, only ``{command}`` is supported as a parameter.
18362963             Defaults to printing the full command string in ANSI-escaped bold.
18363043         :param bool echo_stdin:
18363075             Whether to write data from ``in_stream`` back to ``out_stream``.
18363153             In other words, in normal interactive usage, this parameter
18363225             controls whether Invoke mirrors what you type back to your
18363296             terminal.
18363319             By default (when ``None``), this behavior is triggered by the
18363393             following:
18363417                 * Not using a pty to run the subcommand (i.e. ``pty=False``),
18363495                   as ptys natively echo stdin to stdout on their own;
18363565                 * And when the controlling terminal of Invoke itself (as per
18363642                   ``in_stream``) appears to be a valid terminal device or TTY.
18363721                   (Specifically, when `~invoke.util.isatty` yields a ``True``
18363799                   result when given ``in_stream``.)
18363852                   .. note::
18363880                       This property tends to be ``False`` when piping another
18363958                       program's output into an Invoke session, or when running
18364037                       Invoke within another program (e.g. running Invoke from
18364115                       itself).
18364147             If both of those properties are true, echoing will occur; if either
18364227             is false, no echoing will be performed.
18364280             When not ``None``, this parameter will override that auto-detection
18364360             and force, or disable, echoing.
18364405         :param str encoding:
18364434             Override auto-detection of which encoding the subprocess is using
18364512             for its stdout/stderr streams (which defaults to the return value
18364590             of `default_encoding`).
18364627         :param err_stream:
18364654             Same as ``out_stream``, except for standard error, and defaulting
18364732             to ``sys.stderr``.
18364764         :param dict env:
18364789             By default, subprocesses receive a copy of Invoke's own environment
18364869             (i.e. ``os.environ``). Supply a dict here to update that child
18364944             environment.
18364970             For example, ``run('command', env={'PYTHONPATH':
18365031             '/some/virtual/env/maybe'})`` would modify the ``PYTHONPATH`` env
18365109             var, with the rest of the child's env looking identical to the
18365184             parent.
18365205             .. seealso:: ``replace_env`` for changing 'update' to 'replace'.
18365283         :param bool fallback:
18365313             Controls auto-fallback behavior re: problems offering a pty when
18365390             ``pty=True``. Whether this has any effect depends on the specific
18365468             `Runner` subclass being invoked. Default: ``True``.
18365533         :param hide:
18365554             Allows the caller to disable ``run``'s default behavior of copying
18365633             the subprocess' stdout and stderr to the controlling terminal.
18365708             Specify ``hide='out'`` (or ``'stdout'``) to hide only the stdout
18365785             stream, ``hide='err'`` (or ``'stderr'``) to hide only stderr, or
18365862             ``hide='both'`` (or ``True``) to hide both streams.
18365927             The default value is ``None``, meaning to print everything;
18365999             ``False`` will also disable hiding.
18366048             .. note::
18366070                 Stdout and stderr are always captured and stored in the
18366142                 ``Result`` object, regardless of ``hide``'s value.
18366210             .. note::
18366232                 ``hide=True`` will also override ``echo=True`` if both are
18366307                 given (either as kwargs or via config/CLI).
18366368         :param in_stream:
18366394             A file-like stream object to used as the subprocess' standard
18366468             input. If ``None`` (the default), ``sys.stdin`` will be used.
18366543             If ``False``, will disable stdin mirroring entirely (though other
18366621             functionality which writes to the subprocess' stdin, such as
18366694             autoresponding, will still function.) Disabling stdin mirroring can
18366774             help when ``sys.stdin`` is a misbehaving non-stream object, such as
18366854             under test harnesses or headless command runners.
18366917         :param out_stream:
18366944             A file-like stream object to which the subprocess' standard output
18367023             should be written. If ``None`` (the default), ``sys.stdout`` will
18367101             be used.
18367123         :param bool pty:
18367148             By default, ``run`` connects directly to the invoked process and
18367225             reads its stdout/stderr streams. Some programs will buffer (or even
18367305             behave) differently in this situation compared to using an actual
18367383             terminal or pseudoterminal (pty). To use a pty instead of the
18367457             default behavior, specify ``pty=True``.
18367510             .. warning::
18367535                 Due to their nature, ptys have a single output stream, so the
18367613                 ability to tell stdout apart from stderr is **not possible**
18367690                 when ``pty=True``. As such, all output will appear on
18367760                 ``out_stream`` (see below) and be captured into the ``stdout``
18367839                 result attribute. ``err_stream`` and ``stderr`` will always be
18367918                 empty when ``pty=True``.
18367960         :param bool replace_env:
18367993             When ``True``, causes the subprocess to receive the dictionary
18368068             given to ``env`` as its entire shell environment, instead of
18368141             updating a copy of ``os.environ`` (which is the default behavior).
18368220             Default: ``False``.
18368253         :param str shell:
18368279             Which shell binary to use. Default: ``/bin/bash`` (on Unix;
18368351             ``COMSPEC`` or ``cmd.exe`` on Windows.)
18368404         :param timeout:
18368428             Cause the runner to submit an interrupt to the subprocess and raise
18368508             `.CommandTimedOut`, if the command takes longer than ``timeout``
18368585             seconds to execute. Defaults to ``None``, meaning no timeout.
18368660             .. versionadded:: 1.3
18368695         :param bool warn:
18368721             Whether to warn and continue, instead of raising
18368782             `.UnexpectedExit`, when the executed command exits with a
18368852             nonzero status. Default: ``False``.
18368901             .. note::
18368923                 This setting has no effect on exceptions, which will still be
18369001                 raised, typically bundled in `.ThreadException` objects if they
18369081                 were raised by the IO worker threads.
18369136                 Similarly, `.WatcherError` exceptions raised by
18369200                 `.StreamWatcher` instances will also ignore this setting, and
18369278                 will usually be bundled inside `.Failure` objects (in order to
18369357                 preserve the execution context).
18369407                 Ditto `.CommandTimedOut` - basically, anything that prevents a
18369486                 command from actually getting to "exited with an exit code"
18369562                 ignores this flag.
18369598         :param watchers:
18369623             A list of `.StreamWatcher` instances which will be used to scan the
18369703             program's ``stdout`` or ``stderr`` and may write into its ``stdin``
18369783             (typically ``bytes`` objects) in response to patterns or other
18369858             heuristics.
18369883             See :doc:`/concepts/watchers` for details on this functionality.
18369961             Default: ``[]``.
18369991         :returns:
18370009             `Result`, or a subclass thereof.
18370055         :raises:
18370072             `.UnexpectedExit`, if the command exited nonzero and
18370137             ``warn`` was ``False``.
18370174         :raises:
18370191             `.Failure`, if the command didn't even exit cleanly, e.g. if a
18370266             `.StreamWatcher` raised `.WatcherError`.
18370320         :raises:
18370337             `.ThreadException` (if the background I/O threads encountered
18370411             exceptions other than `.WatcherError`).
18370464         .. versionadded:: 1.0

18391675 a__orig_bases__
18391691 uA container for information about the result of a command execution.
18391762     All params are exposed as attributes of the same name and type.
18391831     :param str stdout:
18391854         The subprocess' standard output.
18391896     :param str stderr:
18391919         Same as ``stdout`` but containing standard error (unless the process
18391996         was invoked via a pty, in which case it will be empty; see
18392063         `.Runner.run`.)
18392088     :param str encoding:
18392113         The string encoding used by the local shell environment.
18392179     :param str command:
18392203         The command which was executed.
18392244     :param str shell:
18392266         The shell binary used for execution.
18392312     :param dict env:
18392333         The shell environment used for execution. (Default is the empty dict,
18392411         ``{}``, not ``None`` as displayed in the signature.)
18392473     :param int exited:
18392496         An integer representing the subprocess' exit/return code.
18392563         .. note::
18392581             This may be ``None`` in situations where the subprocess did not run
18392661             to completion, such as when auto-responding failed or a timeout was
18392741             reached.
18392763     :param bool pty:
18392784         A boolean describing whether the subprocess was invoked with a pty or
18392862         not; see `.Runner.run`.
18392895     :param tuple hide:
18392918         A tuple of stream names (none, one or both of ``('stdout', 'stderr')``)
18392998         which were hidden from the user when the generating command executed;
18393076         this is a normalized value derived from the ``hide`` parameter of
18393150         `.Runner.run`.
18393174         For example, ``run('command', hide='stdout')`` will yield a `Result`
18393251         where ``result.hide == ('stdout',)``; ``hide=True`` or ``hide='both'``
18393330         results in ``result.hide == ('stdout', 'stderr')``; and ``hide=False``
18393409         (the default) generates ``result.hide == ()`` (the empty tuple.)
18393483     :param int pid:
18393503         The process ID of the subprocess that was executed (normally) or is
18393579         executing (when asynchronous or disowned).
18393631         .. versionadded:: 3.0
18393662     :param bool disowned:
18393688         Whether the subprocess was 'disowned' or detached from ourselves; in
18393765         this mode may other attributes or methods of this `Result` will be
18393840         unreliable, see `Runner.run` docs for details. You may want to use your
18393920         own methods to interrogate your operating system about this object's
18393997         ``pid``, however, which will usually be valid.
18394053         .. versionadded:: 3.0
18394084     .. note::
18394098         `Result` objects' truth evaluation is equivalent to their `.ok`
18394170         attribute's value. Therefore, quick-and-dirty expressions like the
18394245         following are possible::
18394279             if run("some shell command"):
18394321                 do_something()
18394352             else:
18394370                 handle_problem()
18394404         However, remember `Zen of Python #2
18394448         <http://zen-of-python.info/explicit-is-better-than-implicit.html#2>`_.
18394528     .. versionadded:: 1.0

18398181 uMarks wrapped callable object as a valid Invoke task.
18398237     May be called without any parentheses if no extra options need to be
18398310     specified. Otherwise, the following keyword arguments are allowed in the
18398387     parenthese'd form:
18398411     * ``name``: Default name to use when binding to a `.Collection`. Useful for
18398491       avoiding Python namespace issues (i.e. when the desired CLI level name
18398568       can't or shouldn't be used as the Python level name.)
18398628     * ``aliases``: Specify one or more aliases for this task, allowing it to be
18398708       invoked as multiple different names. For example, a task named ``mytask``
18398788       with a simple ``@task`` wrapper may only be invoked as ``"mytask"``.
18398863       Changing the decorator to be ``@task(aliases=['myothertask'])`` allows
18398940       invocation as ``"mytask"`` *or* ``"myothertask"``.
18398997     * ``positional``: Iterable overriding the parser's automatic "args with no
18399076       default value are considered positional" behavior. If a list of arg
18399150       names, no args besides those named in this iterable will be considered
18399227       positional. (This means that an empty list will force all arguments to be
18399307       given as explicit flags.)
18399339     * ``optional``: Iterable of argument names, declaring those args to
18399411       have :ref:`optional values <optional-values>`. Such arguments may be
18399486       given as value-taking options (e.g. ``--my-arg=myvalue``, wherein the
18399562       task is given ``"myvalue"``) or as Boolean flags (``--my-arg``, resulting
18399642       in ``True``).
18399662     * ``iterable``: Iterable of argument names, declaring them to :ref:`build
18399740       iterable values <iterable-flag-values>`.
18399787     * ``incrementable``: Iterable of argument names, declaring them to
18399858       :ref:`increment their values <incrementable-flag-values>`.
18399923     * ``default``: Boolean option specifying whether this task should be its
18400000       collection's default task (i.e. called if the collection's own name is
18400077       given.)
18400091     * ``auto_shortflags``: Whether or not to automatically create short
18400163       flags from task options; defaults to True.
18400212     * ``help``: Dict mapping argument names to their help strings. Will be
18400287       displayed in ``--help`` output. For arguments containing underscores
18400362       (which are transformed into dashes on the CLI by default), either the
18400438       dashed or underscored version may be supplied here.
18400496     * ``pre``, ``post``: Lists of task objects to execute prior to, or after,
18400574       the wrapped task whenever it is executed.
18400622     * ``autoprint``: Boolean determining whether to automatically print this
18400699       task's return value to standard output when invoked directly via the CLI.
18400779       Defaults to False.
18400804     * ``klass``: Class to instantiate/return. Defaults to `.Task`.
18400872     If any non-keyword arguments are given, they are taken as the value of the
18400951     ``pre`` kwarg for convenience's sake. (It is an error to give both
18401022     ``*args`` and ``pre`` at the same time.)
18401068     .. versionadded:: 1.0
18401094     .. versionchanged:: 1.1
18401122         Added the ``klass`` keyword argument.

18403374 uDescribes execution of a `.Task`, typically with pre-supplied arguments.
18403449     Useful for setting up :ref:`pre/post task invocations
18403507     <parameterizing-pre-post-tasks>`. It's actually just a convenient wrapper
18403585     around the `.Call` class, which may be used directly instead if desired.
18403663     For example, here's two build-like tasks that both refer to a ``setup``
18403739     pre-task, one with no baked-in argument values (and thus no need to use
18403815     `.call`), and one that toggles a boolean flag::
18403868         @task
18403882         def setup(c, clean=False):
18403917             if clean:
18403939                 c.run("rm -rf target")
18403978             # ... setup things here ...
18404018             c.run("tar czvf target.tgz target")
18404067         @task(pre=[setup])
18404094         def build(c):
18404116             c.run("build, accounting for leftover files...")
18404178         @task(pre=[call(setup, clean=True)])
18404223         def clean_build(c):
18404251             c.run("build, assuming clean slate...")
18404304     Please see the constructor docs for `.Call` for details - this function's
18404382     ``args`` and ``kwargs`` map directly to the same arguments as in that
18404456     method.

18407860 uDetect if given stdin ``stream`` seems to be in the foreground of a TTY.
18407935     Specifically, compares the current Python process group ID to that of the
18408013     stream's file descriptor to see if they match; if they do not match, it is
18408092     likely that the process has been placed in the background.
18408156     This is used as a test to determine whether we should manipulate an active
18408235     stdin so it runs in a character-buffered mode; touching the terminal in
18408311     this way when the process is backgrounded, causes most shells to pause
18408386     execution.
18408402     .. note::

18408496         fail this test, as it starts with "do you have a real ``fileno``?".

18413990 u<metaclass>
18414003 uinvoke.util
18414016 uThread handler making it easier for parent to handle thread exceptions.
18414090     Based in part on Fabric 1's ThreadHandler. See also Fabric GH issue #204.
18414169     When used directly, can be used in place of a regular ``threading.Thread``.
18414249     If subclassed, the subclass must do one of:
18414298     - supply ``target`` to ``__init__``
18414338     - define ``_run()`` instead of ``run()``
18414384     This is because this thread's entire point is to wrap behavior around the
18414462     thread's execution; subclasses could not redefine ``run()`` without
18414534     breaking that functionality.

18498869 uinvoke.watchers
18498886 uA class whose subclasses may act on seen stream data from subprocesses.
18498960     Subclasses must exhibit the following API; see `Responder` for a concrete
18499038     example.
18499052     * ``__init__`` is completely up to each subclass, though as usual,
18499123       subclasses *of* subclasses should be careful to make use of `super` where
18499203       appropriate.
18499222     * `submit` must accept the entire current contents of the stream being
18499297       watched, as a string, and may optionally return an iterable of strings
18499374       (or act as a generator iterator, i.e. multiple calls to ``yield
18499444       <string>``), which will each be written to the subprocess' standard
18499518       input.
18499532     .. note::
18499546         `StreamWatcher` subclasses exist in part to enable state tracking, such
18499626         as detecting when a submitted password didn't work & erroring (or
18499700         prompting a user, or etc). Such bookkeeping isn't easily achievable
18499776         with simple callback functions.
18499817     .. note::
18499831         `StreamWatcher` subclasses `threading.local` so that its instances can
18499910         be used to 'watch' both subprocess stdout and stderr in separate
18499983         threads.
18500001     .. versionadded:: 1.0

18619578 uAllows an SSH server to access a forwarded agent.
18619630     This also creates a unix domain socket on the system to allow external
18619705     programs to also access the agent. For this reason, you probably only want
18619784     to create one of these.
18619813     :meth:`connect` must be called before it is usable. This will also load the
18619893     list of keys the agent contains. You must also call :meth:`close` in
18619966     order to clean up the unix socket and the thread that maintains it.
18620038     (:class:`contextlib.closing` might be helpful to you.)
18620098     :param .Transport t: Transport used for SSH Agent communication forwarding
18620178     :raises: `.SSHException` -- mostly if we lost the agent

18620609 aAgentRequestHandler
18620630 uPrimary/default implementation of SSH agent forwarding functionality.
18620702     Simply instantiate this class, handing it a live command-executing session
18620781     object, and it will handle forwarding any local SSH agent processes it
18620856     finds.
18620868     For example::
18620887         # Connect
18620905         client = SSHClient()
18620934         client.connect(host, port, username)
18620979         # Obtain session
18621004         session = client.get_transport().open_session()
18621060         # Forward local agent
18621090         AgentRequestHandler(session)
18621127         # Commands executed after this point will see the forwarded agent on
18621204         # the remote end.
18621230         session.exec_command("git clone https://my.git.repository/")

18621325 a__clientProxys
18621341 aAgent
18621348 uClient interface for using private keys from an SSH agent running on the
18621422     local machine.  If an SSH agent is running, this class can be used to
18621496     connect to it and retrieve `.PKey` objects which can be used when
18621566     attempting to authenticate to remote SSH servers.
18621621     Upon initialization, a session with the local machine's SSH agent is
18621694     opened, if one is running. If no agent is running, initialization will
18621769     succeed, but `get_keys` will return an empty tuple.
18621826     :raises: `.SSHException` --
18621858         if an SSH agent is found, but speaks an incompatible protocol
18621929     .. versionchanged:: 2.10
18621958         Added support for native openssh agent on windows (extending previous
18622036         putty pageant support)

18638594 uRepresents a partial or complete SSH authentication attempt.
18638657     This class conceptually extends `AuthStrategy` by pairing the former's
18638732     authentication **sources** with the **results** of trying to authenticate
18638810     with them.
18638826     `AuthResult` is a (subclass of) `list` of `namedtuple`, which are of the
18638903     form ``namedtuple('SourceResult', 'source', 'result')`` (where the
18638974     ``source`` member is an `AuthSource` and the ``result`` member is either a
18639053     return value from the relevant `.Transport` method, or an exception
18639125     object).
18639139     .. note::
18639153         Transport auth method results are always themselves a ``list`` of "next
18639233         allowable authentication methods".
18639277         In the simple case of "you just authenticated successfully", it's an
18639354         empty list; if your auth was rejected but you're allowed to try again,
18639433         it will be a list of string method names like ``pubkey`` or
18639501         ``password``.
18639524         The ``__str__`` of this class represents the empty-list scenario as the
18639604         word ``success``, which should make reading the result of an
18639673         authentication session more obvious to humans.
18639729     Instances also have a `strategy` attribute referencing the `AuthStrategy`
18639807     which was attempted.

18658495 asettimeout
18658514 uSet blocking or non-blocking mode of the channel: if ``blocking`` is 0,
18658587         the channel is set to non-blocking mode; otherwise it's set to blocking
18658667         mode. Initially all channels are in blocking mode.
18658727         In non-blocking mode, if a `recv` call doesn't find any data, or if a
18658805         `send` call can't immediately dispose of the data, an error exception
18658883         is raised. In blocking mode, the calls block until they can proceed. An
18658963         EOF condition is considered "immediate data" for `recv`, so if the
18659038         channel is closed in the read direction, it will never block.
18659109         ``chan.setblocking(0)`` is equivalent to ``chan.settimeout(0)``;
18659182         ``chan.setblocking(1)`` is equivalent to ``chan.settimeout(None)``.
18659259         :param int blocking:
18659288             0 to set non-blocking mode; non-0 to set blocking mode.

18672906 u<metaclass>
18672919 uparamiko.channel
18672937 uA secure tunnel across an SSH `.Transport`.  A Channel is meant to behave
18673012     like a socket, and has an API that should be indistinguishable from the
18673088     Python socket API.
18673112     Because SSH2 has a windowing kind of flow control, if you stop reading data
18673192     from a Channel and its buffer fills up, the server will be unable to send
18673270     you any more data until you read some of it.  (This won't affect other
18673345     channels on the same transport -- all channels on a single transport are
18673422     flow-controlled independently.)  Similarly, if the server isn't reading
18673498     data you send, calls to `send` may block, unless you set a timeout.  This
18673576     is exactly like a normal network socket, so it shouldn't be too surprising.
18673657     Instances of this class may be used as context managers.

18682092 a_auth
18682099 uConnect to an SSH server and authenticate to it.  The server's host key
18682172         is checked against the system host keys (see `load_system_host_keys`)
18682250         and any local host keys (`load_host_keys`).  If the server's hostname
18682328         is not found in either set of host keys, the missing host key policy
18682405         is used (see `set_missing_host_key_policy`).  The default policy is
18682481         to reject the key and raise an `.SSHException`.
18682538         Authentication is attempted in the following order of priority:
18682611             - The ``pkey`` or ``key_filename`` passed in (if any)
18682678               - ``key_filename`` may contain OpenSSH public certificate paths
18682756                 as well as regular private-key paths; when files ending in
18682831                 ``-cert.pub`` are found, they are assumed to match a private
18682908                 key, and both components will be loaded. (The private key
18682982                 itself does *not* need to be listed in ``key_filename`` for
18683058                 this to occur - *just* the certificate.)
18683116             - Any key we can find through an SSH agent
18683171             - Any ``id_*`` keys discoverable in ``~/.ssh/``
18683232               - When OpenSSH-style public certificates exist that match an
18683307                 existing such private key (so e.g. one has ``id_rsa`` and
18683381                 ``id_rsa-cert.pub``) the certificate will be loaded alongside
18683459                 the private key and used for authentication.
18683521             - Plain username/password auth, if a password was given
18683590         If a private key requires a password to unlock it, and a password is
18683667         passed in, that password will be used to attempt to unlock the key.
18683744         :param str hostname: the server to connect to
18683798         :param int port: the server port to connect to
18683853         :param str username:
18683882             the username to authenticate as (defaults to the current local
18683957             username)
18683979         :param str password:
18684008             Used for password authentication; is also used for private key
18684083             decryption if ``passphrase`` is not given.
18684138         :param str passphrase:
18684169             Used for decrypting private keys.
18684215         :param .PKey pkey: an optional private key to use for authentication
18684292         :param str key_filename:
18684325             the filename, or list of filenames, of optional private key(s)
18684400             and/or certs to try for authentication
18684451         :param float timeout:
18684481             an optional timeout (in seconds) for the TCP connect
18684546         :param bool allow_agent:
18684579             set to False to disable connecting to the SSH agent
18684643         :param bool look_for_keys:
18684678             set to False to disable searching for discoverable private key
18684753             files in ``~/.ssh/``
18684786         :param bool compress: set to True to turn on compression
18684851         :param socket sock:
18684879             an open socket or socket-like object (such as a `.Channel`) to use
18684958             for communication to the target host
18685007         :param float banner_timeout: an optional timeout (in seconds) to wait
18685085             for the SSH banner to be presented.
18685133         :param float auth_timeout: an optional timeout (in seconds) to wait for
18685213             an authentication response.
18685253         :param float channel_timeout: an optional timeout (in seconds) to wait
18685332              for a channel open response.
18685374         :param dict disabled_algorithms:
18685415             an optional dict passed directly to `.Transport` and its keyword
18685492             argument of the same name.
18685531         :param transport_factory:
18685565             an optional callable which is handed a subset of the constructor
18685642             arguments (primarily those related to the socket and algorithm
18685717             selection) and generates a `.Transport` instance to be used by this
18685797             client. Defaults to `.Transport.__init__`.
18685852         :param auth_strategy:
18685882             an optional instance of `.AuthStrategy`, triggering use of this
18685958             newer authentication mechanism instead of SSHClient's legacy auth
18686036             method.
18686057             .. warning::
18686082                 This parameter is **incompatible** with all other
18686148                 authentication-related parameters (such as, but not limited to,
18686228                 ``password``, ``key_filename`` and ``allow_agent``) and will
18686305                 trigger an exception if given alongside them.
18686368         :returns:
18686386             `.AuthResult` if ``auth_strategy`` is non-``None``; otherwise,
18686461             returns ``None``.
18686492         :raises BadHostKeyException:
18686529             if the server's host key could not be verified.
18686589         :raises AuthenticationException:
18686630             if authentication failed.
18686668         :raises UnableToAuthenticate:
18686706             if authentication failed (when ``auth_strategy`` is non-``None``;
18686784             and note that this is a subclass of ``AuthenticationException``).
18686862         :raises socket.error:
18686892             if a socket error (other than connection-refused or
18686956             host-unreachable) occurred while connecting.
18687013         :raises NoValidConnectionsError:
18687054             if all valid connection targets for the requested hostname (eg IPv4
18687134             and IPv6) yielded connection-refused or host-unreachable socket
18687210             errors.
18687230         :raises SSHException:
18687260             if there was any other error connecting or establishing an SSH
18687335             session.

18693793 uA high-level representation of a session with an SSH server.  This class
18693867     wraps `.Transport`, `.Channel`, and `.SFTPClient` to take care of most
18693942     aspects of authenticating and opening channels.  A typical use case is::
18694020         client = SSHClient()
18694049         client.load_system_host_keys()
18694088         client.connect('ssh.example.com')
18694130         stdin, stdout, stderr = client.exec_command('ls -l')
18694192     You may pass in explicit overrides for authentication and server host key
18694270     checking.  The default mechanism is to try to use local key files or an
18694346     SSH agent (if one is running).
18694382     Instances of this class may be used as context managers.
18694444     .. versionadded:: 1.6

18702657 afinal
18702666 FtuReturn a dict (`SSHConfigDict`) of config options for a given hostname.
18702742         The host-matching rules of OpenSSH's ``ssh_config`` man page are used:
18702821         For each parameter, the first obtained value will be used.  The
18702893         configuration files contain sections separated by ``Host`` and/or
18702967         ``Match`` specifications, and that section is only applied for hosts
18703044         which match the given patterns or keywords
18703096         Since the first obtained value for each parameter is used, more host-
18703174         specific declarations should be given near the beginning of the file,
18703252         and general defaults at the end.
18703294         The keys in the returned dict are all normalized to lowercase (look for
18703374         ``"port"``, not ``"Port"``. The values are processed according to the
18703452         rules for substitution variable expansion in ``ssh_config``.
18703522         Finally, please see the docs for `SSHConfigDict` for deeper info on
18703598         features such as optional type conversion methods, e.g.::
18703665             conf = my_config.lookup('myhost')
18703711             assert conf['passwordauthentication'] == 'yes'
18703770             assert conf.as_bool('passwordauthentication') is True
18703837         .. note::
18703855             If there is no explicitly configured ``HostName`` value, it will be
18703935             set to the being-looked-up hostname, which is as close as we can
18704012             get to OpenSSH's behavior around that particular option.
18704082         :param str hostname: the hostname to lookup
18704135         .. versionchanged:: 2.5
18704167             Returns `SSHConfigDict` objects instead of dict literals.
18704237         .. versionchanged:: 2.7
18704269             Added canonicalization support.
18704313         .. versionchanged:: 2.7
18704345             Added ``Match`` support.
18704382         .. versionchanged:: 3.3
18704414             Added ``Match final`` support.
18704457

18708690 uTry looking up ``hostname`` in an IPv4 or IPv6 specific manner.
18708756     This is an odd duck due to needing use in two divergent use cases. It looks
18708836     up ``AddressFamily`` in ``options`` and if it is ``inet`` or ``inet6``,
18708912     this function uses `socket.getaddrinfo` to perform a family-specific

18711864 u%s.__prepare__() must return a mapping, not %s
18711912 u<metaclass>
18711925 uA dictionary wrapper/subclass for per-host configuration structures.
18711996     This class introduces some usage niceties for consumers of `SSHConfig`,
18712072     specifically around the issue of variable type conversions: normal value
18712149     access yields strings, but there are now methods such as `as_bool` and
18712224     `as_int` that yield casted values instead.
18712272     For example, given the following ``ssh_config`` file snippet::
18712340         Host foo.example.com
18712369             PasswordAuthentication no
18712407             Compression yes
18712435             ServerAliveInterval 60
18712471     the following code highlights how you can access the raw strings as well as
18712551     usefully Python type-casted versions (recalling that keys are all
18712621     normalized to lowercase first)::
18712659         my_config = SSHConfig()
18712691         my_config.parse(open('~/.ssh/config'))
18712738         conf = my_config.lookup('foo.example.com')
18712790         assert conf['passwordauthentication'] == 'no'
18712844         assert conf.as_bool('passwordauthentication') is False
18712907         assert conf['compression'] == 'yes'
18712951         assert conf.as_bool('compression') is True

18771082 apipe
18771097 aOrPipe
18771105 uwraps a pipe into two pipe-like objects which are "or"d together to
18771174     affect the real pipe. if either returned pipe is set, the wrapped pipe
18771249     is set. when both are cleared, the wrapped pipe is cleared.
18771318 uAbstraction of a one-way pipe where the read end can be used in
18771383 `select.select`. Normally this is trivial, but Windows makes it nearly

18799156 aOPEN_FAILED_ADMINISTRATIVELY_PROHIBITED
18799197 uDetermine if a channel request of a given type will be granted, and
18799266         return ``OPEN_SUCCEEDED`` or an error code.  This method is
18799334         called in server mode when the client requests a channel, after
18799406         authentication is complete.
18799443         If you allow channel requests (and an ssh server that didn't would be
18799521         useless), you should also override some of the channel request methods
18799600         below, which are used to determine which services will be allowed on
18799677         a given channel:
18799703             - `check_channel_pty_request`
18799745             - `check_channel_shell_request`
18799789             - `check_channel_subsystem_request`
18799837             - `check_channel_window_change_request`
18799889             - `check_channel_x11_request`
18799931             - `check_channel_forward_agent_request`
18799984         The ``chanid`` parameter is a small number that uniquely identifies the
18800064         channel within a `.Transport`.  A `.Channel` object is not created
18800139         unless this method returns ``OPEN_SUCCEEDED`` -- once a
18800203         `.Channel` object is created, you can call `.Channel.get_id` to
18800275         retrieve the channel ID.
18800309         The return value should either be ``OPEN_SUCCEEDED`` (or
18800374         ``0``) to allow the channel request, or one of the following error
18800449         codes to reject it:
18800478             - ``OPEN_FAILED_ADMINISTRATIVELY_PROHIBITED``
18800536             - ``OPEN_FAILED_CONNECT_FAILED``
18800581             - ``OPEN_FAILED_UNKNOWN_CHANNEL_TYPE``
18800632             - ``OPEN_FAILED_RESOURCE_SHORTAGE``
18800681         The default implementation always returns
18800731         ``OPEN_FAILED_ADMINISTRATIVELY_PROHIBITED``.
18800785         :param str kind:
18800810             the kind of channel the client would like to open (usually
18800881             ``"session"``).
18800909         :param int chanid: ID of the channel
18800954         :return: an `int` success or failure code (listed above)

18803044         made using this key.

18804304 aServerInterface
18804321 uBegin an interactive authentication challenge, if supported.  You
18804388         should override this method in server mode if you want to support the
18804466         ``"keyboard-interactive"`` auth type, which requires you to send a
18804541         series of questions for the client to answer.
18804596         Return ``AUTH_FAILED`` if this auth method isn't supported.  Otherwise,
18804676         you should return an `.InteractiveQuery` object containing the prompts
18804755         and instructions for the user.  The response will be sent via a call
18804832         to `check_auth_interactive_response`.
18804879         The default implementation always returns ``AUTH_FAILED``.
18804947         :param str username: the username of the authenticating client
18805018         :param str submethods:
18805049             a comma-separated list of methods preferred by the client (usually

18823182 uHandler for a subsystem in server mode.  If you create a subclass of this
18823257     class and pass it to `.Transport.set_subsystem_handler`, an object of this
18823336     class will be created for each request for this subsystem.  Each new object
18823416     will be executed within its own new thread by calling `start_subsystem`.
18823493     When that method completes, the channel is closed.
18823549     For example, if you made a subclass ``MP3Handler`` and registered it as the
18823629     handler for subsystem ``"mp3"``, then whenever a client has successfully
18823706     authenticated and requests subsystem ``"mp3"``, an object of class
18823777     ``MP3Handler`` will be created, and `start_subsystem` will be called on
18823853     it from a new thread.

18824013 uProcess an ssh subsystem in server mode.  This method is called on a
18824083         new object (and in a new thread) for each subsystem request.  It is
18824159         assumed that all subsystem logic will take place here, and when the
18824235         subsystem is finished, this method will return.  After this method
18824310         returns, the channel is closed.
18824351         The combination of ``transport`` and ``channel`` are unique; this
18824425         handler corresponds to exactly one `.Channel` on one `.Transport`.
18824501         .. note::
18824519             It is the responsibility of this method to exit if the underlying
18824597             `.Transport` is closed.  This can be done by checking
18824663             `.Transport.is_active` or noticing an EOF on the `.Channel`.  If
18824740             this method loops forever without checking for this case, your
18824815             Python interpreter may refuse to exit because this thread will
18824890             still be running.
18824921         :param str name: name of the requested subsystem.
18824979         :param .Transport transport: the server-mode `.Transport`.
18825046         :param .Channel channel: the channel associated with this subsystem
18825122             request.

18835886 wuahexlify
18835897 aSFTPFile
18835907 uOpen a file on the remote server.  The arguments are the same as for
18835977         Python's built-in `python:file` (aka `python:open`).  A file-like
18836051         object is returned, which closely mimics the behavior of a normal
18836125         Python file object, including the ability to be used as a context
18836199         manager.
18836217         The mode indicates how the file is to be opened: ``'r'`` for reading,
18836295         ``'w'`` for writing (truncating an existing file), ``'a'`` for
18836366         appending, ``'r+'`` for reading/writing, ``'w+'`` for reading/writing
18836444         (truncating an existing file), ``'a+'`` for reading/appending.  The
18836520         Python ``'b'`` flag is ignored, since SSH treats all files as binary.
18836598         The ``'U'`` flag is supported in a compatible way.
18836658         Since 1.5.2, an ``'x'`` flag indicates that the operation should only
18836736         succeed if the file was created and did not previously exist.  This has
18836816         no direct mapping to Python's file flags, but is commonly known as the
18836895         ``O_EXCL`` flag in posix.
18836930         The file will be buffered in standard Python style by default, but
18837005         can be altered with the ``bufsize`` parameter.  ``<=0`` turns off
18837079         buffering, ``1`` uses line buffering, and any number greater than 1
18837155         (``>1``) uses that specific buffer size.
18837205         :param str filename: name of the file to open
18837259         :param str mode: mode (Python-style) to open in
18837315         :param int bufsize: desired buffering (default: ``-1``)
18837379         :return: an `.SFTPFile` object representing the open file
18837446         :raises: ``IOError`` -- if the file could not be opened.

18858880 aCMD_EXTENDED
18858894 ucheck-file
18858906 aget_text
18858916 aget_remainder
18858931 uAsk the server for a hash of a section of this file.  This can be used
18859003         to verify a successful upload or download, or for various rsync-like
18859080         operations.
18859101         The file is hashed from ``offset``, for ``length`` bytes.
18859167         If ``length`` is 0, the remainder of the file is hashed.  Thus, if both
18859247         ``offset`` and ``length`` are zero, the entire file is hashed.
18859319         Normally, ``block_size`` will be 0 (the default), and this method will
18859398         return a byte string representing the requested hash (for example, a
18859475         string of length 16 for MD5, or 20 for SHA-1).  If a non-zero
18859545         ``block_size`` is given, each chunk of the file (from ``offset`` to
18859621         ``offset + length``) of ``block_size`` bytes is computed as a separate
18859700         hash.  The hash results are all concatenated and returned as a single
18859778         string.
18859795         For example, ``check('sha1', 0, 1024, 512)`` will return a string of
18859872         length 40.  The first 20 bytes will be the SHA-1 of the first 512 bytes
18859952         of the file, and the last 20 bytes will be the SHA-1 of the next 512
18860029         bytes.
18860045         :param str hash_algorithm:
18860080             the name of the hash algorithm to use (normally ``"sha1"`` or
18860154             ``"md5"``)
18860177         :param offset:
18860200             offset into the file to begin hashing (0 means to start from the
18860277             beginning)
18860300         :param length:
18860323             number of bytes to hash (0 means continue to the end of the file)
18860401         :param int block_size:
18860432             number of bytes to hash per result (must not be less than 256; 0
18860509             means to compute only one hash of the entire segment)
18860575         :return:
18860592             `str` of bytes representing the hash of each block, concatenated
18860669             together
18860691         :raises:
18860708             ``IOError`` -- if the server doesn't support the "check-file"
18860782             extension, or possibly doesn't support the hash algorithm requested
18860863         .. note:: Many (most?) servers don't support this extension yet.
18860937         .. versionadded:: 1.4

18861026 uTurn on/off the pipelining of write operations to this file.  When
18861094         pipelining is on, paramiko won't wait for the server response after
18861170         each write operation.  Instead, they're collected as they come in. At
18861248         the first non-write operation (including `.close`), all remaining
18861322         server responses are collected.  This means that if there was an error
18861401         with one of your later writes, an exception might be thrown from within
18861481         `.close` instead of `.write`.
